articles.title: Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership. - Meduza
articles.summary: Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership.  MeduzaThe Future of Russian-European Relations Is Bleak  Carnegie Endowment for International PeaceNATO gegen Russland: Überlegenheit auf dem Papier, Verwundbarkeit in der Wirklichkeit  Xpert.Digital - Konrad WolfensteinEurope is considering two scenarios for ending the war in Ukraine, according to the Financial Times  UA.N...
articles.full_text:
European leaders are rethinking their approach to the Kremlin, Financial Times foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman writes. More politicians in the European Union now agree that negotiations with Vladimir Putin should not remain the exclusive prerogative of the United States. European countries could soon open their own talks with the Kremlin. Channels of communication are already in place, he says.
EU policy toward Russia has rested on two main pillars until now: support for Ukraine and sanctions. European leaders have tried to shape the negotiations by influencing Donald Trump’s position, but those efforts are growing less effective. Europe also fears Trump is more interested in business deals with Moscow than in security issues.
In any direct talks, Putin could be offered two options for ending the war, Rachman writes: freezing the conflict along the front line in exchange for a guarantee that Ukraine will not join NATO, or ceding all of the Donbas to Moscow’s control, after which Kyiv could join the alliance.
Meanwhile, relations between Kyiv and Washington are going through a new crisis, triggered by an energy crisis and Trump’s push to lower diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections to Congress.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries and declare an energy truce. After diplomatic failure, he struck a deal with Moscow on diesel supplies. Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States had “chosen the side” of Russia. Trump responded that it was easier for him to reach an agreement with Putin than with Zelensky, adding that Ukraine needs to hold elections.
Relations between the two leaders are at their “lowest point” since the clash in the Oval Office in 2025, the WSJ writes. The latest exchange took place a day earlier: Trump accused Zelensky of not wanting to end the war, while Zelensky said Ukraine is being pressured to capitulate.
Amid this, U.S. Vice President JD Vance has spoken out against Ukraine joining NATO: “We don’t have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They’re not in NATO. I don’t think that they should be in NATO,” he said. Vance also refused to call Kyiv an ally of Washington, saying they have “divergent interests from time to time.”
War in photographs. Komyshuvakha.
Residents of Komyshuvakha, a front-line village in the Zaporizhzhia region, are being evacuated because of the threat of Russian drone strikes. These photos were taken October 19, 2026.

articles.title: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine - Euronews
articles.summary: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine  Euronews‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal  Al JazeeraTrump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going  BBCOpinion | Trump wants to make Zelenskyy his midterms scapegoat  MS NOWTrump’s Push for Deals With Russia Powers His Frustration With Ukraine  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he wanted his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia as he complained that the United States had received "nothing back" for its support for Kyiv.
Speaking to the media in the White House, Trump said: "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal."
"He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," he continued, seemingly referencing the pair's heated exchange during a meeting in early 2025. "He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer."
Zelenskyy and Trump have endured a volatile relationship since the US president began his second term in January last year, but it has soured further in recent weeks after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.
On Tuesday, Trump - who is gearing up for key midterm elections to determine the make-up of Congress for his final two years in office - seemed to pin the blame for the ongoing war on Zelenskyy, repeatedly saying he had had the opportunity to make a deal and that the US had got nothing in return for its help "except grief, death," and "tremendous monetary loss."
"We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump added. "The American taxpayers are tired of it."
"It's time to make a deal," he said.
Zelenskyy's Oslo talks
Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is scheduled to travel to Russia for a meeting with Putin on Wednesday.
Following the talks in Oslo, which also involved Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Zelenskyy had appeared relatively positive, telling journalists he had recently held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and calling for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin.
Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with the Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now."
"I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.
In a post on social media later in the evening, Zelenskyy added: "It was constructive because all of us want peace – Ukraine, Europe, the United States. And we will see what happens tomorrow."

articles.title: European steel and downstream industries call for comprehensive EU CBAM expansion - SteelOrbis
articles.summary: European steel and downstream industries call for comprehensive EU CBAM expansion  SteelOrbis
articles.full_text:
European industry representatives and trade unions have issued a joint statement calling on the European Parliament, Council of the EU and European Commission to agree on the broadest possible extension of the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to downstream products during ongoing trilogue negotiations.
The signatories include the European Federation of Steel, Tubes and Metals Distribution & Trade (EUROMETAL), Electromechanics Synergy Network, European Steel Tube Association (ESTA), European Non-Integrated Wire Rod Processors Association (EUNIRPA), European Steel Association (EUROFER), European Federation of National Forging Associations (EUROFORGE), European Confederation of Associations of Manufacturers of Insulated Wires and Cables (Europacable), European Aluminium, European Federation of Steel Wire Rope Industries (EWRIS), Federation of the European Cookware, Cutlery and Housewares Industries (FEC), Metal Packaging Europe, Steel for Packaging Europe and industriAll European Trade Union.
EU ETS free allowance phaseout raises concerns over carbon leakage
According to the statement, extending CBAM coverage is necessary to protect European industrial value chains, investments and employment against carbon leakage and competition from imported products that are not subject to equivalent carbon costs.
The signatories warned that European manufacturers face increasing carbon costs throughout steel- and aluminum-intensive value chains, while competing finished and semi-finished products imported from third countries may continue to enter the EU market without bearing comparable costs.
These risks will become more pronounced as free emissions allowances under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) are gradually phased out. Broader CBAM coverage would help address differences in carbon costs between European manufacturers and competing imports.
Downstream steel and aluminum sectors face import competition
Several downstream sectors exposed to competition from carbon-intensive imports include energy, automotive and other mobility applications, machinery, construction, packaging, clean technologies and defense. Other affected sectors include household appliances, cookware, cutlery, catering equipment, hand tools and other metal products.
Products included within CBAM's scope would benefit from more balanced competitive conditions, while products excluded from the mechanism could face greater risks of import substitution and production relocation to countries with lower carbon costs. The organizations therefore called on EU policymakers to build on the positions adopted by the European Parliament and Council and ensure comprehensive coverage of downstream products in the final agreement. They also urged the EU institutions to prioritize European industrial production, investment and employment, emphasizing their importance for the region's economic security, industrial competitiveness and climate transition.

articles.title: The Ministry of Economy should step up its efforts with the EU to delay the CBAM — EBA - ЭкоПолитика
articles.summary: The Ministry of Economy should step up its efforts with the EU to delay the CBAM — EBA  ЭкоПолитика
articles.full_text:
The Ministry of Economy and Environment must step up its cooperation with the European Commission and EU Member States so that Ukraine can finally benefit from special conditions for the application of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
The European Business Association addressed the ministry with this appeal.
Enormous losses for the state and pressure on businesses
Data from the GMK Centre indicates that, between 2026 and 2030, losses to Ukrainian exports due to the impact of the mechanism could ‘skyrocket’ from $372 million to $1.754 billion.
Ukraine’s GDP losses will be many times higher. Their potential total by 2030 could reach $7,248 billion.
At the same time, as the cost of SVAM certificates rises, so too will the burden on businesses. And the price is not stable — in the third quarter it stood at €82.32, which is 10 per cent higher than in the second quarter.
The scope of the mechanism is not fixed either — the list of products subject to the carbon ‘duty’ may include hundreds of derivative goods with a high steel and aluminium content.
Key areas of work
In its statement, the EBA calls on the Ministry of Economy to focus on two areas of work:
Strategic. This involves the development of a special regime for Ukraine, as provided for in Regulation (EU) 2023/956. It differs for the two periods:
- during the period of martial law — a deferral of payments for embedded emissions arising from imports into the EU. Subsequent settlement of financial obligations under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) must take place through verified decarbonisation and environmental modernisation projects;
- From the end of martial law until integration with the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS), revenues from the Domestic Emissions Trading Scheme (SVA) should be accumulated in a special fund. The funds in this scheme should be used to finance decarbonisation projects.
EVA proposes introducing regular joint consultations between the business community and the Ministry of Economy. The business community believes this will help to jointly formulate proposals for Ukraine’s negotiating position.
The practical component involves the following activities:
- a review of the default emission factors for Ukrainian steel and cement products;
- developing mechanisms for verifying actual emissions in wartime;
- exemption of Ukrainian cement and cement clinker from the accounting of indirect emissions.
"This approach will make it possible to minimise the negative impact of the CBAM on Ukrainian industry, preserve enterprises’ export opportunities and investment potential, whilst at the same time creating the conditions for decarbonisation and Ukraine’s gradual integration into the European climate system," the Association emphasised.

articles.title: Rubio in Samarkand: Trump’s Russia Sanctions U-Turn Reshapes the US–China–Russia Power Game - Pagenews.gr
articles.summary: Rubio in Samarkand: Trump’s Russia Sanctions U-Turn Reshapes the US–China–Russia Power Game  Pagenews.gr
articles.full_text:
English Edition
Rubio in Samarkand: Trump’s Russia Sanctions U-Turn Reshapes the US–China–Russia Power Game
Πηγή Φωτογραφίας: AP Photo//Rubio in Samarkand: Trump’s Russia Sanctions U-Turn Reshapes the US–China–Russia Power Game
Samarkand Becomes a Strategic Battleground for Three Major Powers
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, highlights Central Asia’s growing geopolitical importance as a region positioned between Russia, China and the strategic trade and energy corridors of Eurasia.
Washington is seeking to expand its economic and strategic presence through investment, commercial agreements and access to American financing.
However, the diplomatic initiative comes at a time when President Donald Trump’s administration has altered its approach to certain sanctions measures targeting Russia.
The suspension of new restrictions, combined with Washington’s agreement to import Russian diesel, has raised questions about the durability and predictability of American economic pressure.
For Central Asian governments, this development represents more than uncertainty.
It could become an additional bargaining advantage.
The region possesses natural resources, strategic infrastructure and trade routes that are increasingly important to all three major powers.
The central question is whether Washington can secure economic and strategic cooperation without weakening the mechanisms it has established to pressure Moscow.
More Than 100 American Companies Accompany Rubio
Marco Rubio arrived in Samarkand on Sunday, October 18, for his first visit to Central Asia as US secretary of state.
The American delegation includes representatives of more than 100 companies, underscoring the economic importance of the initiative.
Critical minerals, rare earth elements, energy resources, trade corridors and financing for major investment projects are at the center of the agenda.
Washington’s strategy extends beyond strengthening diplomatic relations.
Its objective is to establish economic partnerships that provide Central Asian countries with alternatives to Russian and Chinese influence.
Central Asia holds significant reserves of uranium, tungsten and other raw materials essential to defense manufacturing, advanced technology and the energy transition.
For the United States, securing access to these resources is both an economic competitiveness issue and a national security priority.
Two Days Before the Summit, Trump Changes the Equation
The American delegation arrives following a significant decision by the White House.
On October 16, Donald Trump issued an executive order suspending the implementation of provisions in new sanctions legislation he had signed the previous month.
The legislation, associated with an initiative by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal, authorized substantial tariffs against countries purchasing Russian energy or facilitating sanctions evasion.
According to the analysis underlying the debate, the proposed tariffs could reach 100%.
Kazakhstan was among the countries potentially exposed to the new measures.
The suspension followed the October 9 agreement concerning imports of Russian diesel into the United States.
Together, these decisions have created a different political environment.
Sanctions remain an instrument of American foreign policy, but the recent suspension demonstrates that the implementation of certain new measures can change according to Washington’s political and economic priorities.
That is precisely what Central Asian governments are watching.
Central Asia: A Transit Route Into Russia’s War Economy
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Central Asian trade routes have become increasingly important for shipments of goods entering the Russian market.
Some of these products appear on Western high-priority lists because they can serve both civilian and military purposes.
They include electronic components, microchips, machine tools and parts potentially used in unmanned systems.
According to research cited by Eurasianet, Kazakhstan’s exports to Russia of certain high-priority dual-use products increased by more than 400% in 2022.
These flows declined significantly over the following two years as the risk of secondary sanctions increased.
However, the same research identified renewed growth in certain trade flows through Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan in 2025.
Importantly, the findings did not establish systematic involvement by Kazakhstan’s government in circumventing sanctions.
Geographical proximity to Russia, established commercial networks and Kazakhstan’s membership in the Eurasian Economic Union create conditions in which export controls are particularly difficult to enforce.
The challenge therefore concerns not only government policy but also the behavior of private companies and intermediary trading networks.
Why Secondary Sanctions Depend on Credibility
Secondary sanctions allow the United States to exert pressure on companies and financial institutions in third countries that conduct business with sanctioned entities.
Their effectiveness does not depend exclusively on penalties already imposed.
It also depends on how businesses assess the likelihood of future enforcement.
A company considering the export of machine tools to a Russian buyer must evaluate not only existing legislation but also the risk of future investigations and penalties.
The more consistent and predictable enforcement appears, the stronger the incentive to comply.
Conversely, when governments observe that significant provisions can be suspended or become part of political negotiations, their calculations change.
This does not mean companies are released from existing legal obligations.
It means uncertainty over future enforcement acquires economic and diplomatic value.
The credibility of sanctions is therefore not merely a legal matter.
It is also a question of expectations.
Kazakhstan: A Case Study in Multivector Foreign Policy
Kazakhstan illustrates how Central Asian governments seek to maintain partnerships with competing major powers.
To the United States, it offers access to critical minerals, investment opportunities and commercial agreements.
With Russia, it maintains substantial economic, energy and institutional ties.
To China, it offers access to overland trade corridors and alternative transportation routes connecting Asia with Europe.
This multivector foreign policy is not new.
However, intensifying competition between Washington, Moscow and Beijing has increased its strategic significance.
Kazakhstan can attract American investment without severing its economic relationships with Russia.
It can also develop cooperation with China without excluding Western financing and technology.
For Astana, the challenge is to preserve these relationships without becoming exposed to sanctions or creating dependencies that restrict its strategic autonomy.
The $25 Billion Investment Push and the Battle for Critical Minerals
Washington’s engagement with Central Asia has already acquired a substantial economic dimension.
At the White House summit with Central Asian leaders in November 2025, agreements worth approximately $25 billion were announced.
Among them was a tungsten project in Kazakhstan valued at approximately $1.1 billion.
Tungsten is particularly important for industrial and defense applications, while secure supply chains have become an increasingly important American priority.
Washington is also interested in uranium and rare earth elements.
Developing new investment projects could provide regional governments with additional financing and export opportunities.
At the same time, American businesses are seeking access to markets where Russia and China maintain established positions.
The unresolved question is whether these commercial agreements will include specific commitments concerning export controls and sanctions compliance.
Rosatom: Russia Retains a Powerful Energy Footprint
Despite growing American interest, Russia continues to play a significant role in Kazakhstan’s energy strategy.
Russia’s state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, has secured the contract to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant.
Under the reported terms of the arrangement, Russia is expected to finance approximately 85% of the project.
The agreement demonstrates the depth of the economic relationship between Astana and Moscow.
Large energy projects establish long-term technological, financial and operational partnerships.
Consequently, a stronger American presence does not automatically translate into diminished Russian influence.
Kazakhstan is seeking to develop relationships with multiple partners rather than committing itself exclusively to one geopolitical bloc.
The Russian Oil Corridor and the Importance of Sanctions Exemptions
Kazakhstan’s reliance on transportation routes through Russia is another critical factor.
Approximately 80% of the country’s oil exports reach international markets through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which terminates on the Black Sea.
Kazakh-origin oil transported through this route has been exempted from Western restrictions targeting Russian oil.
This exemption differs fundamentally from a temporary political suspension of sanctions.
It is an established arrangement allowing specified energy flows to continue under defined conditions.
By contrast, when the implementation of new sanctions is suspended through a political decision, companies must assess how durable that change will be.
The distinction between stable legal exemptions and discretionary political decisions is essential to the functioning of international markets.

Beijing is interested in maintaining and expanding overland trade routes connecting China with Europe through the region.

articles.summary: Natural Gas and Oil Forecast: Houthis Target Saudi Oil, Can WTI Break $99.72?  FXEmpireOil parked above $110 a barrel as IEA warns energy markets won’t return to normal next year  CNNBrent hits five-month high as attacks on ships, Saudi sites fuel supply worries  CNBCOil slips after Trump's Russia sanctions waiver  RTE.ieThe Commodities Feed: Sustained Middle East flows fail to dent oil prices  ing think
articles.full_text:
Oil Holds Its Risk Premium as Houthi Strikes Offset Russia Relief
Crude markets start the week with uncertainty after the US softened its stance on buying Russian oil, while the attack on Saudi’s energy facilities last weekend drew wider concern.
Brent: Saudi Supply in the Crosshairs
Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for multiple attacks over the weekend, including attacks on Saudi energy and airport infrastructure and the Shaybah oilfield. According to ING, the market remains at risk premium due to the heightened war risk.
Russian supplies are also coming under increased pressure. A series of drone attacks by Ukraine over the weekend set fire to an oil terminal and a nearby depot in St. Petersburg. The terminal, according to Kpler, exports approximately 120,000 bpd of refined petroleum products.
However, the other way on the scale is President Trump’s executive order from Friday, which removed sanctions and tariffs relating to Russia, including penalties on countries buying Russian energy.
WTI: Inventories Back in Focus
Inventories are likely back in focus for WTI after a week of solid gains last week. The Cushing stock build last week was smaller than expected and markets will now look toward EIA inventory data for further insight.
A Reuters poll showed crude and products stockpiles are expected to have dropped last week. Data shows US stockpiles have been declining over the last couple of weeks, which keeps the focus on domestic supply ahead of the EIA’s report this week. The Nov WTI contract expires on Tuesday.
Natural Gas: Mild Weather Versus Record LNG Pull
On Monday, expectations for milder weather cut forecasts for heating demand, which countered bullish factors like small storage builds, lower production and LNG demand. On average, LNG feedgas has been at 18.1 bcfd. Lower 48 production averaged 111.3 bcfd.
Two opposing factors influenced the gas and LNG market this week. LNG feedgas hit a new high at 20.7 bcfd. Meanwhile, Columbia Gas restored 1.9mn Dth/d of capacity, bringing supply back to Appalachia. While that has increased supply in the US, the attack on ships in the Middle East has limited global LNG supply, making it more difficult for Europe to restock for the winter.
Natural Gas Technical Analysis: NG Slips Below $3.03 as $2.97 Support Comes Into Focus
Natural gas is currently trading at around $3.01/MMBtu, and what’s notable is the sustained selling following last week’s triangle breakdown. The most recent bounce ended at $3.09 and price has fallen below the previous support of $3.03 and $3.05. The moving averages are both falling, and the faster moving average is still below the slower moving average, which keeps the short-term trend bearish.
The first major support I’m looking at is at $2.97. If that support is breached, then $2.91 would be the next support and that would also be a breakdown of the previous uptrend that started from the early October lows. If that happens, then $2.87 would be the next support.
Resistance is at $3.03, $3.09 and $3.15. The RSI is at 34, and still bearish. A recovery above $3.03 would also negate the bearish case, and so would a move above $3.09. I would also add that if $3.09 is broken, then a more serious move to the upside could take place. From there a return to $3.15 would still be in the realm of possibility.
WTI Technical Analysis: USOIL Holds $98.09 as $99.72 Remains the Key Breakout Test
WTI crude is at $98.67 on the 1 hour chart. On the upward channel from mid-October, the price has tested lower levels and been defended by the lower level of the channel. Twice the price has tried to break out at $99.72 and has formed a double top with the last high from October 10th. For now, the price is above both moving averages.
$99.72 is the first major resistance. If this breaks, $100.86, and the channel upper level, would be the next target. $98.09 and the lower channel line would provide support, followed by $97.65. Even lower $96.73 and $95.34 would provide support.
RSI is at 55 and falling, signaling that a drop may occur, but the lower level of the channel continues to be defended, so a drop may be short-lived.
If $98.09 and the channel lower level is defended, I would view the outlook as slightly bullish. A break of $99.72 would provide a better outlook. A close below $96.73 would flatten the channel.
Brent Technical Analysis: UKOIL Holds $109.97 as $111.07 Comes Into Focus
Brent is trading at $109.92 as of the 1-hour chart. What I find important is how strongly the breakout from the contracting triangle held. The previous resistance at $107.00 to $107.57, which rejected price 3 times, has since turned to support. A rising trendline is also supporting the lows, while both moving averages are still far from price and are pointing up.
The first resistance I am looking at is $111.07, where the last leg of the move higher stopped. Breaking through that would bring $112.08 into play. Supporting the move lower would be the $109.97 pivot level, then the rising trendline and $108.83. Further down, the $108.14 level and the previous breakout of $107.57 would come into play.
RSI is at 59, and is headed lower, and has slipped just below the signal line at 62. That suggests bullish momentum and a mild uptrend is still in place. However, that may change if price breaks below $108.83.
I am leaning slightly bullish, and would expect $108.83 to act as support. I would also expect $111.07 to be a stiff resistance, and possibly a breakout level to the upside. A close below $107.57 would bring the contracting triangle into question.

articles.title: France and Germany Push "Hard Tool" on China Trade, But Europe's Internal Reforms Still Missing - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: France and Germany Push "Hard Tool" on China Trade, But Europe's Internal Reforms Still Missing  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sent a joint letter in early October to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, calling on Brussels to respond more swiftly to persistent market distortions and proposing a new mechanism that could ultimately restrict foreign companies' access to the EU single market. The Franco-German document does not name its target, but it is widely seen as aimed at China.
Under the proposal, economic measures put forward by the European Commission would take effect automatically under a "reverse majority" rule—unless enough member-state governments explicitly oppose them with a qualified majority. German officials liken the design to Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, arguing that Europe likewise needs the ability to respond within days.
It marks a clear shift in Berlin's economic policy toward China. For nearly two decades, Paris has focused on reciprocal openness, industrial sovereignty and strategic dependency risks, while Berlin long believed that expanding trade and economic ties with China was broadly beneficial to the German economy. That assumption is now eroding.
The Shifting Competitive Landscape Behind a Widening Deficit
Data show Germany's exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025 while imports from China rose 8.8%, leaving a bilateral deficit of €89.3 billion (approximately $100.2 billion). In the first five months of 2026, German exports to China fell another 14.5% year on year while imports continued to climb, with auto exports hit especially hard. For the EU as a whole, goods imports from China totaled €559.4 billion (approximately $627.6 billion) in 2025 against exports of €199.6 billion (approximately $223.9 billion), a deficit of €359.8 billion (approximately $403.6 billion); compared with a decade ago, exports rose 37% and imports rose 89%.
Jeromin Zettelmeyer, director of Bruegel, summed up the shift in a single sentence during an interview on the sidelines of the Bund Summit in Shanghai on October 19: "In a sense, China is the new Germany." He argued that Chinese companies have reached the technological frontier in some fields while retaining cost advantages, meaning that even if the so-called overcapacity dispute is eased, Europe will still face structural competition from Chinese manufacturing.
In his view, European policymakers sometimes overemphasize protection without sufficiently advancing industrial restructuring. Trade policy should be judged industry by industry, rather than treating all Chinese goods as targets. Citing air conditioners as an example, he noted that as climate change drives up demand for cooling equipment in Europe, being able to import quality products at lower cost has real value.
Tariffs Can't Cure Europe's Internal Ills
Supporters of the Franco-German initiative see the trade deficit as a signal of declining competitiveness, but the scoreboard itself is easily misread. The bilateral goods deficit ignores trade in services—according to Chinese statistics, China ran a $48.3 billion services trade deficit with the EU in 2025, with the EU being the largest source of China's services trade deficit; it also ignores ownership and value added—surpluses earned by European-owned companies in China, with profits, design, patents and brand returns flowing back to Europe in large volumes. Overall, the EU still runs a goods surplus of roughly €128 billion to €133 billion (approximately $143.4 billion to $149.2 billion) with the rest of the world.
The real problems lie more within Europe itself. A European Investment Bank (EIB) survey shows that 62% of EU companies encounter difficulties when exporting to other member states, and that fragmented rules—not Chinese subsidies—are what prevent nearly two-thirds of companies from doing business within the single market. Yet Brussels is at this moment investigating whether Chinese companies distort competition.
In recent years Brussels has leaned on defensive tools. In 2024 the EU decided to impose countervailing duties on Chinese electric vehicles, on the logic of offsetting the effects of subsidies. But tariffs can only raise the prices of competitors' products; they cannot lower European companies' costs of producing batteries, shorten the cycle for developing new models, or integrate fragmented capital markets. Data show that after the EU imposed duties on Chinese EVs, sales of Chinese hybrid vehicles in Europe surged, and Brussels is now considering restrictions on hybrids—exposing the policy paradox.
Data from Rhodium Group and the Mercator Institute for China Studies show that Chinese direct investment in the EU and the UK rose 67% in 2025 to €16.8 billion (approximately $18.8 billion), with greenfield investment reaching a record €8.9 billion (approximately $10.0 billion). What tariffs mainly change is the location of production—Chinese companies are shifting toward local production, local plant construction and local hiring in Europe. The EU is thus caught in a contradiction: on one hand it wants to restrict Chinese goods, on the other it needs the jobs and supply chains that Chinese greenfield investment brings; on one hand it speaks of "de-risking," on the other Chinese companies are embedding themselves more deeply within Europe.
Who Ultimately Pays the Bill
The U.S. experience offers a reference. Papers by economists Mary Amiti, Stephen Redding and David Weinstein confirm that the tariffs imposed by the United States in 2018-2019 were almost entirely passed through to import prices, and that by the end of 2018 the U.S. had lost real income of about $1.4 billion per month—paid by American importers and consumers.
If Europe repeats the mistake, the bill will likewise fall on European companies, downstream industries and ordinary households. According to media reports, if the EU fully excluded Chinese companies and equipment in 18 sectors, EU countries would bear at least €840 billion (approximately $942.3 billion) in losses. At the same time, the EU is itself mired in energy risk: energy costs have stayed high since the Ukraine crisis, and U.S. and Israeli military strikes on Iran have further tightened global energy supplies, pushing EU natural gas prices up 50% and adding €3 billion (approximately $3.4 billion) in extra costs.
The German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK) has warned against a trade war, noting that labor costs, energy prices and bureaucratic procedures are obstacles Europe has created for itself. Spain's Público newspaper argued that it is ultimately European citizens who will pay for a trade war, suffering both higher prices and declining industrial competitiveness, and criticized EU protectionism for exposing a "double standard." Britain's The Economist, in an article titled "Europe's Industrial Woes Have Nothing to Do With Global Imbalances," argued that if Europe wants a thriving industry, it should focus on fixing its own internal problems rather than shutting competitors out.
A report published by BNP Paribas on October 5 argued that trade rebalancing cannot be achieved through trade tools alone, and that Europe should avoid repeating the U.S. government's mistake of treating the bilateral deficit as the core criterion for tariff policy. The report highlighted two keys: first, R&D spending, where the gap between Europe and China has widened markedly in recent years; second, deepening the European single market, which directly affects whether European companies can achieve the economies of scale enjoyed by China's large corporate champions.
Market Power and the Window of Time
The Franco-German initiative is not an isolated move. The Anti-Coercion Instrument adopted in 2023 is explicitly aimed at deterrence: if a third country uses economic pressure to force the EU or a member state to change policy, Brussels can respond with tariffs, services, investment and public procurement tools. When U.S. President Trump threatened to impose 30% tariffs on European goods, EU governments approved potential retaliatory tariffs on $9.3 billion of U.S. exports, with France and Germany the most active advocates of putting the Anti-Coercion Instrument on the negotiating table.
Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe, Russia and Eurasia program at Chatham House, wrote in Foreign Policy that Europe has for decades possessed a vast geopolitical asset: some 450 million relatively affluent consumers concentrated in a single regulatory space, with foreign companies eager to enter the market, so that EU rules have in effect shaped corporate behavior beyond the EU's borders—the so-called "Brussels effect."
But he also cautioned that market power is useful only as long as Europe remains indispensable to China's economy, and that balance is shifting rapidly, especially in key industries such as batteries, clean technology and electric vehicles. Trade defense alone will not bring cheaper energy or create technological leadership. Protecting an industry and making it competitive are two different things. The Franco-German document is a positive signal, but the bigger challenge is that Paris and Berlin still need to push reforms to revive flagging competitiveness; once the so-called unfair competition issue is resolved, the real hard battle—domestic economic reform—will only just be beginning.
The European Union Chamber of Commerce in China's 2026 survey shows that 94% of member companies consider China an important sourcing location, and 48% believe Chinese companies are more innovative than European competitors. A DIHK survey in early September showed that 83% of respondents felt intensifying competition from Chinese companies, yet 88% still wanted to continue the businesses affected; in response, 60% chose to rely on innovation, 50% on cost reduction and 39% on opening new markets.

articles.title: Kallas: Russian Black Sea strikes deepen ‘perfect storm’ for world food supplies - Euronews
articles.summary: Kallas: Russian Black Sea strikes deepen ‘perfect storm’ for world food supplies  EuronewsNato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks  The GuardianNATO to send planes and drones to Black Sea after attacks on shipping  ReutersSeven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast  BBCRussia trying to limit Ukrainian export routes - Kallas  RTE.ie
articles.full_text:
Ukraine is losing an estimated €60 million a day in export earnings as Moscow is accused of targetting the routes it uses to ship grain abroad.
Suspected Russian drone strikes on civilian shipping in the Black Sea are piling further pressure on global food supplies, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned.
Addressing the European Parliament on Tuesday, Kallas said vessels had come under attack six times in 10 days, describing it as "a dangerous and unacceptable escalation".
The strikes have hit ships off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, both EU and NATO members, prompting alarm across Europe.
Kallas, the High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, accused the Kremlin of trying to choke off Ukraine’s income while Russian troops make little progress on the battlefield. She said Ukraine was losing around €60 million a day in export revenue.
Ukraine is one of the world’s leading exporters of wheat, maize and barley, most of which leaves the country by sea.
Kallas said global grain reserves were in better shape than in 2022, when a Russian blockade left 20 million tonnes of Ukrainian grain stranded.
"Global grain stockpiles are larger than in 2022," she said. "But the global food system is now facing a perfect storm: a super El Nino, drought in both hemispheres, and conflict in the Middle East, straining fertiliser exports."
But she warned of a combination of threats: a super El Niño, drought in both hemispheres, and conflict in the Middle East disrupting fertiliser exports.
"Russia’s actions make it harder to put food on people’s plates across the world," she said.
Back-up routes at risk
Since 2022, the EU has built overland "solidarity lanes" to carry Ukrainian goods through its member states instead of across the Black Sea. Kallas said these were now under threat too, as Russia targets border crossings with Moldova, Romania and Poland.
Last week, EU leaders called for safe passage for civilian shipping in the Black Sea to be restored immediately.
NATO to deploy 'additional assets'
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart announced later on Tuesday that the alliance would be sending "additional assets" to the Black Sea region following the recent wave of drone incidents.
"NATO will be sending additional assets to the region, including support for surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensics," Hart wrote in a post on social media.
"We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe."

| The JRC released new Version 4 of the Global Forest Cover map for the year 2020 | 
| Dear subscribers, We are pleased to inform you on that the European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) has released map Version 4 of the Global Forest Cover map for the year 2020 (GFC2020).
The new Version 4 integrates newest data on forest height, forest management and types, improving the spatial representation of forest.
Most significant changes are notable in Mesoamerica, the Northern Andes, the Cerrado region of Brazil, Western and Eastern Africa and Eastern China.
Map Version 4 is available through several portals: via the EU Observatory on deforestation and forest degradation, the General JRC access, or as Web Mapping Service (simply copy this link into your GIS).
It can also be downloaded as 10x10 degree tiles, as tiles, or single file from the JRC Big Data Analytics Platform.
Analysis-ready data can also be accessed through Google Earth Engine or the IMPACT Toolbox (EUDR module).
(Caption for the Figure: Net area differences in 1x1 degree cells between GFC2020 Version 4 and 3.
) Looking ahead, the JRC is updating the Global Forest Type map for the year 2020 (GFT2020).
A technical report covering both maps is expected to be released in December 2026 or January 2027.
What is the EU Observatory? The EU Observatory on deforestation and forest degradation provided by the Commission is a free tool for all stakeholders that helps determine the global forest cover of 2020, aimed at supporting operators and competent authorities in the implementation of the EUDR.
It is non-exclusive, non-mandatory and carries no legal value.
Public and private stakeholders can use any maps or other data that they see fit for the purpose of their due diligence exercise or checks.
Further detailed information on EU Observatory on deforestation and forest degradation and the Global Forest Maps can be found on the Commission Website.

articles.title: LAWRENCE EDWARDS AND NICOLA WILLS | The CBAM wake-up call: decarbonisation is now an export survival issue - Business Day
articles.summary: LAWRENCE EDWARDS AND NICOLA WILLS | The CBAM wake-up call: decarbonisation is now an export survival issue  Business Day
articles.full_text:
South Africa has spent years worrying about the damage a slow-growing, carbon-intensive economy is doing to its international competitiveness. Now the EU has put a price on one of our biggest weaknesses.
Since January 1 the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) has entered its definitive phase, requiring importers of specified goods to pay for the carbon emissions embedded in those products.
Our new study, recently published as an Economics Research Southern Africa (Ersa) working paper, suggests that its impact could be severe, particularly for two South African industries with significant EU exports — iron and steel (about R33.6bn worth of exports a year) and aluminium (R12bn).
The study warns about the risks facing these industries and highlights the importance of getting South Africa’s energy and industrial policies to work in sync to help these exporters become more competitive. This means treating electricity sector decarbonisation as both a climate and a trade competitiveness issue — something that will be crucial if border carbon adjustment mechanisms become widespread internationally, as seems likely.
For the iron, steel and aluminium products we study, the CBAM covers only direct emissions at this stage — those produced by the factory or production process itself. It does not yet cover indirect emissions from the electricity used in production. This distinction is particularly important for South Africa, where much of the electricity supply comes from “dirty” coal-fired power stations.
Extending the CBAM to cover indirect emissions, as is currently under consideration, would place South African producers at an even greater disadvantage relative to producers in countries that use a higher share of clean, renewable energy.
Emission variations
The first noteworthy feature of our study is that the emissions associated with apparently similar products can vary enormously within a sector. So, while most older studies use sector averages to estimate CBAM costs per country, our paper uses far more granular product-level trade data. Even these differences can be understated, as emissions can vary substantially between individual firms producing similar products.
Second, we find that average total emissions expressed as tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of output (tCO₂e/t) vary considerably across countries, ranging from 0.6 (Switzerland) to 5 (India) for iron and steel, and from 0.5 (Switzerland) to 16.7 (South Africa) for aluminium.
The reason South Africa’s aluminium sector has the highest average total emissions intensity (direct and indirect emissions) of the 16 major countries sampled is mainly because its production uses enormous amounts of electricity — and South Africa still generates much of its electricity from coal. The same holds for other high-emitting, middle-income economies, including India, China and Russia. In contrast, advanced economies such as Switzerland, Norway and Iceland make more extensive use of renewable energy.
Unsurprisingly, in our iron and steel simulations South Africa, India, Russia and Ukraine are among the countries facing the biggest risk of reductions in their EU exports. But it is not simply because these countries are “dirty” producers — the interaction between emissions intensity and the import price of the product is also important.
The reason South Africa’s aluminium sector has the highest average total emissions intensity (direct and indirect emissions) of the 16 major countries sampled is mainly because its production uses enormous amounts of electricity — and South Africa still generates much of its electricity from coal.
Given that the carbon charge is a fixed cost per tonne of emissions, it represents a smaller percentage of the price of a high-value product than of a cheaper one. So a relatively cheap product with high embedded emissions (a typical emerging-country combination) could face a larger percentage increase in its effective price in the EU market.
Previous studies have largely overlooked that products with identical embedded emissions can face different percentage price increases, with larger increases for lower-priced imports and, consequently, sharper reductions in EU import demand for those products. It suggests that the CBAM could impose larger adjustment costs on some emerging economies than justified solely by the carbon content of their imports. But it also implies there is another route to reducing exposure: moving towards higher-value products.
Huge implications
The implications for South Africa are striking. At an assumed carbon price of €80 tCO₂e our model suggests that the average EU import price of South African aluminium would rise by about 32% and that of iron and steel by about 31%, when direct and indirect emissions are included. These price effects are the highest of all the counties surveyed.
The simulated consequences for trade are even more dramatic. For South African iron and steel, our model estimates a roughly 48% decline in EU imports when only direct emissions are considered, rising to about 76% when indirect emissions are included.
For aluminium the corresponding decline rises from about 7% to nearly 75%. These figures combine the direct EU import demand reduction and the anticipated trade diversion effects (when importers switch between suppliers). Overall, the paper finds that the CBAM hurts exporters mainly because higher effective prices reduce EU demand, although trade diversion adds to the decline in South Africa’s case.
These findings should alarm policymakers. But as the most severe results for South Africa arise when indirect emissions are included, our findings are useful as a warning about the vulnerability of exporters to future changes in the system.
As such, the CBAM provides an important industrial policy signal. Clearly, it would be a mistake to regard it simply as a new trade tax or a climate-policy problem. Responding to this serious threat is going to require our industrial and energy policies to work together to increase our export competitiveness.
The potential losses in iron, steel and aluminium — and the investments required to change to cleaner production technologies — are sufficiently large that the government cannot reasonably leave exposed firms to absorb the additional costs and hope that they will decarbonise themselves.
Government’s role
The government therefore has a role to play in easing the transition by, for instance, recycling carbon tax revenue to incentivise decarbonisation, introducing investment tax credits, concessional finance or recapitalisation funds, and supporting reliable systems for measuring, reporting and independently verifying emissions.
Since South African firms’ international competitiveness are likely to increasingly depend on the carbon intensity of our electricity system, we argue in favour of expanding low-carbon electricity generation, modernising the electricity network, improving grid reliability and allowing companies to procure renewable electricity through power-purchase agreements.
So, is the CBAM a disaster in the making for key South African exporters? Certainly, there is no escaping that our carbon-intensive production is becoming a competitive disadvantage in an increasingly carbon-conscious world. But the CBAM also provides an opportunity in that it reinforces the economic rationale for South Africa’s energy reforms by increasing the trade-competitiveness benefits of decarbonisation.
Viewed that way, the EU has created a new reason for South Africa to fix problems it needed to fix anyway. We can allow the CBAM to dictate our competitive disadvantage, or we can use the pressure to accelerate investment in both cleaner production methods and cleaner forms of electricity.
• Professor Edwards is director of policy research in international services at the University of Cape Town’s School of Economics and an Ersa research fellow. Wills is a doctoral student in the School of Economics. This article draws on the Ersa working paper, “Measuring EU CBAM Incidence at the Product Level: A Multi-country Partial Equilibrium Analysis”.

articles.title: France’s coming bond crisis is a test for Europe’s double standards - City AM
articles.summary: France’s coming bond crisis is a test for Europe’s double standards  City AMFrench bond sell-off spreads across Europe  The TelegraphA ‘Doom Loop’ Threatens France as Populism Confronts Markets  The New York TimesFrance hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors  The GuardianPolitical Risk Makes France a Go-To Market for Short Sellers  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
As Greek government bonds yield lower interest than France’s, the Eurozone faces a critical test over whether European institutions will enforce fiscal rules consistently or protect politically influential member states, says Tim Focas
If someone had told investors during the eurozone debt crisis of 2012 that Greece would one day borrow more cheaply than France, you would have put them in a straitjacket. Yet here we are at the back end of 2026, and French ten-year government bonds are yielding 4.9 per cent, against Greece’s 4.36 per cent. The country once synonymous with sovereign bankruptcy is now being charged less to borrow than one of the European Union’s founding powers. Welcome everyone, roll up roll up, and look to see the Eurozone’s spectacular see through the looking-glass economy.
But an Alice in Wonderland production this certainly is not. For anyone who was unlucky enough to have lived through the Greek debt crisis, this turning of the tables puts a ginormous elephant in the room and begs the question, when the next sovereign debt crisis does hit Europe, whose interests will the EU really protect?
Investors who still have the scars to prove what happened last time will inevitably be asking themselves this question right now. Back in 2012, Greece completely rearranged its government debt, and imposed a 53.5 per cent nominal reduction in the amount of debt owed on private bondholders. Unfortunately, this only masqueraded over the true destruction of investors’ wealth. The remaining 46.5 per cent wasn’t handed back in cash and much came in the form of long-dated, low-interest bonds worth much less than their face value.
Meanwhile, the Eurosystem’s holdings escaped as Greece retrospectively inserted collective-action clauses into bonds issued under Greek law which allowed most creditors to force restructuring terms upon disgruntled investors. To put it another way, the rules were basically rewritten after investors had bought the bonds. At the same time though, the European Central Bank and national central banks had exchanged their eligible Greek bonds for securities outside the restructuring and, as a result, their holdings were protected while private investors absorbed enormous losses. Then, just to make sure everything was watertight, the European Court of Human Rights subsequently accepted that the restructuring interfered with investors’ property rights, but concluded that the interference was justified by the exceptional circumstances and wider public interest. Legally permissible perhaps, but the question that still lingers to this day is was it really equitable?
Political risk
Unlike Greece though, France is the lifeblood of the EU budget and, alongside Germany, is the cornerstone of political power in Brussels. That makes its precarious borrowing position particularly uncomfortable for those passionate about protecting the Eurozone at all costs. Now let’s not get things twisted, France is certainly not Greece if only because it has a much larger and more liquid debt market. Nevertheless, investors shouldn’t forget that sovereign bonds carry huge political as well as credit risk. Staunch ECB’s defenders will of course make the case that protecting central-bank holdings was imperative to prevent financial contagion.
Nobody would dispute this, but at the same time, it doesn’t erase the losses imposed on private creditors. If France’s public finances get worse, would financial institutions across the bloc really tolerate a Greek-style treatment of creditors? Or would we suddenly see a more “flexible” interpretation of Europe’s precious rules-based system when the country that just so happens to have its fiscal feet to the fire is too politically important to make an example out of?
That is the double-standards predicament confronting Europe, which they have no choice but to face head on once again. And, if this wasn’t uncomfortable enough, the yield advantage offered by French bonds over Greek bonds is currently not even one full percentage point. Would any investor in their right mind accept a modest premium of 0.36 per cent in return for all the political uncertainty? With many still licking their wounds from how quickly contractual protections can be overwhelmed by sovereign necessity, surely they would have to think very carefully.
Pricing inflation, interest rates and assessing default probabilities is just what markets naturally do. However, pricing in the likelihood of European institutions tweaking the rules when it politically suits doesn’t come as naturally to investors as Greece taught them at extraordinary cost. With France now firmly in the firing line, we may soon find out whether Europe has learned its lesson.
Tim Focas is head of capital markets at Aspectus Group

articles.title: EU to Classify ChatGPT as VLOSE Under Digital Services Act - TechRepublic
articles.summary: EU to Classify ChatGPT as VLOSE Under Digital Services Act  TechRepublic
articles.full_text:
The European Commission is likely to classify ChatGPT as a ‘Very Large Online Search Engine’ under the Digital Services Act (DSA), subjecting the developer, OpenAI, to more stringent compliance requirements.
According to the German daily Handelsblatt, which cites unnamed sources within the EC, the classification of ChatGPT will take place in the next few days.
The DSA mandates applying the designation of Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE) or Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) to digital services that reach over 45 million active monthly users in the EU, with providers obliged to update user figures every six months.
OpenAI’s own data indicates that ChatGPT search reached 120.4 million monthly EU-based users in the six months to the end of September 2025.
LLMs to be regulated under DSA on ‘case-by-case basis’
Officially, the EC is still weighing up the prospect of slapping ChatGPT with the VLOSE classification.
Spokesperson Thomas Regnier told Reuters that classifying large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT under the DSA would have to be decided on a “case-by-case” basis, indicating that the EC would not automatically designate any LLM that passed 45 million monthly active users.
“OpenAI has published user numbers for ChatGPT above the 45 million DSA threshold for designation,” Regnier said. “The Commission services are currently assessing this information.”
As of April 1, the EU classifies 21 service providers as either VLOPs or VLOSEs, including such usual suspects as Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Twitter (also known as X).
Other classified providers included Booking.com, AliExpress, Infinite Styles Services (Shein), LinkedIn, Zalando, and Pinterest.
OpenAI may face higher operating costs
Providers have four months to comply once designated as either a VLOP or VLOSE, during which period they must introduce points of contact between regulators and users, report criminal offences and regulatory violations, implement “user-friendly” terms and conditions, and provide transparency as to advertising and content moderation.
Newly designated providers must also provide the Commission with an assessment of any risks arising from their services, particularly those pertaining to illegal content, fundamental civil and consumer rights, public and electoral security, and physical and mental health.
Highlighting how the DSA becomes more demanding for VLOPs and VLOSEs, providers not only have to establish internal compliance functions but also have to undergo an annual independent audit and adopt measures recommended by the corresponding auditor.
They even have to share relevant monitoring data with the EC and national regulators, and permit “vetted” researchers to access information and data that would aid with research into any systemic, EU-wide risks posed by their platforms.
Assuming that the Commission does classify ChatGPT as a VLOSE, OpenAI could face a considerable increase in its operating costs in the EU, although it does already comply with the DSA under its current status.
It will have to help finance the EU’s supervision of its services, contributing a maximum of 0.05% of its annual worldwide net income.
While there is no reliable data on the average cost of ensuring internal compliance with a VLOP or VLOSE classification, the EC collected €54.8 million in supervisory fees last year.
The cost of noncompliance can also be very steep for very large providers, with the Commission fining X €120 million last December for contravening transparency requirements.

articles.title: NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin Opens as Germany Advances AI Partnership and European Investment - Konsulteer
articles.summary: NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin Opens as Germany Advances AI Partnership and European Investment  Konsulteer
articles.full_text:
Highlights:
- NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin runs from October 20–22, with CEO Jensen Huang scheduled to deliver the keynote on October 21.
- Germany has signed a memorandum of understanding with NVIDIA to advance industrial AI, although further details remain undisclosed.
- The event features more than 100 sessions covering accelerated computing, agentic AI, robotics, physical AI and open models.
- NVIDIA’s European expansion includes startup investments and partnerships spanning industrial software, robotics and AI infrastructure.
- Vera Rubin deployment and the economics of AI inference remain important questions for assessing the next phase of AI infrastructure growth.
NVIDIA Brings Its AI Ecosystem to Berlin
NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin conference opened on October 20, bringing developers, researchers, technology companies and industrial leaders together to examine the next phase of artificial intelligence infrastructure and deployment.
Running through October 22, the event places particular emphasis on accelerated computing, agentic AI, physical AI, robotics, open models and the infrastructure required to run AI systems at scale. CEO Jensen Huang is scheduled to deliver the keynote on October 21.
The gathering comes as NVIDIA expands its European presence beyond supplying chips to building relationships across the region’s AI ecosystem. These include technology partnerships, startup investments and collaborations aimed at bringing AI into manufacturing and other industrial environments.
The strategic shift is significant. As enterprises move from experimenting with AI models to operating them in production, infrastructure requirements increasingly extend beyond individual processors. Computing systems, networking, software, data management and application-specific tools must work together to support reliable deployment.
NVIDIA is positioning its AI factory approach around this broader stack, with the goal of providing infrastructure that can support the development, deployment and operation of AI applications.
GTC Berlin provides a platform for the company to demonstrate how that strategy could develop across European markets, particularly in manufacturing and industrial automation.
Germany Advances a Government-Backed AI Partnership
Germany’s industrial AI ambitions are a major focus of NVIDIA’s European expansion.
The German government has signed a memorandum of understanding with NVIDIA, according to reporting published on October 19. The cooperation is intended to promote AI adoption in German industry, with applications spanning physical AI, robotics, autonomous driving and industrial AI models.
The initiative is expected to involve German industrial and technology companies, including Siemens, Audi and Black Forest Labs. Deutsche Telekom’s industrial AI cloud infrastructure is also part of the broader collaboration landscape described ahead of the announcement.
The partnership builds on Germany’s interest in developing AI capabilities that can strengthen its manufacturing base while supporting European digital sovereignty objectives.
Germany has substantial industrial engineering expertise and established manufacturing networks. Applying AI to those environments could help companies develop more capable robots, improve production processes and build systems that respond more effectively to changing operational conditions.
Physical AI is especially relevant to this ambition. Unlike software applications that operate primarily on digital information, physical AI systems must interpret and interact with the real world. Examples include robots, autonomous vehicles and intelligent industrial equipment.
The government-backed initiative could provide a framework for developing and training AI systems for these applications.
However, the memorandum does not by itself establish that all planned projects are funded, operational or commercially deployed. The precise funding arrangements, implementation milestones and division of responsibilities require further detail.
NVIDIA’s European Investment Strategy Expands
NVIDIA’s activity in Europe extends beyond Germany.
Before GTC Berlin, Huang indicated that NVIDIA would announce approximately $2 billion in additional European AI investments or deals within the following week. The company had already invested approximately $8 billion in Europe over the preceding year, according to the supplied report.
If the additional commitments materialize as described, they would bring the combined figure close to $10 billion. That projection should not be interpreted as a confirmed total of completed investments, as the precise composition and status of the anticipated commitments remain unclear.
NVIDIA has also announced financing for several European startups.
In France, the companies named include health technology business Doctolib, robotics AI company Genesis AI, software provider Pigment and AI materials company Entalpic. In the United Kingdom, NVIDIA identified AI and technology companies including Boltz, Prima Mente, Hiverge, Riverlane and Foresight.
The range of companies suggests that the strategy is not confined to traditional semiconductor infrastructure. NVIDIA is building relationships across areas such as physical AI, materials discovery, industrial software and other applications that could use its computing platforms.
For NVIDIA, these relationships can help expand the ecosystem of developers and businesses building on its technologies. For European startups, access to computing resources, capital and technical partnerships may support the development of new products.
The longer-term economic impact will depend on how these relationships translate into deployed applications, business growth and sustained demand for AI infrastructure.
GTC Puts AI Factories at the Centre of the Discussion
NVIDIA’s AI factory concept is central to its broader infrastructure strategy.
An AI factory combines computing resources, networking, software and operational systems to produce AI capabilities at scale. Instead of viewing a GPU as an isolated component, the approach treats the entire infrastructure environment as a system designed to train, deploy or serve AI models.
This model becomes increasingly relevant as enterprises deploy AI agents that perform multi-step tasks, interact with tools and coordinate operations. Such workloads can create different infrastructure demands from conventional AI applications, particularly when systems must handle sustained inference requests and complex workflows.
NVIDIA’s official GTC programme features more than 100 sessions covering the AI technology stack, including accelerated computing, agentic AI, physical AI, robotics and open models.
The conference is therefore relevant not only to hardware buyers but also to software developers, cloud providers, industrial companies and organizations evaluating how to integrate AI into their operations.
For European enterprises, the practical question is whether these infrastructure developments can translate into useful applications that meet local requirements for performance, security, cost and control over data.
The growing emphasis on sovereign AI infrastructure reflects that concern. Governments and companies want access to advanced AI capabilities while retaining greater influence over where their data is processed and how systems are operated.
NVIDIA’s strategy seeks to address these requirements through partnerships with local technology providers and industrial organizations, although the extent of control and independence achieved will vary by deployment.
Vera Rubin Deployment and Inference Economics Remain Key Questions
The deployment progress of NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform is another important area to watch as the company advances its next-generation computing roadmap.
NVIDIA has positioned Vera Rubin as a full-stack platform for demanding AI workloads, encompassing computing and supporting infrastructure. For customers, the commercial significance will depend not only on the platform’s technical capabilities but also on when systems become available and how effectively they perform in production.
Large cloud providers are particularly important to this assessment because their deployment decisions can influence infrastructure availability and the economics of AI services.
A second consideration is inference cost, including the cost of generating each token. Lower inference costs can make it more economical to serve larger volumes of AI requests and support applications that would otherwise be too expensive to operate.
However, per-token costs depend on more than hardware specifications. Model architecture, software optimization, utilization, workload characteristics and infrastructure configuration all affect the economics of serving AI systems.
The available preview does not establish that major cloud providers have entered a new phase of large-scale Vera Rubin deployment or that a particular reduction in inference cost has been achieved. Those outcomes require confirmation through deployment announcements and comparable performance data.
The GTC keynote may provide additional information, but expectations should remain separate from confirmed product, deployment and performance announcements.
Industrial AI Could Become a European Growth Opportunity
Germany’s involvement highlights a potential route for NVIDIA to expand its business through industrial applications rather than relying solely on conventional data-center demand.
Manufacturing companies can apply AI to production planning, inspection, robotics, simulation and engineering. These applications may require a combination of AI models, physical simulation, computing infrastructure and specialized industrial software.
The partnership with Germany creates an opportunity to connect those requirements with NVIDIA’s technology ecosystem and the country’s industrial base.

articles.title: Euro drops amid high energy prices and street riots in France - Yahoo! Finance Canada
articles.summary: Euro drops amid high energy prices and street riots in France  Yahoo! Finance Canada
articles.full_text:
By Stefano Rebaudo
Oct 19 (Reuters) - The euro fell on Monday as high energy prices compounded concerns over political stability in France, where weekend riots and looting amounted to some of the country's worst unrest in years.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday he had asked some local municipalities to impose partial curfews.
Analysts said the euro's reaction in early October was much more dramatic and followed a familiar playbook: The single currency tends to come under sustained pressure only if French political tensions spill beyond national borders and weigh on sentiment across the euro zone.
The euro dropped 0.20% to $1.1218. It fell more than 1% at the turn of the month after the spread between French OATs and safe-haven German Bunds widened by about 40 basis points to above 150 bps within days, increasing risk premiums of other countries of the bloc. The French spread was last up 2 bps at 144 bps on Monday.
Analysts argued that investors reassessed their narrative about the forex market last week after robust US economic growth and equity market gains driven by the AI boom had supported the greenback for months.
They are increasingly focused on the risk that AI-driven spending could slow down due to a weaker outlook for investment in the sector, which would likely weigh on US growth while reducing borrowing needs — a combination that could drag both the dollar and Treasury yields lower.
The interest-rate outlook returned as a main market driver, also helped by the Fed's September rate hike which reassured investors that US policymakers remained committed to tackling inflation.
"For the euro/dollar, it is currently less the oil price itself that matters than how the Fed and ECB respond to it," Thu Lan Nguyen, head of forex and commodity research at Commerzbank, said.
"As long as markets do not expect the Fed to react much more forcefully to the inflationary shock, the dollar will struggle to fully capitalize on the fundamental advantage provided by higher oil prices," she added.
Since the conflict in Iran erupted in March, higher oil prices have supported the dollar while weighing on energy-importing currencies such as the euro and yen. Brent crude futures slipped from a five-month high but were still above $100. Natural gas prices hit a fresh four-year high at €89.74.
Markets see an 85% chance that the Fed will keep rates unchanged this month, while pricing in 75 basis points of easing by the end of 2027. Expectations for the European Central Bank have followed a similar trajectory.
