articles.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Germany adopts CRA Implementation Act as national enforcement regimes take shape across the EU - Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
articles.summary: EU Cyber Resilience Act: Germany adopts CRA Implementation Act as national enforcement regimes take shape across the EU  Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
articles.full_text:
Don't just teach AI, use it
On 14 October 2026, the German Parliament adopted the Implementation Act for the EU Cyber Resilience Act (“CRA”), determining how the EU’s cybersecurity rules for products with digital elements will be supervised and enforced in Germany. The German Federal Office for Information Security (“BSI”) takes a key role as market surveillance authority, notifying authority and CSIRT, through an amendment of the Act on the Federal Office for Information Security (“BSIG”). In this article, we outline the BSI’s new powers and when they apply, compare Germany’s approach with the CRA implementation status in other EU Member States, and set out the steps companies should take now.
1. Background
The CRA (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) establishes essential cybersecurity requirements for "products with digital elements", including many hardware and software products and their remote data processing solutions (see a high-level step-by-step guide on the CRA's material scope here).
Most obligations under the CRA apply to manufacturers, importers, distributors and other actors from 11 December 2027. However, the manufacturer reporting obligations under Art. 14 CRA have applied since 11 September 2026 (see our summary here) and Chapter IV on the notification of conformity assessment bodies has applied since 11 June 2026 (Art. 71 CRA).
Although the CRA, as an EU regulation, applies directly in all EU Member States it still requires national implementation in several respects. Chapter V of the CRA requires EU Member States to designate the market surveillance authorities for the enforcement of the CRA alongside the Market Surveillance Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2019/1020), including through the imposition of administrative fines (Art. 52 and Art. 64 CRA). Further, national frameworks for notifying conformity assessment bodies need to be implemented (Art. 36 CRA).
The German CRA Implementation Act aims to establish this legal framework for CRA enforcement and implementation in Germany.
2. Key content of the German CRA Implementation Act
The BSI is designated as the national authority competent for the national implementation of the CRA. To this end, a new Part 8 of the existing BSIG, titled „Cybersecurity of Products with Digital Elements“, is inserted. Part 8 of the BSIG assigns the BSI four key tasks: it acts as the competent national market surveillance authority, as the notifying authority for conformity assessment bodies and as the CSIRT under the CRA, and it supports economic operators, in particular microenterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises, including open-source software stewards, in complying with the CRA.
Further amendments to the Telecommunications Act (Telekommunikationsgesetz) and the Energy Industry Act (Energiewirtschaftsgesetz) are expressly only of editorial nature and do not constitute a substantive change.
2.1. Competent national market surveillance authority
Under the new BSIG, the BSI is designated as the sole competent national market surveillance authority for the purpose of ensuring the effective implementation of the CRA under Art. 52(2) CRA.
An exception applies for products with digital elements that are high-risk AI systems under Art. 6 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (“AI Act”), for which the German Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) or another market surveillance authority designated under the AI Market Surveillance and Innovation Promotion Act (Gesetz zur Marktüberwachung und Innovationsförderung von künstlicher Intelligenz, “KI-MIG”) (Art. 52(14) sentence 1 CRA) will act as the competent authority for CRA purposes. In such scenarios, the competent authority under the AI Act shall cooperate with the BSI (Art. 52(14) sentence 2 CRA).
Wherever a product with digital elements also falls within the scope of another harmonization regulation under the New Legislative Framework (“NLF”) listed in Annex I of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 or is governed by another supervisory authority under sector-specific cybersecurity regulations, such as DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), the BSI is to cooperate closely and in a spirit of mutual trust with the other relevant supervisory authorities.
As the competent market surveillance authority, the BSI has the following tools available for supervision under the CRA:
a. Enforcement measures
The BSI may implement the enforcement measures set forth in Chapter V CRA as well as those in the Market Surveillance Act (Marktüberwachungsgesetz, “MüG”) where necessary (Art. 52(1) CRA). These measures include, in particular,
- requiring the economic operator to take all appropriate corrective actions to bring a non-compliant product with digital elements into conformity, to withdraw it from the market, or to recall it within a reasonable period (Art. 54 CRA);
- requiring corrective action, withdrawal from the market, or recall of a product with digital elements that is compliant with the CRA but nonetheless presents a significant cybersecurity risk or other public-interest risk (Art. 57 CRA);
- restricting or prohibiting a product from being made available on the market, or requiring that it be recalled or withdrawn, where formal non-compliance (such as missing or incorrect CE marking or an incomplete EU declaration of conformity) persists (Art. 58 CRA);
- participating in EU-wide coordinated control actions ("Sweeps") of particular products or product categories, including test purchases under a cover identity (Art. 60 CRA); and
- imposing administrative fines, as described below.
b. Administrative fines
The new Sec. 68 and 69 BSIG align the administrative fines regime with the requirements of Art. 64(2) to (4) CRA:
- Non-compliance with the essential cybersecurity requirements set out in Annex I of the CRA and the obligations set out in Art. 13 and 14 CRA is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 million or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 2.5 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 64(2) CRA).
- The other infringements specified in Art. 64(3) CRA are subject to fines of up to EUR 10 million or, for undertakings, up to 2% of that turnover, whichever is higher.
- Supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or market surveillance authorities in reply to a request is subject to fines of up to EUR 5 million or, for undertakings, up to 1% of that turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 64 (4) CRA).
As provided for in Art. 64(7) CRA, the German provisions exclude administrative fines against public authorities and other public bodies within the meaning of Sec. 2(1) or (2) of the Federal Data Protection Act (Bundesdatenschutzgesetz, “BDSG”) (new Sec. 70(2) BSIG).
c. Complaints body
Lastly, under the new Sec. 65(3) BSIG the BSI, as the competent national market surveillance authority, has to establish a complaints body where consumers can submit complaints that could indicate non-compliance with the CRA (Art. 52(11) CRA).
2.2 Notifying authority
The BSI is also designated as the notifying authority under Art. 36(1) CRA. The assessment and monitoring of conformity assessment bodies are assigned to the German national accreditation body (Deutsche Akkreditierungsstelle, “DAkkS”). The BSI may carry out the assessment itself where there is a public interest in the notification of the conformity assessment body; in that case, it is also responsible for monitoring that body (new Sec. 66(1) to (3) BSIG).
Where the BSI determines that a conformity assessment body meets the requirements of Art. 39 CRA, based on an accreditation certificate or its own assessment (new Sec. 66(2) and (3) BSIG), it designates the body to perform conformity assessments and notifies the European Commission and the other EU Member States (new Sec. 66(4) BSIG).
The designation under the new Sec. 66(4) BSIG is a non-discretionary administrative act: the BSI must designate the body in question if the accreditation certificate, or its own assessment, confirms that the body meets the requirements of Art. 39 CRA.
2.3 CSIRT
The new Sec. 5(3) sentence 2 no. 6 BSIG provides that the BSI performs the tasks of a national computer security incident response team (“CSIRT”) under the CRA. Manufacturers’ notifications under Art. 14 CRA are submitted via ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform (“SRP”) to the CSIRT designated as coordinator in the Member State of the manufacturer’s main establishment. For manufacturers with their main establishment in Germany, this will be the BSI (Art. 14(1), (7) and Art. 16 CRA). See here for more information on ENISA’s SRP.
2.4. Support measures for microenterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises, including open-source software stewards
Further, the BSI is obligated under the new Sec. 67 BSIG to support affected economic operators, especially microenterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises, including open-source software stewards, in complying with the cybersecurity requirements of the CRA. This support is provided primarily through
- the organization of specific awareness-raising and training activities about the application of the CRA; and
- the establishment and operation of a cyber resilience regulatory sandbox. Such a regulatory sandbox shall provide for controlled testing environments for innovative products with digital elements to facilitate their development, design, validation and testing for the purpose of complying with the CRA for a limited period of time before the placing on the market (Art. 33(1) and (2) CRA).
3. Entry into force
The German CRA Implementation Act follows a staggered implementation timeline. Certain provisions will already apply from the day following the promulgation of the German CRA Implementation Act (Art. 4(1) of the German CRA Implementation Act). This include the provisions
- adding the BSI’s tasks as the competent market surveillance authority (new Sec. 3(1) sentence 2 no. 30 BSIG),
- designating the BSI as the no

articles.title: Pound to Euro Nears Best Exchange Rate in Over Two Years - CurrencyNews.co.uk
articles.summary: Pound to Euro Nears Best Exchange Rate in Over Two Years  CurrencyNews.co.uk
articles.full_text:
The Pound Euro (GBP/EUR) exchange rate moved higher on Tuesday after an unexpected drop in UK unemployment gave Sterling a boost.
At the time of writing, GBP/EUR was trading at €1.1896, marking a 0.3% gain for the session.
The Pound (GBP) gained ground early on Tuesday as the latest UK employment figures pointed to a stronger labour market than economists had anticipated.
Data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) revealed that unemployment fell from 4.9% to 4.7% in the three months to August, reaching its lowest level in more than a year.
The unexpected improvement provided further evidence that the UK labour market remains resilient, despite earlier signs of slowing employment growth.
For the Bank of England (BoE), the figures strengthened the case for another interest rate increase in November.
Following the release, markets were pricing in a 95.5% probability of a rate hike next month, alongside expectations for three additional increases during 2027.

The prospect of tighter monetary policy helped Sterling strengthen against several major currencies, with GBP/EUR extending its recent advance towards the €1.1900 level.
The Euro (EUR), meanwhile, came under pressure after Germany's latest economic sentiment figures disappointed expectations.
The ZEW economic sentiment index fell from 34.7 in September to 28.1 in October, missing forecasts for a more modest decline to 30.
The deterioration suggested that confidence in the Eurozone's largest economy remains fragile, with businesses and investors facing continued uncertainty over the growth outlook.
Germany's weaker figures added to existing concerns surrounding the Eurozone economy.
Political and fiscal instability in France also continued to weigh on the single currency, with investors questioning whether the French government can secure sufficient parliamentary support for its proposed budget measures.
With economic confidence deteriorating in Germany and French fiscal concerns unresolved, the Euro struggled to attract fresh demand.
Near-Term GBP/EUR Forecast: UK Inflation Could Push Pound Above €1.19
Wednesday's UK consumer price index (CPI) release will provide the next major test for the Pound to Euro exchange rate.
Economists expect annual headline inflation to accelerate from 3.1% to 3.4% in September, while core inflation is forecast to increase from 2.6% to 2.8%.
Following Tuesday's stronger-than-expected employment figures, another rise in inflation could reinforce expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates in November.
A stronger-than-forecast reading could provide Sterling with enough momentum to challenge the €1.1900 level.
However, with markets already assigning a 95.5% probability to a November rate increase, much of the anticipated tightening may already be reflected in exchange rates.
A softer inflation reading could therefore trigger a more substantial reaction, particularly if investors begin questioning the need for additional BoE tightening beyond November.
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey is also scheduled to speak on Wednesday afternoon, with investors looking for further clues about the central bank's policy outlook.
For the Euro, attention will turn to comments from European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde.
Nevertheless, developments in France may remain an important influence, with further political instability or renewed pressure on French government bonds potentially limiting any recovery in the single currency.

articles.title: Romania’s political crisis gets 6-month truce as new government formed - POLITICO.eu
articles.summary: Romania’s political crisis gets 6-month truce as new government formed  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
Romania ended five months of political paralysis Tuesday with its parliament voting in Luca Niculescu as prime minister after three failed attempts to form a government — but the deal comes with a six-month deadline for the parties to strike a more lasting agreement.
The threat of snap elections, which would likely see the populist right-wing Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) party surge, helped push the center-right National Liberal Party (PNL) and the center-left Social Democrats (PSD) to agree on a government led by independent Niculescu, a former journalist and diplomat who was nominated as prime minister by moderate President Nicușor Dan earlier this month. The socialists will join the cabinet, but the liberals will stay out.
Romania has the sixth-largest population in the EU and plays a critical role in NATO’s defense of southeastern Europe as home to a major military base and a U.S. missile shield site. The country has been plagued by political instability and a mushrooming budget deficit in recent years, fueling a surge in support for hard-right nationalist politics.

articles.title: Back in the eye of the storm: A Trump-Putin deal would require much more to protect Ukraine and EUrope - EPC, European Policy Centre
articles.summary: Back in the eye of the storm: A Trump-Putin deal would require much more to protect Ukraine and EUrope  EPC, European Policy Centre
articles.full_text:
It is currently being reported that Putin, Trump and Xi Jinping will meet in November to attempt to end the conflict in Ukraine, now in its fourth year, without involving Ukrainian President Zelensky. In the light of these claims, Fabian Zuleeg revisits and updates his February 2025 exploration of Trump’s earlier ceasefire plans and finds that all his conclusions still hold: EUrope might have bought some time by appeasing Trump but we are still facing the same fundamental dilemma as we did nearly two years ago.
Peace at last?
As President-elect, Donald Trump publicly stated that he wanted to bring the war in Ukraine to an end quickly, aiming also potentially to absolve the US from its responsibility to continue to support Ukraine militarily, financially and politically. He did not succeed at the beginning of his administration, but reports suggest that he may be preparing for another try. By so imposing a ceasefire he would be ignoring that this war was started illegally by Russian aggression, that Russia committed crimes against humanity, as well as various war crimes, or that significant parts of sovereign Ukrainian territory are not only occupied by Russia but have been illegally annexed by Moscow. Making a deal and getting domestic relief for his self-inflicted high energy prices through imports from Russia are Trump’s only aims. But voices around the world believe that the most important goal is to stop the killing immediately. However, any deal must guarantee security in the longer term. If not, the conflict will return in future and is likely to escalate then.
Of course, we do not know whether Trump will be successful. Even if he makes a deal, Ukrainians might not acquiesce, given the existential nature of the threat, although it is very costly to maintain their defences without US support. It is also not clear what Putin wants; this will depend partly on the attached conditions and partly on how the war is developing with the ongoing withdrawal of US support.
Potential implications for Ukrainian and European security
The challenge for the EU and its member states will be to prepare for a working mode of managing the unreliability of Europe’s key security provider. This requires thorough “what if” preparations in Brussels and in European capitals. If Trump approaches the new potential ceasefire in his usual way, what will this mean for Ukrainian and wider European security?
In part, this will depend on the conditions attached to the ceasefire. Who will be the guarantors of any deal? Who will enforce the deal when Russia starts to disregard its provisions, as it has done in the past? Will Kyiv be given the ability to continue to build up its capabilities to resist Russian aggression? Will Ukraine become a part of the EU (now or with a credible path towards membership)? What happens to occupied territories and to sanctions on Russia?
While many in Europe and especially in Ukraine will not believe in such a ceasefire, they must try to set at least some guardrails for the conditions under which it could be agreed and regarding the role of the EU and its members in any settlement touching the very core of European security for years to come.
A ceasefire is not a lasting peace
It is important to emphasise that this is a discussion around ceasefire, not peace. Whatever is achieved now will most likely be an interlude before the next act of Russian aggression – we have been here before. Putin is unlikely to resist the temptation to pick off an already weakened Ukraine if he is not deterred from doing so. It will not be so much a frozen conflict as a temporarily paused one. Even more worryingly, Russia will, sooner or later, turn its eye to other victims. Moldova and Georgia, even the Baltic States, have long been in the firing line of Russian covert warfare and might be next in Putin’s expansionist path, in addition to continued Russian meddling in Europe, Africa and the Middle East. His continuing close alliance with North Korea links the conflict into the Asia-Pacific region.
In addition, a Russian victory would signal to the world that the only guarantor for independence and territorial integrity is nuclear weapons, leading to nuclear proliferation across the board. It would also bury any idea of upholding the UN Charter in future, creating greater insecurity by casting doubt on the independence and borders of all countries with a strong aggressive neighbour.
Putin will also not stop pursuing his stated aim to reverse some of the repercussions of the end of the Soviet Union, continuing to threaten the Baltic States, as well as the whole of NATO’s Eastern flank. With a perceived weakening of the commitment of the US to European security, the temptation to crank up the covert warfare that is already impinging on Western sovereignty will increase. While it is unlikely that he would seek a military confrontation in the short term, a continual testing of the West’s defences strongly increases the risk of a potentially catastrophic accident. In the medium term, it should not be forgotten that Putin’s Russia is expansionist by nature, seeking domination over its neighbourhood. In a few years’ time, Russia will have recovered militarily and might well surpass its pre-war capabilities in a number of areas. Eventually, the next confrontation will become inevitable.
A conditional deal
A ceasefire at this moment in time under these conditions is bad for Ukrainian and European security, as well as for global stability. Rather than resolving the situation and reducing human suffering, it vastly increases the risk of a future confrontation, with even more catastrophic outcomes. But, given the US president’s plans and objectives, it is the most likely next stage in Russia’s long-running war against free Europe.
So, what can the EU and its member states do?
While we could, and should, have done more to support Ukraine to comprehensively win the war, this has been beyond reach for some time. In the near future, it is about damage limitation. This means ensuring that any ceasefire deal contains as many favourable conditions for Ukraine as possible, including credible security guarantees. This must be done in close coordination with Kyiv. At the same time, there should be no limitations enshrined in the deal for Ukraine to arm itself or to be armed, or on any technology Ukraine needs. And Europe should be willing to put boots on the ground in case of a ceasefire; it is the only way to ensure such a ceasefire would hold.
EU membership, or a credible path and timeline to membership, should also be part of the deal, at the very least ensuring that Russia does not exercise a veto on Ukraine’s European future. However, it does not seem that this is a Trumpian priority, given his disdain for multilateral institutions in general and the EU in particular. The Union should nevertheless put this on the table, although it is unclear whether the political will within exists.
Any easing of sanctions should be contingent on the return of illegally occupied territory, as well as mandating the use of Russian funds for reconstruction, which many in the US also advocate, although there is likely to be strong pushback from Russia. Other conditions, linked to Ukraine’s Peace Formula, such as returning prisoners of war, as well as the Ukrainian children abducted by Russia, guaranteeing free passage through the Black Sea and provisions to guarantee nuclear safety all need to be part of the deal. The complete withdrawal of all 8,500 North Korean troops must also be part of any ceasefire.
Putin might not be willing to accept these conditions, but if this leads to a breakdown in negotiations between Trump and Putin, so much the better. However, chances are that in return for a favourable ceasefire, Putin will accept many conditions, even if he intends to break them later on. The challenge will be to ensure that Trump includes these conditions in his dealings with Putin. Appealing to his vanity might help: Trump always needs to win, so if the “best deal ever” is presented as being dependent on these conditions, it might induce him to push for them, i.e. his deal is “great” if, and only if, these conditions are included.
A crucial battleground for EUrope and Ukraine will be US domestic politics. Trump might be constrained in his actions, given that there are many in the US who are opposed to a US–Russia deal. This might become even more salient after the mid-term elections.
Europe will have to do more, not less, in case of a ceasefire
Much of what will need to be delivered under a ceasefire will have to come from Europe, including a commitment to a further continuous strengthening of Ukrainian armed forces and significant funding and risk guarantees for Ukrainian reconstruction. Europe must continue to further strengthen its defence industry, so that it is able to produce the weapons required to defend itself against an expansionist Russia, as well as buying more US weapons. European defence spending will need to continue to rise substantially, consistent with NATO’s June 2025 commitment to invest the equivalent of 5% of GDP in defence and security by 2035. This may entail borrowing more both at national and EU level, potentially also outside the current Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) given the time pressure to strengthen EU capabilities in the immediate future. In many instances, Europe will be expected to sacrifice its economic interest in return for a continuation of the US security guarantee, albeit that this guarantee will be more tentative under Trump than under previous presidents.
As a result, should a Trump-imposed ceasefire become a reality, Europe will have to do – and commit – more rather than less. Europe must listen to the countries bordering Russia, and to Ukraine in particular, to apprehend the nature of Putin’s Russia and the continuous and increasing threat it poses, given the border countries’ correct assessment in the past. Beijing warns London of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it aligns with EU import curbs on EVs
Ministry of Commerce responds to British minister’s call for London and Brussels to ‘work together’ on measures targeting Chinese carmakers
As London considers aligning with EU trade measures targeting imports of Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), Beijing has warned of “firm countermeasures” if the UK imposes restrictions.
“We hope the UK will abide by World Trade Organization rules and think twice before acting, rather than blindly following the EU,” the Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. “China will closely monitor developments and take firm countermeasures if the UK insists on restricting Chinese electric vehicles.”
The ministry’s statement was in response to remarks last week by Anas Sarwar, the United Kingdom’s trade minister, who said Britain and the European Union must “work together and act in lockstep” to address China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
The British government was continuing discussions with the EU on potential tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, he said.

articles.title: New carbon tax could leave British farmers worse off, NFU warns - FarmingUK
articles.summary: New carbon tax could leave British farmers worse off, NFU warns  FarmingUK
articles.full_text:
New carbon tax could leave British farmers worse off, NFU warns
British farmers could face higher fertiliser bills under a new carbon border tax, while imported food avoids equivalent charges, the NFU has warned.
The union is urging the chancellor to introduce safeguards in the upcoming budget to prevent domestic food producers from being placed at a competitive disadvantage.
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), due to take effect on 1 January 2027, will apply carbon-related charges to certain imported goods, including fertilisers.
The mechanism is designed to tackle carbon leakage by ensuring imported products face carbon costs comparable to those paid by UK manufacturers.
However, the NFU fears that additional charges on imported fertiliser could ultimately be passed on to farmers already struggling with rising production costs.
The warning follows the government's publication of illustrative CBAM rates on 16 October, ahead of the tax's introduction next year.
The provisional fertiliser rate stands at £1.45 per tonne of CO2-equivalent emissions, although the final rate for early 2027 has yet to be confirmed.
Rates will be reviewed quarterly, reflecting changes in carbon pricing and other factors, creating uncertainty over future costs.
NFU Deputy President Paul Tompkins warned that Britain's reliance on imported fertiliser supplies could leave farmers particularly exposed.
“Fertiliser is essential for British farmers and growers as we work to produce the nation’s food.”
He highlighted that ammonia used in fertiliser production is no longer manufactured in the UK, leaving the industry dependent on overseas supplies.
The union argues that additional import costs could place further pressure on farm profitability, particularly where producers have limited ability to absorb increases or pass them on.
Mr Tompkins said: “A tax on those fertiliser imports is most likely to be felt by farmers who are already operating on the tightest of margins and can't simply absorb these extra costs or pass them on.”
A major concern is the potential imbalance between British food producers and overseas competitors.
While domestic farmers could face higher fertiliser costs under CBAM, imported food grown using fertiliser overseas would not face an equivalent charge under the mechanism.
The NFU believes this risks making British agricultural production less competitive against imported food.
Mr Tompkins warned: “Unbelievably, food grown overseas with fertiliser will not be subject to the same tax, leaving domestic food production at a competitive disadvantage.”
The union is calling on the government to ensure the new mechanism does not undermine domestic food production or weaken the competitiveness of British agriculture.
It wants the upcoming budget to include measures that reduce production costs, strengthen farm business resilience and restore confidence across the sector.
The NFU argues that protecting food security must remain a central consideration as ministers introduce new environmental and taxation policies.
Mr Tompkins said: “If government is true to its word that ‘food security is national security’, then the chancellor must announce measures at the budget that actually reduces the cost of producing food, not increases it, builds resilience in the sector and restores farm business confidence.”

articles.title: The ‘Total Strike’ Has Come for France - Tribunemag.co.uk
articles.summary: The ‘Total Strike’ Has Come for France  Tribunemag.co.ukThe Failures of Emmanuel Macron  The New York TimesRiots leave France divided as Macron enters his final stretch  The Washington PostDarkness in the city of light  Engelsberg IdeasNous sommes le pouvoir: Crisis and Struggle in France  Honi Soit
articles.full_text:
It’s like a traffic accident: a fatal junction, a death. Macronism is dying at the crossroads for which it has always been destined: the intersection of capital and people. Here, capital appears in its purest form — the form of money that makes money, without mediation: finance capital. And opposite it: the fire. The Financial Times ran an early headline: ‘France Caught Between the Bond Market and the Barricades.’ There we are: right to the bone.
Four decades of neoliberal rot are now coming to a head at this point of terminal crisis — the point where two incompatible principles of sovereignty collide: the financial markets’ claim to sovereignty, as they seek to control all public policies, shape them according to their wishes, and nip in the bud any they dislike; and the sovereignty of the people. Macronism is the party of the former sovereignty against the latter: choose France, please the markets — as for the rest: riot police, eye-gouging, mutilations.
It took until 2017 for capital to get a man of capital elected. Previously, there had been lingering delays, awkward timidity, hesitation, sometimes even backtracking. But with Macron, everything has become clear. It is no coincidence that the sovereign debt crisis erupted at the same time as the political crisis (let’s stop talking about a ‘social’ crisis): these are characteristic features of a global order headed for ruin, when all their internal processes synchronise, signalling that fundamental contradictions of the matrix have reached a critical moment. The matrix has created its own impasse — its total impasse.
How did we get here? 1) Sanctify the financial markets, applaud their complete control over the economy, and celebrate their role as watchdogs of the neoliberal order: distant, abstract, incomprehensible, beyond the reach of any protest movement — perfect. 2) Enact the Tax Law: exempting both the rich and capital from being taxed. 3) Watch as the deficit inevitably widens and the debt balloons. 4) Invoke ‘the debt’ (self-imposed) and ‘the markets’ (deliberately enshrined) to begin the rampage: cut, impoverish, privatise, commodify. 5) Turn the people protesting into enemies and subdue them with weapons of war. Until the day when — no. No more. Then, the bunker that the rich thought they had built turns against them: the final explosion of the matrix.
The final adjustment variable — the one on which the rich had staked everything, the variable of voluntary servitude — has just collapsed. The daily of the bourgeoisie, Le Monde, is ‘dismayed’ by the ‘accumulation of crises’. One can see why these people are despondent, situated at the intersection of blabocracy (the government of loudmouths) and morocracy (the government of idiots). They cannot understand a thing unless they are destroying things. Their impasse is total. Their equation has no solution; there is no way out. The people have broken free from the straitjacket and forced Prime Minister Lecornu into it. This unfortunate man is under orders to announce a fiscal recovery plan just as the entire country rises up to tell him: No, not this time.
A formidable nemesis: it’s no longer even about Parcoursup, or the de-indexing of pensions, or housing assistance; it’s about everything. No authority can reassert itself when everything is called into question. That is to say, when the primal sovereignty of the people — denied by the usurping sovereignty of capital and the markets — rises up. This gigantomachy was bound to happen eventually. Now its time has come.
But poor Lecornu hasn’t seen anything yet. Like the media morocrats, he doesn’t realise that the real financial cyclone — the one involving private debt, AI, private credit and private equity, as well as household debt — hasn’t hit yet; it’s still gathering strength. It will ravage the US financial system and thus the entire neoliberalised world system. Banks and insurance companies will go under and will have to be bailed out. Yet again. With public money. The ensuing recession will be devastating. Deficits will skyrocket. Why? Because this is a crisis of everything: ‘La Totale’.
‘La Totale’ is also a historic opening. Under the guise of youth — astonishing in every respect — popular sovereignty is surging forward. We know the bourgeois order’s only response: to terrorise. But these ‘solutions’ are only temporary. Their scope is limited. The sum total of everything that is unbearable — high schools, colleges, diesel, food, wages, firefighters, healthcare, public services, pensions — has crashed up against the sum total of all those who can no longer bear the unbearable. Behind the high school students spearheading the movement, the larger battalions are beginning to grow restless. The fatal error of Macronism: because it corrupts everything, everything can work towards its overthrow.
When everything comes into play, the balance shifts. The Nahel revolt — from which the current movement draws much of its legacy — had seen the police teeter on the brink of collapse: too many red lights flashing on the ‘big board’ in the Interior Ministry’s crisis room, too many hotspots in too many places across the country, impossible to keep track of — so in came the police brigades, the RAID, the BRI, the madness of a regime already on the ropes. Now, we wait for nothing more than for the working class rise from its strongholds and take the stage: refinery workers, transit workers, sanitation workers. Picket lines everywhere, blockades everywhere: the Total Strike — but ours. From one Total Strike to another: the Total Strike of the uprising against the Total Strike of the bourgeois crisis. The police are overwhelmed, resorting to extremes that will fuel hatred against them to levels where fear is transformed into a desire for revenge.
Whatever happens from here on out, this regime has lost. In ten years, Macronism has quite literally destroyed the country, before sinking into shame and disgust. We have long awaited the moment to present it with the bill. And here it is. Macronism is not only morally delegitimised but also symbolically defeated. No movement in France since May ’68 has produced such a wealth of imagery. TikTok has become the channel of vitality, invention and creativity: when we aren’t trembling with rage at videos of police violence, we’re crying with laughter — or simply crying because it’s so beautiful. Who would have thought: TikTok, the return of Simone Weil’s ‘pure joy’.
A tyrannical regime cannot beat it. Here, high school students sing Aznavour’s ‘Emmenez-moi’ beneath the sunlight; there, eruptions of energy right under the bullies’ noses. We don’t know where to look. A radio broadcast arrives from the blockade at none other than the École Alsacienne, the famously elite private school, where a ‘woman in fur’ is asked for her view of the students. The woman in fur says ‘I support them.’ In the background, we hear the protesters sing the final verses of The Internationale at the top of their lungs. Only times of extreme crisis produce scenes so absurd, so joyful. The symbolic disaster is total. There is no recovering from this convergence of images.
La Totale marks the culmination of a bourgeois state that has been looming on the horizon for quite some time: a state reduced to two ministries — the Ministry of the Budget and the Ministry of the Interior. Or, to put it another way: the Ministry of Friends (the markets) and the Ministry of Enemies (the people). As the first runs up against the economic impasse of neoliberalism, the second comes to hold all the power. It is nothing more than a gathering of sadistic thugs at every level; this is indeed the novelty of Macronism.
Even Pasqua, even Pandraud, even Sarkozy, even Hortefeux knew when to stop. The new rulers do not. They take pleasure in beating people, gouging out eyes, maiming, strangling young women or groping them. The levels of sexual violence in police custody are staggering. The police are nothing more than a degenerate force, made up of degenerates. We are living in an era where the police now inspect protest signs. What little bell is jingling inside an officer’s head when he decides which are allowed and which are not? Who gives such instructions? It’s true, as we are often told, that there are lawless zones in the country: they are called ‘the Ministry of the Interior’ and ‘the police stations’.
Such is the hideous spasm of powers on the wane. Macron, a sham ruler and a puppet of historical forces that overwhelm him on all sides, came to power to carry out neoliberalism — that is, to bring it to an end. He has now been overthrown, and by whom? By kids. An abject disgrace on top of a historic failure. A young girl protesting sums up the situation: ‘I don’t understand why they tell us not to revolt’, she says, ‘when our curriculum is literally full of people who revolt — Arthur Rimbaud, La Boétie, Olympe de Gouges’. Suddenly, the morocrats of the 24-hour news channels — old, white, bourgeois — find themselves ridiculed. The unfathomable hypocrisy of bourgeois culture, which cares nothing for what it reads, what it sees, what it claims to revere — which celebrates merely to embalm and neutralise — is exposed. Only young people, from the depths of their integrity, can rediscover it.
Among the avalanche of photos destined to go down in history, one will undoubtedly stand out. It shows a child, sitting on the ground against a police van, handcuffed, beneath the two thugs who arrested him. Everything in the frame is dark: the street, the police vehicle, especially the helmeted officers. But a patch of light radiates, leaping out of the image: the face of this child looking directly at the camera. It’s as beautiful as a Rembrandt.
The entire period has become melodramatic, full of stark polarities — from Rembrandt to Hugo, so to speak. But one subsumes all others. There is the struggle, which is life, and the bourgeoisie, which is death.

articles.title: The European cities facing protests as continent gripped by cost of living crisis - The Independent
articles.summary: The European cities facing protests as continent gripped by cost of living crisis  The IndependentFrom Paris to Porto, from Tirana to Milan: protests across Europe – in pictures  The GuardianItaly, Spain, Belgium, Portugal: Social unrest spreads across Europe amid soaring energy prices and a housing crisis  Le Monde.frAs France erupts, Europe's far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections  ReutersFrance Protests Show Europe’s Shift Away From Ce...
articles.full_text:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
Violent protests have broken out across Europe amid growing frustration over the cost of living crisis, a lack of affordable housing and deteriorating school conditions.
As many as 550,000 people turned out across France on Saturday, according to authorities, to demonstrate against declining public services. Protests turned violent in Paris as shops were looted and cars set on fire in some of the city’s worst violence in years.
Young people waved Italian flags and let off flares in Milan as they rallied against the rising cost of living in scenes that were condemned by prime minister Giorgia Meloni.
Police used water cannon and teargas to break up the crowds after some masked rioters clashed with authorities and set off fires.
Tens of thousands of people meanwhile marched through central Lisbon in protest of the soaring cost of living and a deepening housing crisis, echoing weeks of demonstrations in Spain that prompted prime minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election.
Pressure was also on Albania’s prime minister Edi Rama after a week of protests over poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption, which saw hours-long violent clashes with police on Sunday.
Here we look at the factors behind the protests sweeping the continent and the latest developments.
France
Marseille is set to impose a curfew on minors each night until Friday in response to the violent protests that have rocked France.
On Monday night, the French government imposed partial curfews across the country, including in Paris and Nice, after riots and looting amid nationwide protests over the weekend.
It came after thousands of rioters were arrested during the weekend’s widespread protests, with justice minister Gérald Darmanin promising an “unrelenting” response to violence. The unrest gathered momentum from student-led demonstrations that began last month in response to overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages.
Authorities said more than half a million people turned out to march on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris alone. Organisers put the figure closer to 800,000.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
French president Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday as some of the protests boiled over into violent clashes with police. The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting.
More than 2,400 people were arrested across France, while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the government. Police fired teargas in Paris on Sunday afternoon and protesters set fire to piles of bicycles.
One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in the capital.
Spain
Tens of thousands of people have turned out across Spain in recent weeks following the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, from her Madrid home.
The pensioner was forcibly removed from her flat of 70 years after the property was bought by the investment firm Urbagestion, which tried to increase her rent by 230 per cent. She died suddenly in early October, two weeks after she was evicted.
Maricarmen’s death reinvigorated a movement long frustrated by home shortages and surging rents across the country.
Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez last month called a snap general election for 29 November after parliament rejected his government’s proposals to address a mounting housing crisis.
Several people who received eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months.
Spain's minimum wage is €1,221 (£1,025), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around €1,130 (about £949), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansión.
Italy
“Italia in Piazza,” or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators against crumbling public services and the rising cost of living.
Milan police clashed on Sunday with protesters throwing stones and looting shops. Meanwhile, police in riot gear fired teargas and used water cannons after several hundred hooded protesters broke shop windows and set bins on fire in the area near central Piazza Duomo, sources told Reuters, adding that more than 60 protesters had been detained for checks.
A total of 28 protesters were arrested after similar clashes erupted on Saturday in northern cities including Milan, Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, according to a police report on Sunday.
Ms Meloni, facing an election next year, condemned the violence and announced a government meeting on Monday to discuss how to address the situation.
Now a newly formed group calling itself the “17 October Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilization” to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy.
Portugal
Fifty-five people were arrested as Portuguese police dismantled housing crisis protest camps in the central squares of Lisbon and Porto before dawn on Tuesday.
Activists pitched roughly 200 tents in Lisbon’s Rossio square on Saturday, while Porto’s Dom Joao I square had been occupied for 10 days. Protesters say low wages are failing to keep pace with housing costs and the rising cost of living, leaving many people struggling to make ends meet.
Portugal faces an acute housing affordability crisis, where buying costs have more than doubled since 2017 and new lease rents have almost doubled.
Urban areas feel the greatest strain, compounded by backlash against excessive tourism and digital nomads. Activists want the centre-right government to drop a bill easing evictions and removing rent caps on new leases, which passed its first reading after the far-right Chega party abstained.
Tens of thousands of people also marched through central Lisbon on Saturday. Portugal's biggest union, CGTP, which called the rally, said “many tens of thousands” packed one of the capital's main avenues.
Portugal’s inflation hit 3.6 per cent in September, driven by rising food and fuel prices, the latter up 15 per cent year-on-year following an increase in tensions in the Middle East.
Albania
Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania's capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Rama has condemned the protesters as “ideologized and radicalized” by antifa, an umbrella term for loosely organized far-left militants in the United States, where President Donald Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organization.
Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama's government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website.
Serbia
Tens of thousands of people are expected to march in Serbia’s capital Belgrade on Thursday as part of an election rally led by student activists.
For nearly two years, Serbian university students have driven mass anti-corruption protests. Now they share a broader aim: defeating the nation's powerful populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in this weekend's early parliamentary election.
Following the 25 October vote, the former authoritarian president is seeking a return as prime minister to extend his right-wing party's 14-year rule. Having previously rattled the populists during their demonstrations, Serbia's youth movement is the sole barrier in his way.
Unlike high school students in France who are rallying for better education, Serbia's student movement started out as a struggle for justice after a train station tragedy in the country's north killed 16 people in November 2024. The students' call for accountability for the deaths, which they blamed on rampant corruption, found widespread support. Protests spread, forcing a government collapse and rattling Vucic.
Much is uncertain ahead of Sunday's vote. Tensions remain high alongside the stakes. Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, and the student-supported Students' List are thought to be running close, leaving the outcome uncertain and raising fears of potential violence.

articles.title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show - The Guardian
articles.summary: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show  The GuardianMonaco's yachting industry approaches €660 million in annual turnover  Riviera RadioWhat’s new and hot in the world of high-end yachting, courtesy of the launches at MYS 2026  Wallpaper*Monaco’s yachting industry explores new markets and future trends  GlobeNewswire“Superyachts of 2026: Pioneering Design and Functionality at Monaco Yacht Show”&nbs...
articles.full_text:
Who knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?
To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.
For now, though, I’m boarding my first vessel: a relatively modest Zeelander 8 – 23.9 metres (79ft) long, built in the Netherlands. It has a rather retro look about it, with pleasing curves and a rear end not unlike a Porsche’s. I could imagine James Bond at the wheel. It’s fast too, reaching 40 knots (46mph); I could be in Saint-Tropez in a little over an hour.
Downstairs there’s a huge owner’s cabin, plus a couple of double guest cabins, all en suite, with lots of nice details, such as a cream-coloured leather floor. In the less opulent crew quarters, there’s room for two or three. How much does it cost? This one is not actually for sale – some of the boats here are, others are for charter, some just for show. But I could order one just like it, it would take a year and a half to build and cost me about €9.5m (£8m).
Tempting, certainly, but I need to see a few more before rushing into anything. I can’t help noticing that, compared with some of the others packed into Port Hercules, the Zeelander 8 is a bit … well, small. Is it even a superyacht? There seems to be some debate about how long a yacht has to be to be super – some say 24 metres, others 30.
No question about this one – a Fast50, made by Italian builders Baglietto, with room for 12 guests and a crew of nine. It’s not as fast as the Dutch one, despite the name. Its four engines take it to 30 knots, but that’s actually very quick for a 50 metre boat. Perhaps more importantly, its gross tonnage, referring to internal volume, is 499; a sub-500GT yacht isn’t subject to the more stringent safety and environmental rules under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) that yachts over 500GT are, so they require less frequent surveys and have fewer restrictions on crew size and certification. My favourite features are the large “beach club” (the open deck at the back) and the Jacuzzi right up at the pointy end. Imagine it: sitting with a glass of fizz, in the bubbles, at 30 knots, Céline Dion blasting out … where do I sign?
Oh, again. Not for sale. The first Fast50, fresh from the shipyard, is already sold, but they won’t tell me how much for or who to (superyacht owners can be quite shy). The search continues.
The trouble with superyachting, I’m finding here in Monaco, is that you think you’ve found the perfect vessel, and then you look over there and there’s a bigger, better one. It’s not just me – this is reflected in the Global Order Book, published by Boat International, which tracks construction projects. The 2026 GOB counts the number of yachts over 24 metres under construction globally at 1,093. In 2016, it counted 755 vessels under construction. This year’s figure is actually down 3.95% from last year, but that’s balanced by an increase in average length and gross tonnage. In other words, a few fewer, but they’re getting bigger. New prefixes are required, “mega” and “giga”, but for simplicity’s sake we’ll stick with superyacht. Here at MYS 2026 there are 118 superyachts, with a combined length of 5,508 metres, and a value of €4.5bn.
Despite the sock shame, I’m beginning to feel more comfortable. Most people are friendly. It’s a lovely day on the Côte d’Azur – I’m offered ice-cream, branded fans and straw hats. It’s not just the yachts, there are stands for everything connected. Would I like to come to a wine tasting later “exploring superyacht wine trends”? Of course I would. Am I interested in yachting in Saudi Arabia? Hmmm, maybe next year. There are loads of toys on show – jetskis, eFoils, even submersibles. And if you’re still finding life at sea boring, there’s a portable golf simulator, with cameras and sensors, plus a screen, with hundreds of real courses programmed into it. So after dropping anchor off St Barts you can play a round at St Andrews. It costs €170,000 (£143,000).
And so on to Nixie, built by Lürssen in Germany, owned by co-founder and CEO of Revolut, Nik Storonsky: 102 metres long, with a helipad, glass-bottomed infinity pool, dedicated spa and wellness zone, and a crew of 34, one of whom is busy polishing a stainless steel cleat on the lowest of its decks. Access, though, is “reserved exclusively for direct, potential clients,” says the Lürssen PR. Perhaps they think the average Guardian reader is not in the market to rent a boat the length of a football pitch. Nixie costs €2.4m a week to hire. A lot, I know, but if you split it between the 12 of you …
Anyway, it’s not even the biggest here, which I will be allowed on. First though I pass another – Boardwalk V, only 76.5 metres long and five years old, but this one is for sale, at a discount price! Down €14m, to just €135m. Not including the helicopter. Boardwalk V … it’s ringing a bell. Got it! And now the twin flags on the helicopter’s tail – the American stars and stripes and the tricolore of Italy – make sense. This boat belongs to Tilman Fertitta, billionaire owner of restaurants, hotels, casinos, and the Houston Rockets basketball team, and now Donald Trump’s ambassador to Italy. He made the news in June when hundreds came out to protest after he parked his brand new 117-metre yacht (also named Boardwalk, but without the V) in Venice. He’s got an upgrade – that’s why he’s selling this one.
To be honest there are some proper horrors on show. This one looks like a supersized 80s caravan, that one more like a bridge than a boat, another is bright red – like some kind of firefighting ship. “I don’t understand the clients,” says Rick. “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” Rick is also pretty disparaging about the people who sell these boats, the brokers. “They’re like real estate agents, they say: ‘Look at the master cabin, look at all the light, the big windows,’ it’s all about the interior space.”
Guess what Rick does? Yup, yacht broker. It’s why we’ve changed his name. He also points out something about the way they look. “I don’t know if you’ve heard the analogy, but they look like irons.” As in electric irons, to do the ironing with, and oh my God, he’s so right – that shape, pointy at the bow, then rising and widening as you go aft, with a squared off swim platform … As Rick says, “once you see it, you can’t unsee it.”
In a 2024 study, Oxfam identified 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires and estimated the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. For an average citizen of the world it would take 860 years to produce the same amount.
Oxfam zoomed in further to one family, the Waltons, heirs of the Walmart chain and owners of three superyachts (at this level you’re not talking about the haves and the have-yachts, you’re talking about the have-yachts and the have-lots-of-yachts). They travelled 56,000 nautical miles in a year with a combined carbon footprint of 18,000 tonnes. That’s equivalent to the carbon emissions of about 1,700 Walmart employees.
Superyachts use an awful lot of fuel – some of the bigger ones use more than 500 litres of diesel per hour, releasing CO2 as well as nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide into the atmosphere. The recreational boating sector as a whole – including yachts – produces about 16m tonnes of CO2 annually. It’s not just when they’re going along; at anchor they operate onboard generators to run their “hotel loads” (for air conditioning, stabilisation systems, lighting, galleys, hot tubs, etc) which emit further CO2. In addition, the vessels’ big anchors and chains act like the grim reaper’s scythe on the Posidonia seagrass which grows on the Mediterranean seabed and is a vital habitat for sea life as well as a source of oxygen.
And there are more and more of them. The big increases came in 2022 and 2023 when, as Boat International puts it, “orders soared as UHNWIs sought private holiday cocoons.” UHNWIs, you’ll know, are ultra-high net worth individuals, but why the big boom? Because a superyacht is “the best way to practise social distancing in a very safe and very comfortable way,” says Grégory Salle. Covid was brilliant for the superyacht sector, in other words. Salle is talking to me by video from Lille where he works at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. He’s also author of the thoroughly researched and surprisingly entertaining book Superyachts: Luxury, Tranquility and Ecocide, which has a whole chapter devoted to Posidonia seagrass.
Ecocide is not the superyacht’s only crime. “It has really become the symbol of excessive, unjustifiable wealth,” Salle says. Even though the gap between most of us and the people who have them is virtually unfathomable, “it looks like provocation, especially when all you’re hearing and reading about is crisis, austerity, poverty – including child poverty.”
Superyachts are also a kind of floating paradox that Salle calls “conspicuous seclusion. On the one hand they’re meant to be noticed, they’re massive, you can’t miss them. But at the same time the interior is hidden and of course it can sail away and escape ordinary people.”
Salle uses words and phrases such as “plutocracy”, “oligarchy” and the new “global super-bourgeoisie” about the people who own them, a “transnational capital

articles.title: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech - BBC
articles.summary: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech  BBCBritain seeks to break Apple's grip on contactless payments  ReutersCMA outlines proposals to unlock contactless technology on Apple iPhone  GOV.UKApple Pay rivals to be allowed on iPhones under crackdown  The TelegraphUK Antitrust Regulator Wants Apple To Open Up iPhone NFC Access  Engadget
articles.full_text:
UK smartphone users could benefit from new payment, ticket and travel apps if Apple widens access to its contactless payment tech, the competition watchdog says.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) also wants the fees Apple charges firms to use its contactless tech to be "substantially lower".
It believes the iPhone maker's current fees and charges are "blocking" financial technology firms and others from innovating and growing - and is consulting on proposals it believes would cause these fees to fall.
Apple maintains that widening access could undermine security, and that its current arrangements do not stop innovation.
Nearly 2 in 5 payments are now contactless, the watchdog said, with nearly 60% of people using digital wallets - with Apple's the most popular in the UK.
In a statement Apple told the BBC that the current arrangements had permitted developers in the UK and around the world to securely offer contactless transactions directly within their apps, for everything from in-store payments and transit passes to car keys and event tickets.
"This solution enables developers and banks to create innovative products and services for their customers and facilitates competition between wallets, while ensuring users' sensitive data remains protected by the highest security standards".
"We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."
Last year Apple warned UK regulators against following the same path as the EU which forced it to open up a range of its technologies to rivals.
However, the CMA argued that, unlike the EU, it is focused on ensuring the interoperability of particular aspects of Apple's tech, such as digital wallets and watches.
The proposed measures would force Apple to grant access to apps that make payments via a widely used alternative contactless technology standard, called Host Card Emulation (HCE), which the firm does not currently permit in the UK.
New wallets, IDs and digital keys
The UK is one of the world's leading fintech hubs, the CMA said, generating more than £214 billion in turnover and supporting more than 360,000 jobs.
But Apple's fees and rules contactless payments are restricting growth and innovation, it argued.
Changes could enable the development of a wide range of new products, such as account-to-account payments, digital IDs, travel passes and digital keys, it claimed.
The regulator said moves to open up the tech in the EU had resulted in the creation of new businesses.
In the six months since the EU forced Apple to widen access to its tech, an alternative payment app Vipps launched, followed by PayPal, Klarna, Curve, and BBVA.
Apple argues however that the these new apps could easily have been launched prior to the changes.
But in the UK not a single firm has launched a wallet-type product to compete with Apple's the watchdog argued.
The CMA said it was not proposing to set the price and terms Apple could demand for use of its devices contactless tech, but the effect of its plans would be that prices would fall.
Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA said it had been told that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology made it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete.
"By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services," she said.
