articles.title: Andy Burnham expected to make major Keir Starmer U-turn - AOL.co.uk
articles.summary: Andy Burnham expected to make major Keir Starmer U-turn  AOL.co.ukCarmakers face smaller cut in UK EV sales targets  Financial TimesSigns that you’re ready to make the switch to an electric car  Belfast News Letter‘The zero-emission vehicle mandate is a major climate test for Burnham’  LabourListU.K. Auto Industry Needs Urgent Policy U-Turn To Survive  Forbes
articles.full_text:
Andy Burnham could be set to green-light a major U-turn over Keir Starmer's Labour plan, according to reports. The Financial Times claims that Andy Burnham's Government is considering reducing the UK's electric car sales targets with updates to Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) Mandate rules. Mr Burnham's Government is believed to have sounded out manufacturers on whether a 60% EV sales target could be supported.
Under the current policy, manufacturers must ensure that as many as 80% of new cars sold are electric by 2030. This is a U-turn in itself, but the move could go against Sir Keir Starmer's previous plan, which would have cut targets by even more.
Peter Kyle, business secretary under Mr Starmer had plans to cut EV sales targets to 50% to back manufacturers. However, Mr Starmer left office before the plans could be realised. The Department for Transport (DfT) is currently consulting on the future of the ZEV Mandate, with the Government seeking views on the current trajectory and yearly headline targets.
The consultation is set to close on October 23, with stakeholders asked to pick whether the 80% sales target should be maintained or updated. Among the ideas on the table is a 70%, 60% and 50% EV sales target. However, under all of the plans companies will need to ensure all vehicles sold are fully electric by 2035.
Meanwhile, petrol and diesel cars will still be banned by 2030, with the difference likely to be made up by plug-in models. Mr Burnham's new target could still put him at odds with some car manufacturers, with concern that the targets could still be too high.
Last week, Renault boss François Provost told the UK that ZEV mandate rules were "not realistic" and put "too much pressure on the system". Ford UK boss Lisa Brankin was among those demanding an "urgent review" into the UK's ZEV mandate rules.
Earlier this summer, Lisa said: "Ford believes in a zero-emissions future. That isn't in question. What is in question is whether the current policy path reflects how people actually buy and use vehicles today."
The DfT told the Express: "It has never been easier or cheaper to own an EV - with sales up by 36% in September thanks to our £7.5 billion investment in the market, and nearly 2 million EV drivers saving up to £1,750 a year in running costs.
"We recognise manufacturers are facing challenges, and are reviewing the Mandate to ensure it continues to deliver for British consumers and industry. Our consultation is ongoing and no decisions have been made."
The Express has contacted the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) for comment.

articles.title: Bradford station rebuild gets government backing - Construction Enquirer
articles.summary: Bradford station rebuild gets government backing  Construction EnquirerNew Bradford railway station will ‘transform travel across the north’  The GuardianNew station puts city at heart of network - mayor  BBCGovernment confirms new Bradford Interchange station to be delivered in 2030s  Rail MagazineFull steam ahead: new station for Bradford  GOV.UK
articles.full_text:
The existing 1970s station site has been picked for the Northern Powerhouse Rail hub, which will spearhead regeneration of Bradford’s Southern Gateway.
Ministers have settled the location but have yet to announce a construction budget or detailed building programme.
Network Rail has been carrying out engineering and cost studies. Amey has separately secured the integration role across six projects making up NPR’s first phase, including the Bradford to Leeds corridor. This covers engineering coordination rather than building the station.
Bradford wants a through station to end the need for trains to reverse out of the existing terminus. But the final layout, platform numbers and track arrangements remain to be settled.
Wider rail plans include electrifying the Bradford to Leeds route via New Pudsey and developing a future fast connection to Huddersfield and onwards to Manchester.
The new station will link with the proposed West Yorkshire mass transit network, helping unlock land for thousands of homes and new commercial space.
Bradford’s 126ha Southern Gateway regeneration area has potential for 5,000 homes and 440,000 sq m of offices, alongside shops, leisure facilities and green spaces.
Arup is progressing the regeneration masterplan for Bradford Council, building on earlier work by WSP.
Transport secretary Heidi Alexander said: “By bringing Northern Powerhouse Rail into the heart of the city, we are unlocking the huge potential Bradford offers – improving connections, supporting economic growth and setting the foundations for new homes, jobs and opportunities across the region.”
West Yorkshire mayor Tracy Brabin said: “Today is an exciting and important milestone for Bradford, with an ironclad commitment to a new station in the city centre.”
The wider NPR programme carries a £45bn lifetime funding cap, with £1.1bn allocated for development during the current spending review period.

articles.title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says | Ukraine - The Guardian
articles.summary: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says | Ukraine  The GuardianUkrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC  BBCZelenskiy says Ukraine got no warning as Russian missiles rain in  ReutersUS gave Kyiv just 60 seconds’ warning of ballistic missile attack  The Telegraph‘Tell that to the families’: Polish FM hits back at Hegseth over Afghanistan remarks  TVP World
articles.full_text:
Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.
Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian air force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at about 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.
“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.
“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
Zelenskyy is grappling with recent US moves benefiting the Russian president, Vladimir Putin.
On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia, telling Congress the pause on the legislation, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.
The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Trump also told reporters on Monday that he would consider a trilateral meeting with Russia and China. He said: “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation. If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it.”
For years, the US has warned Ukraine before Russia launched ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskyy and Trump.
Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”
US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.
The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink, the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.
Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through the PURL scheme, where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St Petersburg.
The Russian barrage on Sunday evening hit 28 substations and other critical energy facilities, depriving more than 500,000 people of electricity, heat and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media. Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine by attacking trains, shopping centres, fuel stations and supermarkets, among other sites.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, Zelenskyy said, and officials in the capital reported that a 21-year-old woman had been killed.
Later drone strikes on a public park in the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people, including young children. The regional governor, Oleg Synegubov, said on Telegram that three of the dead in the attack on Nova Vodolaha were children, including one in a pushchair. Seven children were among the 14 wounded. Police posted pictures showing damaged playground equipment.
Synegubov condemned “another terrorist act by the Russian Federation”, saying “the enemy strikes a recreational park in the middle of the day, knowing that there is no military infrastructure there at all”.
Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Zelenskyy on Monday to discuss the embattled city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, according to a Vatican statement. He told the Ukrainian president that he had asked Putin for a humanitarian ceasefire during a call with the Russian leader on Friday.
Residents of Oleshky face a worsening humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food and medication, as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops. The Vatican said that Leo had expressed deep concern about conditions in the city and sought a ceasefire to permit aid deliveries and evacuations.
The call to Zelenskyy came two days after Leo, 71, was discharged from a hospital in Rome where he underwent a lung cancer operation on Tuesday.
The Kremlin said on Friday it had explained to Leo what it called “the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation”.

articles.title: Ed Miliband’s clean energy company is being split apart - POLITICO.eu
articles.summary: Ed Miliband’s clean energy company is being split apart  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
LONDON — Labour swept to power with a big, expensive promise: to create a government-owned energy company, hand it billions to invest in British renewables, and watch it grow, eventually, to rival other state-owned energy giants.
Two years on from the foundation of Great British Energy, that isn’t what has happened.
Analysis from POLITICO shows billions of pounds from its budget have been redirected to schemes not included in GBE’s initial remit, stripping away some of the cash earmarked for costly, large-scale renewable energy projects like wind and solar. Those funds are being used instead for very different purposes, like planning new nuclear schemes and reviving Britain’s creaking electricity grid.

articles.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism - BBC
articles.summary: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism  BBCRussia, sensing victory, cheers Trump’s latest shift against Ukraine  The Washington PostTrump has finally abandoned the West for Putin. This is what the UK and Europe must do next  The IndependentAs America turns against Ukraine, Europe stands alone  The EconomistMaybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.
But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?
In some ways, we've been here before.
After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.
The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.
Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.
Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.
Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks applied to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
"It's inexplicable and saddening."
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.
Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.
A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.
A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.
Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.
Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

Key Points

Bank Pictet & Cie Europe AG cut its holdings in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Ltd. (NYSE:TSM - Free Report) by 2.4% during the third quarter, according to the company in its most recent Form 13F filing with the SEC. The firm owned 260,438 shares of the semiconductor company's stock after selling 6,436 shares during the quarter. articles.title: Trade Wars Are No Cure for Europe's Economic Ills: Addressing the Root Causes of Europe's Challenges - 36Kr
articles.summary: Trade Wars Are No Cure for Europe's Economic Ills: Addressing the Root Causes of Europe's Challenges  36Kr
articles.full_text:
If a company has lagged behind in R&D investment for ten consecutive years, suffered high energy costs, and had internal departments refusing to supply each other, yet blames its losses on the lower-priced supplier at its doorstep and imposes extra taxes on that supplier, what kind of operation is this? Is it a strategy? I think it is more like a financial trick.
The so-called "de-risking" of China by the EU today is actually similar. It just erases the decline of European industrial competitiveness from its own balance sheet and records it in the "state subsidy" account of China.
The problem is that the global industrial chain is not an emotional ledger. Tariffs will not create batteries, software and economies of scale out of thin air, they will only pass the bill on to European consumers, the Global South and climate goals.
Therefore, the EU's economic security policy towards China, named "de-risking", is essentially "selective de-globalization + risk transfer". Its effect of reducing risks is limited. Instead, it arbitrages the risk of internal structural failure in Europe into tough political gains against external parties; it internalizes the benefits of globalization and externalizes the costs of globalization.
The final cost will only be jointly borne by European enterprises, European consumers, global trade rules and the green transition.
The EU has miscalculated the ledger with the deficit as the scoreboard
European public opinion repeatedly emphasizes that the daily trade deficit with China is about 10 billion euros, and Germany's deficit with China in the first eight months of the year has expanded to 76 billion euros, which seems very scary... But the bilateral goods deficit is very easy to be misread.
First, it ignores trade in services. According to Chinese statistics, China's trade in services deficit with the EU reached 48.3 billion US dollars in 2025, and the EU is China's largest source of trade in services deficit.
Second, it ignores ownership. A large part of China-EU trade is realized by European enterprises in China, forming a situation where "the surplus belongs to China and the profit goes to the European side".
Third, it ignores added value. For a German-brand car assembled in China, the export statistics are counted under China's name, but a large amount of profits, design, patents and brand income flow back to Europe.
In essence, a country's trade balance is essentially the difference between savings and investment. The EU as a whole still has a goods surplus of about 128 billion to 133 billion euros with the rest of the world.
This does not look like an economy with a collapsing export sector.
The decline in Germany's exports to China and the rise in its imports from China more reflect Germany's problems in industrial competitiveness, energy costs and demand structure, which cannot be explained by China's "subsidies". Germany's exports to China fell by 12.9% year-on-year in the first eight months of the year, imports from China rose by 10.1%, and the trade deficit with China expanded to 76 billion euros. German industrial and commercial circles point out that the uncertainty of trade policy and insufficient enterprise competitiveness are still restricting exports. Although industry associations have slightly raised the full-year export forecast, the problem of lack of sustained momentum for Germany's export recovery remains prominent.
The German federal government has raised its 2026 economic growth forecast from 0.5% to 1.3%, but the recovery is still not solid.
Energy price pressures brought by the Iran conflict, international trade frictions and domestic structural problems may still constrain subsequent growth.
Treating the bilateral deficit as a scoreboard for winning or losing is caused by the "surplus worship". Trade is not a zero-sum war. Deficit does not mean defeat, and surplus does not mean victory.
The real problems lie within Europe: energy costs, labor costs, bureaucratic procedures, and fragmentation of the single market.
A survey by the European Investment Bank shows that 62% of EU enterprises have difficulties in exporting to other member states. What hinders nearly two-thirds of EU enterprises is the fragmented rules, not Chinese subsidies. Yet Brussels is investigating whether Chinese enterprises are distorting competition.
This is ironic. Eliminating these barriers can allow enterprises to invest more assets, and the investment promotion effect generated by tariffs cannot be compared with it.
Europe has too many, too big and too deep problems of its own. According to the survey of the European Investment Bank, 62% of the surveyed EU enterprises said that they have difficulties in exporting to other EU member states. What hinders nearly two-thirds of EU enterprises from doing business in the single market is the fragmented rules, not China's subsidies.
At the same time, Brussels is investigating whether Chinese enterprises are distorting competition. The European Investment Bank estimates that eliminating these barriers can allow enterprises to invest more assets, and the investment promotion effect generated by tariffs cannot be compared with it.
Brussels relies on defensive tools. The countervailing tariffs imposed on Chinese electric vehicles decided in 2024 are intended to offset the impact of subsidies.
But tariffs will only raise the price of competitors' products, cannot reduce the cost of EU enterprises producing batteries, cannot shorten the cycle for EU enterprises to develop new car models, cannot integrate the fragmented capital market, nor can it give birth to world-class European technology enterprises.
Therefore, the EU has miscalculated the ledger with the deficit as the scoreboard.
If statistical illusions are taken as a judgment of competitiveness, the policy will prescribe the wrong prescription, and when the prescription is wrong, tariffs will come into play.
Tariffs cannot cure Europe's problems, they will only raise its own medical bills
The EU imposes countervailing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles with the logic of offsetting the impact of subsidies, but tariffs can only raise the price of competitors' products, cannot reduce the cost of EU enterprises producing batteries, cannot shorten the cycle of developing new car models, cannot integrate the fragmented capital market, nor can it give birth to world-class European technology enterprises.
Some data show that after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, the sales of Chinese hybrid vehicles in Europe increased sharply, but the EU wants to restrict hybrid vehicles again.
This directly exposes the political and economic paradox in Europe: tariffs do not change the total export capacity, but only change the product structure and production location. Data from Rhodium Group and Mercator Institute for China Studies show that China's direct investment in the EU and the UK increased by 67% in 2025 to reach 16.8 billion euros; greenfield investment reached a record 8.9 billion euros. Tariffs mainly change the production location, and Chinese enterprises shift to local production, local factory construction and local employment in Europe.
As a result, the EU falls into policy contradiction: on the one hand, it wants to restrict Chinese goods, on the other hand, it needs the jobs and industrial chain brought by Chinese greenfield investment; on the one hand, it talks about "de-risking", on the other hand, Chinese enterprises are more deeply embedded in Europe.
If restrictions are imposed in the name of security again, Europe may lose investment, technology and jobs.
This is "reverse embedding": the more you want to decouple, the more entangled you become.
Looking at the example of the United States, the paper by economists Mary Amiti, Stephen Redding and David Weinstein confirms that the tariffs imposed by the United States from 2018 to 2019 were almost entirely passed on to the prices of imported goods. They estimate that by the end of 2018, the actual income loss of the United States was about 1.4 billion US dollars per month.
The ones who pay the bill are American importers and consumers, and the Chinese do not pay for it.
If the EU repeats the same mistake, the bill will also fall on European enterprises, downstream industries and ordinary families.
According to media reports, if the EU completely excludes Chinese enterprises and equipment in 18 fields, EU countries will bear at least 840 billion euros in losses. Who will pay for this money? The pockets of European people, Europe's green transition, and Europe's digital competitiveness.
What is more ironic is that while the EU talks about "de-risking", it is deeply mired in energy risks.
After the Ukraine crisis, energy costs remained high, and the military strikes on Iran by the United States and Israel have further intensified global energy tensions. EU natural gas prices rose by 50%, resulting in an additional expenditure of 3 billion euros.
In this case, launching a trade war against China can hardly be called strategic autonomy, but rather strategic self-harm.
Because protectionism can gain buffer time for a short time, but it cannot create core competitiveness. If it is regarded as a substitute for competitiveness, it is costly self-deception.
The Association of German Chambers of Industry and Commerce warned against launching a trade war, pointing out that labor costs, energy prices and bureaucratic procedures are the self-imposed obstacles in Europe.
Tariffs cannot change these facts.
It only provides the most convenient explanation for "why development is stagnant", that is, to attribute its own failure to external factors, and then package it as determination.
According to these arguments, we find that in fact, the inside of Europe is not monolithic.

articles.title: Macron seeks Gulf fuel supplies as conflict disrupts energy markets - سانا
articles.summary: Macron seeks Gulf fuel supplies as conflict disrupts energy markets  سانا
articles.full_text:
Capitals, Oct. 20 (SANA) French President Emmanuel Macron began a tour of four Gulf countries on Monday to seek additional oil and diesel supplies as regional conflict disrupts energy markets, threatens shipping routes and compounds pressure on French households facing rising living costs.
The tour, which runs through Wednesday, includes Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar. According to the French presidency, Paris aims to secure additional fuel supplies while strengthening economic and defense ties and supporting efforts to restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Representatives of French energy companies TotalEnergies and Engie are accompanying Macron, highlighting the focus on translating political discussions into practical arrangements for energy supplies.
In a televised address on Sunday following violence in Paris and other French cities, Macron linked rising living costs and fuel prices to the economic consequences of the conflict in the Gulf. He said France had not participated in the war but was bearing some of its economic repercussions.
Macron said he had taken international initiatives to secure French supplies of fuel and gas and would continue those efforts during his Gulf tour.
Shipping disruption complicates energy security
France’s efforts come amid continuing disruption to energy transportation in the Gulf since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February. Restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which handled around one-fifth of global oil supplies before the war, have increased supply risks and transportation and insurance costs.
Macron’s talks are expected to address not only additional fuel supplies but also maritime security and alternative transportation routes, including potential overland pipeline corridors.
The Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key route for trade between Europe and Asia, is another strategic concern because of its importance to oil and goods shipments.
Francis Perrin, an energy expert at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, told Agence France-Presse that Gulf countries were keen to continue supplying global markets, including France. However, he said firm commitments remained difficult amid regional instability.
Broader economic and defense ties
The tour also aims to expand French business and investment opportunities in the Gulf and strengthen cooperation in defense, security, technology and infrastructure.
In Kuwait, the first stop, Macron met Emir Sheikh Meshal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah to discuss bilateral economic, trade and investment ties, as well as regional and international developments.
The visit also included steps to strengthen defense cooperation and announcements of intentions to support the renewal of Kuwait Airways’ fleet, cooperation in maintenance and training, and projects involving technology and artificial intelligence.
According to the French presidency, Macron’s visit to the United Arab Emirates, scheduled for Monday evening, is expected to focus on defense, security and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. In Bahrain, discussions are expected to address economic and defense ties, while the Qatar leg will focus on expanding the strategic partnership and cooperation on regional and international issues.
Domestic pressures add urgency
The diplomatic initiative comes as France faces domestic economic and political challenges, including difficulties in passing the national budget, rising public debt-servicing costs and declining confidence in government performance.
With France’s next presidential election scheduled for 2027, addressing pressure on household budgets remains a significant political challenge for Macron’s administration.

articles.title: Europe’s energy transition will be won project by project - Enlit World
articles.summary: Europe’s energy transition will be won project by project  Enlit World
articles.full_text:
Dr Frederik Doyé of Siemens Energy on why the energy transition will be built through partnerships, not individual achievements
Europe has the targets, the technology and the expertise to deliver its energy transition. What it lacks, argues Dr Frederik Doyé, senior vice-president and head of Europe at Siemens Energy, is speed and coordination. In this interview, Doyé explains why standardisation could unlock 25% more projects.
What is preventing greater collaboration across Europe's energy sector?
Europe has no shortage of expertise, technology or ambition. What we often struggle with is collaboration and speed. Building grids, integrating renewables, strengthening energy security and supporting industrial competitiveness require many stakeholders to move in the same direction. What often slows progress is not willingness to work together, but the complexity of coordinating investments, regulations and timelines.
A good example is the expansion of Europe's grid infrastructure. Technology exists, the business case is clear, and the need is widely recognised. But projects can still be delayed by permitting processes, fragmented regulation or differing priorities.
As the transition accelerates, our ability to turn ideas into action will become increasingly important.
What needs to change to turn shared ambition into action?
We need to shift the focus to relentless execution. Europe has set clear targets. The real challenge now is how we deliver on them while maintaining affordability, security of supply and industrial competitiveness.
A good example is the Rybnik power plant in Poland. As recently as 2023, around 60% of the country's generating capacity still came from coal. The challenge is not simply to replace that capacity overnight, but to do so in a way that maintains reliability, affordability and energy security. That's why the Rybnik project is so interesting.
Together with PGE, Siemens Energy is replacing coal-fired generation with high-efficiency gas turbine technology, delivering cleaner and more efficient power generation while supporting Poland's broader energy transition. A modern CCGT plant emits around 330g of CO₂ per kWh – approximately three times less than the emissions from coal-fired generation producing the same amount of electricity. We should prioritise solutions that deliver measurable impact now while creating the foundation for a more electrified and lower-carbon energy system in the future.
The energy transition will not be won through targets alone. It will be won project by project, investment by investment, and by making pragmatic choices to move forward.
Interesting read: Poland’s PGE signs deals for 1.2GW of new gas-fired capacity
What does Europe need to do to deliver affordable, competitive, resilient energy by 2030?
Europe needs to reduce complexity, and it needs to do so quickly. Let me give you an eye-opening example: to deliver an offshore grid connection today, manufacturers must navigate around 23,000 pages of technical requirements. Stacked on top of each other, it would be roughly 2.3 metres high, about the height of a room ceiling.
In our company preparing for a single bid can involve up to 150 experts for six months. And these 23,000 pages can look different for every project. Greater standardisation and harmonisation would make an enormous difference. Put simply, we all would spend less time navigating complexity and more time building critical infrastructure.
In fact, it could enable us to deliver 25% more projects across Europe and complete them up to two years faster. That is the kind of practical change that would significantly accelerate the energy transition and help Europe meet its goals.
To deliver an offshore grid connection today, manufacturers must navigate around 23,000 pages of technical requirements.
What do industry, energy providers and infrastructure operators need from one another to accelerate the energy transition and what commitments should each be prepared to make?
What we need is earlier dialogue and closer alignment on execution.
Bornholm Energy Island shows what is possible when countries collaborate around a shared objective. By connecting the Danish and German grids through a 3 GW offshore hub, it creates a more integrated and resilient energy system while making better use of offshore wind resources.
Scaling this type of collaboration across Europe will require earlier engagement, common standards, shared investments, and faster decision-making. If we can get those fundamentals right, delivering our energy and climate objectives becomes much more achievable.
Looking ahead to 2030, which parts of today's energy system will look most different and which assumptions about the transition do you think we are getting wrong?
By 2030, I believe the biggest difference will be the scale of electrification. Electricity demand will keep growing, driven by industry, transport, digitalisation and AI. To succeed, we first need a realistic view of what the transition means and challenge some myths.
One is the idea that the transition is simply about switching to renewables. Renewables are essential, but they are only one piece of the puzzle. The energy transition is a complex transformation of every aspect of the energy system - including low- and zero-emission generation, grid infrastructure and energy efficiency in industrial processes.
Another myth is that rising demand can be met simply by adding more generation capacity. Electricity must also be transported where and when needed. The current grid infrastructure is outdated. By 2040, more than 80 million kilometres of electrical grid will need to be significantly expanded and upgraded to handle renewables and increased demand. And when additional grid capacity is required, the answer is not always to build more transmission lines. In many cases we also need grid stabilisation technologies, digital grid management, and selected equipment updates.
By 2030, I think the conversation will be less about individual technologies and more about how the entire energy system works together. That is the essence of energy realism: turning ambition into practical solutions that are sustainable, reliable, affordable and resilient.
Where can shared investment or new commercial models strengthen both competitiveness and resilience?
Competitiveness and resilience increasingly go hand in hand. The challenge is that many of the investments needed for the energy transition are too large, too interconnected and too strategic for a single company to solve alone.
One of the most compelling examples is again grid infrastructure. Across Europe the energy transition is no longer primarily constrained by generation capacity, but our ability to build, modernise and expand the grid.
This is where new approaches can make a real difference. Beyond financing, we need greater transparency, earlier commitment, and a more balanced sharing of risk across the value chain. Building transformers or HVDC systems requires years of planning, investments and capacity expansion. Suppliers cannot wait until orders are placed before investing in people and manufacturing capacity.
The earlier there is visibility on future demand, the earlier the industry can prepare.
The energy transition will be built through partnerships, not individual achievements.
Beyond efficiency gains, where could AI fundamentally change how energy companies operate, make decisions or manage risk?
Beyond efficiency gains, AI has the potential to fundamentally change how energy companies understand and operate complex systems. AI enables a shift toward continuous decision-making, where assets, grids, supply chains, projects and markets are monitored and optimised - almost in real time.
For example, a minute temperature fluctuation in a transformer or an irregular load cycle might be indistinguishable from "noise" to a human operator, but AI can identify an early warning of equipment stress. This allows operators to intervene early, preventing unplanned outages and ensuring the grid remains reliable.
The same principle applies to power generation, where AI can continuously analyse operating conditions, market signals, and plant performance to ensure efficient operations. Also, as extreme weather events become more frequent, the ability to simulate a crisis is as vital as the ability to respond to one using a large set of data. AI can help operators simulate scenarios, identify vulnerabilities, and strengthen resilience across critical infrastructure.
The real opportunity is not simply automating tasks. It is giving people the insights to make better decisions, earlier and hopefully with greater confidence.
If you had a magic wand, what is one thing you would implement today?
If I had a magic wand, I would make the power of cooperation stronger than the habit of working in silos. The energy transition will be built through partnerships, not individual achievements. The greatest opportunities ahead of us are simply too big for any one company, industry or country. But together, we have everything we need to build a more sustainable, resilient and competitive energy future in Europe.

articles.title: Von der Leyen: EU needs whole puzzle of actions for lowering energy prices - SightLine | U308
articles.summary: Von der Leyen: EU needs whole puzzle of actions for lowering energy prices  SightLine | U308
articles.full_text:
The European Union is rolling out a range of measures against the surge in energy prices, including the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel and extending the temporary state aid framework, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said after the meeting of the European Council. EU leaders are yet to agree on a more comprehensive joint approach to the energy crisis and the tradeoff with carbon pricing. Von der Leyen reiterated the core climate pledges: replacing foreign fossil fuels with affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources and electricity. “We need a whole puzzle of actions,” she pointed out.
The two-day negotiations between EU institutions and member states in Brussels were “long and dense,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged. Speaking alongside European Council President António Costa after their latest summit, she said “there is no silver bullet” for the energy crisis as all countries have different energy mixes.
“We need a whole puzzle of actions,” Von der Leyen pointed out. She noted that since the start of the war in the Middle East, costs for imported fossil fuels have increased by EUR 106 billion, without a single additional molecule of energy. Gas prices have risen 140% since late February, and diesel prices have doubled, Von der Leyen said.
The EU is releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel reserves
The EU is releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel reserves over the next four months. In addition, it is extending in scope and time the temporary state aid framework introduced in February for vulnerable segments of industrial production. Another recent response with short-term effect was to postpone the Methane Regulation, for monitoring emissions for imported oil and gas, until January 2028.
Von der Leyen noted that the European Commission is opening a strategic dialogue on European refineries, mainly to have more of them operating. Such facilities have been cutting capacity and closing down for years. Their profit margins have substantially narrowed or even gone negative in the past few months. It all translates to a greater dependence on fuel imports.
Transition from imported fossil fuels toward nuclear, renewables is essential
The heads of state and government and top EU executives didn’t find much common ground on the longer-term path forward regarding the tradeoff between climate objectives and expensive energy. For the joint statement, they decided to stick with the core climate pledges from the programs of the previous administration such as REPowerEU, Fit for 55 and the European Green Deal.
“As long as Europe depends on imported oil and gas, our prosperity remains exposed to events beyond our control. This is why it is so important to stay the course of the transition that is a transition towards affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources – nuclear and renewables. We must change the way we consume energy, that is replacing foreign fossil fuels by electricity produced in Europe,” Von der Leyen stressed.
The European Commission’s chief said the grid has to be modernized and improved. Von der Leyen highlighted the 80 GW of renewables capacity installed last year. Six times more is waiting for network connection approval, she asserted.
Member states have specific individual circumstances
The current situation urgently requires a coordinated European response of targeted and temporary measures, taking into account the member states’ specific circumstances and safeguarding the single market, the European Council underlined.
The body welcomed the initiatives of the European Commission to bundle energy demand voluntarily, for joint purchases.
The energy transition remains the most effective strategy for achieving Europe’s strategic autonomy, strengthening resilience and structurally lowering energy prices, the European Council said
“Recalling the overarching imperative of reducing the EU’s dependence on volatile fossil fuel markets, the European Council stresses that the energy transition remains the most effective strategy for achieving Europe’s strategic autonomy, strengthening resilience, structurally lowering energy prices, and delivering the clean, abundant and homegrown energy needed to power the economy of the future, by accelerating electrification and deploying renewable and low-carbon energy sources, grids and energy storage, as well as fostering energy efficiency,” the conclusions read.
The European Council said the legislative process on the Market Stability Reserve should be accelerated with a view to moderating price volatility. It is a mechanism within the European Union’s Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) designed to fix imbalances between the supply and demand of carbon emission allowances – EUAs. They can be pulled from the market or released back to ease price movements.
In the context of the ongoing review of the ETS system and to support European industrial competitiveness, the European Council repeated that a well-functioning, transparent and predictable carbon market is necessary to effectively protect against carbon leakage, to reduce the volatility of the carbon price and mitigate its impact on electricity prices, while preserving the essential role of the ETS in the climate and energy transition through a market-based price signal for carbon emissions that drives investment and innovation.
The most urgent matter, though, is an agreement on the 27-member bloc’s 2028-2034 budget, needed by the end of this year.
Eurelectric: Beyond short-term response, any measure must be targeted, temporary
In a response to the European Council’s update on energy and climate policy, Eurelectric – Union of the Electricity Industry commended the short-term measures to ease the pressure on bills.
But it pointed out that any further measure must be targeted and temporary, so it does not disrupt the market signals that drive investment.
“Europe must keep its industry competitive while unlocking the investment needed for affordable, secure and decarbonised energy. Eurelectric’s message to leaders is clear: electrification delivers both,” the statement adds. Mirroring the conclusions from the meeting, the association said the energy transition remains the most effective way to lower prices for good and secure Europe’s energy.
There was little word in the European Council about ETS 2 and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Eurelectric said policymakers need to implement ETS 2 rather than reopen it, backed by strong enabling policies and funding instruments like the Social Climate Fund. Early, targeted use of its revenues would protect vulnerable households and give investors certainty, the statement adds.
SolarPower Europe calls for making electrification affordable
SolarPower Europe highlighted the need to ensure a level playing field between electricity and gas. It argued that fairer energy taxation and a strong, predictable carbon price are essential to making electrification the affordable choice.
“Faster deployment of rooftop solar is a proven and swift solution for lowering citizens’ energy bills, while large-scale batteries can store cheap abundant renewable electricity and push out expensive gas peakers when electricity demand is high. These are practical, easy-to-deploy measures that can help shield European households and businesses before next winter,” Deputy Chief Executive Officer Dries Acke said.

articles.title: Uber wins bid to throw out £200m black cab claims - BBC
articles.summary: Uber wins bid to throw out £200m black cab claims  BBCUber wins bid to throw out UK mass lawsuit by black cab drivers  ReutersUber sees off £340m claim by London cabbies  Yahoo Finance UKJudge throws out case against Uber brought by 13,000 black cab drivers  The IndependentUber dodges £340M cabbie lawsuit after drivers miss legal deadline  The Register
articles.full_text:
Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about £340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms.
The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012.
But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true.
Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity.
About 13,000 drivers were seeking nearly £200m in damages, Reuters reported, while a claim on behalf of Kabbie and Iride, two private hire firms that have since closed, sought about £140m.
The lawsuits were filed in 2024, and Uber argued they fell outside the six-year limit for bringing such claims.
In a written ruling, Mr Justice Birt said the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018.
RGL Management, which ran the cases for the claimants, said it was very disappointed and was considering its options with the legal team.
Since gaining its licence, Uber has taken much of the trade once dominated by black cabs.
The company faces a separate case next week, when it challenges HM Revenue and Customs in a tax dispute worth more than £1bn.

articles.title: Germany Drops Boeing MQ-28 Ghost Bat Rapid Procurement Plan - TWZ
articles.summary: Germany Drops Boeing MQ-28 Ghost Bat Rapid Procurement Plan  TWZGermany Drops Direct MQ-28 Ghost Bat Purchase  MiGFlugGermany changes course on plans to buy MQ-28 drone wingman: Boeing official  Breaking DefenseMQ-28 Ghost Bat: The Loyal Wingman Reshaping Air Combat  The Defense PostGermany Drops Direct MQ-28 Ghost Bat Buy, Forces Three-Way CCA Contest, None Will Meet 2029 Deadline  Defense Express
articles.full_text:
Germany appears to have dropped plans to directly procure the larger, Block 3 version of Boeing’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat collaborative combat aircraft (CCA), leaving doubts over Berlin’s ambitions to field uncrewed combat aircraft alongside its crewed fighters before the end of the decade.
Boeing confirmed to Breaking Defense that Germany’s Ministry of Defense had informed the company it would not proceed with a direct acquisition of the drone, which had previously been lined up. The decision, first reported by Politico, represents a setback for Boeing’s effort to position the Ghost Bat as a candidate for Berlin’s planned CCA capability, something that had seen it announce a partnership with Rheinmetall, the largest arms manufacturer in Germany, earlier this year.
“With Boeing Defense Australia as a partner, we are laying the groundwork to optimally tailor the MQ-28 to the Bundeswehr’s requirements,” said Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall AG, in March of this year. “As a system integrator, we ensure that integration, operation, and further development come from a single source while simultaneously strengthening industrial value creation in the form of an industrial hub in Germany and Europe. We see revenue potential for Rheinmetall in the range of three-digit millions of euros.”
The move does not necessarily mean the MQ-28 is out of contention for Germany’s wider program. Instead, Berlin appears set to move toward a different acquisition approach, with competing designs potentially having an opportunity to demonstrate their capabilities before a selection is made.
A Boeing spokesperson told Breaking Defense the company “stands ready to support” its German customer on the next steps, while referring questions about the decision to the German Ministry of Defense.
The ministry declined to discuss the specific procurement with the same outlet, citing regulations governing public contracting and the need for such matters to be addressed by parliament.
“[As a] matter of principle — and regardless of the specific case in question — we cannot provide information regarding potential procurement projects,” a ministry spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
Germany has set an ambitious goal of fielding CCAs by 2029. These uncrewed aircraft are intended to operate alongside crewed fighters such as the Eurofighter, extending their reach, adding sensors and weapons, and giving air forces additional options for conducting high-risk missions.
However, the reported change in Berlin’s acquisition plans raises questions about whether that deadline remains achievable.
According to Politico, Germany is now looking toward the early 2030s for the capability to arrive, with flight testing expected to begin in 2027. That would suggest the original target was based around the introduction of the MQ-28, which has already undergone extensive testing, rather than a newer design. The reshuffle could now give prospective suppliers additional time to demonstrate their designs.
The reported new timeline suggests that Germany’s CCA effort could be entering a more competitive and potentially longer development phase.
There is also a question about the degree of operational capability that will initially be fielded by the given date. Getting a CCA into meaningful frontline service is a very significant task, calling for integration with crewed fighters, communications systems, mission-planning networks, weapons, and sensors. Then there is also testing, certification, training, and the establishment of supporting infrastructure. For Germany in particular, getting a military drone, let alone an armed one, cleared to operate routinely in commercial airspace has long been an issue.
If Germany acquired the Ghost Bat directly, it would have offered a route to a CCA capability without having to begin an entirely new aircraft development effort.
However, the MQ-28 was always one of a larger field of candidate aircraft.
A week ago, Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions announced the first flight of their U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, a Europeanized version of the XQ-58A Valkyrie. Airbus is simultaneously working on its larger U760 Ravenstorm, intended for service in the early 2030s, and the company has previously pitched a stealthy CCA-like concept known as Wingman.
Other entrants include Anduril, General Atomics partnered with Germany’s INTEC, as well as Lockheed Martin. Meanwhile, Helsing and Hensoldt are pursuing the homegrown CA-1 Europa, very much an MQ-28 lookalike.
Germany may not be looking for a single drone to do everything, a point we have discussed in the past:
“One option might be a split high-low approach that could pair more capable, longer-range systems for deep-strike missions with cheaper, attritable collaborative combat aircraft that can fly alongside crewed fighters. At this point, it should also be noted that CCAs could also give older fourth-generation fighters a new lease on life, boosting their lethality and survivability by extending their sensor reach, adding weapons capacity, and allowing uncrewed aircraft to take on more dangerous tasks.”
At the same time, Germany continues to define its requirements for a capability described in media reports as a Jagdbomberdrohne, or fighter-bomber drone. Berlin has yet to publicly clarify its intended concept of CCA operations, including whether the Luftwaffe envisions an uncrewed wingman operating alongside crewed fighters, a platform capable of carrying out long-range strike missions independently, or a system designed to perform both roles.
There are signs that the strike mission is being prioritized, at least initially, with a reduced emphasis on air-to-air missions. This is essentially the reverse of the U.S. Air Force’s CCA effort.
Since Germany is set to receive the F-35 stealth fighter, there is also an argument that Berlin could place more orders for the crewed jet. This could have the dual role of filling the gap left by the collapse of the pan-European Future Combat Air System (FCAS), specifically its sixth-generation crewed fighter, and the delayed introduction of the first operational CCAs. Germany is also looking forward to receiving more Eurofighters.
Germany’s evolving CCA plans form part of a broader effort by Western air forces to develop uncrewed aircraft capable of working alongside advanced fighters. These systems are intended to expand the number of available platforms, distribute sensors and weapons across a larger force, and potentially take on missions that would otherwise expose pilots and expensive crewed aircraft to greater risk.
Boeing’s Ghost Bat could still have an opportunity to compete, depending on the structure of the eventual acquisition process and the requirements Berlin establishes.
However, with testing reportedly planned from 2027 and operational fielding potentially slipping into the early 2030s, the original 2029 ambition for an operational German CCA appears increasingly uncertain.

articles.title: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots - BBC
articles.summary: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots  BBCWhy are French police so violent? Their job is to protect the state, not the people  The GuardianIs it safe to travel to Paris right now? Latest advice  The TimesMacron abandons France and leaves door open to Le Pen  The TelegraphIs France spinning out of control?  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"
Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.
I'd stopped her and her friend to ask what they thought of what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.
"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."
But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.
Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.
The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.
French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.
French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.
A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections.
The mass looting of what's said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?
Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. President Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.
Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts has lead former French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.
Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's Interior minister Bernard Quintin, warned of the 'TikTokisation' of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liege on "known far left groups".
In France, Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu and his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire," said Nunez. On Tuesday Mr Lecornu spoke of "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".
Previously he'd accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.
It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.
Mélonchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.
What do the students say?
In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians.
"Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.
But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."
France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.
The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.
Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist Prime Minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy."
Mélonchon went on to apparently imply Mr Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances."
France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.
As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's Interior Minister admitted there weren't enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance. Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.
Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration, National Rally Party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.
She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said.
She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness".
She ended her video by reminding French voters they'd have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in 6 months time.
Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed border message and, like US President Trump and Vice US President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday.
Teacher, Mar, complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services," she said.
"Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."
But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system".
That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium.
These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives.
What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask?
Voters increasingly say they are losing faith in traditional or governing political parties to listen to concerns and address them. The young look at climate change, social inequality, impossible housing prices and AI potentially threatening their place in the job market.
According to opinion polls conducted by this year by Pew, 69% of people in France are dissatisfied with democracy. In Spain, it's 68% and in Italy, 62%. (The US is experiencing similar disillusionment with 69% saying they are dissatisfied with how democracy is working.)
So many people I've spoken to in France since Saturday's riots emphasise the importance in making a clear distinction between angry but peaceful protestors, and those intent on wreaking violent havoc.
Politics aside, is what we're now seeing in Europe's protest wave perhaps a powerful cocktail of a bubbling over of frustration, cries for help for the authorities to listen but also, for some, a dark sense there's little left to lose?
