articles.summary: US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy  The GuardianZelensky says intelligence sharing on Russian strikes 'works now' and Ukraine 'thankful' to US  BBCUkraine war latest: Elon Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink, report claims  Sky NewsTrump’s not out to get you, Rubio assures Zelensky  The TelegraphWorld in Brief: Ukraine says US intelligence is back; SpaceX revenues soar  The Economist
articles.full_text:
The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.
He said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives.
The Ukrainian president said: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”
Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy in Norway. The US envoy would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, a US official told Reuters.
The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.
On Tuesday Trump again suggested Zelenskyy was the main obstacle to an agreement. “We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office,” he said.
Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard – an American taken prisoner by Russian forces in occupied Ukraine – in a further sign of his growing public alliance with Moscow.
The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video for the talks. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.
Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”
He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.
Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.
Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, the Wall Street Journal reported.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”
The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.
Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.
The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.
“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.
Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.
US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.
Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.
At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.

articles.title: New EU Plan for Arctic Warily Eyes Influence of Russia, US - Tempo.co English
articles.summary: New EU Plan for Arctic Warily Eyes Influence of Russia, US  Tempo.co English
articles.full_text:
October 21, 2026 | 06:21 am
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The EU on Tuesday presented a new Arctic Strategy that outlines the bloc's priorities in the key region amid challenges such as security threats, climate change and mining.
Russia is building up its military power in the Arctic, and US President Donald Trump has threatened Greenland, saying the Danish territory is needed for American security interests but later signed a deal with Denmark over US military access to the territory. China is also investing in the region and has shipping ambitions there.
The northern parts of Finland and Sweden, along with Greenland are located within the Arctic, meaning part of the region is in the European neighborhood. Iceland and Norway, two other Arctic states, are also involved in the European single market.
'Tectonic plates of geopolitics' colliding in Arctic
"The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned security in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture," she added.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia "has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons" in the Arctic.
"Drone incursions, GPS jamming and the sabotage of undersea cables undermine Arctic security," Kallas continued. Russia's shadow fleet, which is an attempt to circumvent Western sanctions, is active in the Arctic.
On Arctic security, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub in the region "to facilitate information sharing form seabed to space." The bloc also intends to expand European icebreaker capacity and extend its satellite surveillance program in the region.
However, the EU does not intend to compete with NATO in the region, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela told DW. Twenty-three EU countries are members of NATO.
"NATO will remain basically the center of defense and the center of deterrence, but NATO doesn't have a budget, the member state has," Sikela said. "This is first about the proper focus and the proper use of resources of the NATO member states and about better coordination."
EU to boost climate research as Arctic faces ice melting crisis
In regard to the climate, the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. The melting of ice and glaciers in the Arctic pose risks to Europe such as prolonged heatwaves, drought and flooding.
Sikela said, "Collaboration among the Arctic is very difficult," adding, "We're not getting information about the permafrost from the biggest part of the Arctic territory."
Sikela accused Russia of "unprecedented" actions in the Arctic and said the "catastrophic level of drilling and opening new mines" in the region is contributing to its rapid warming. The Arctic is rich in critical minerals and rare earth elements such as nickel.
As part of the EU Arctic Strategy, the bloc intends "to strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring" and launch flagship projects utilizing AI to "anticipate extreme weather and cascading disasters such as coastal flooding."
Although Russia and other non-EU countries such as Norway drill in the Arctic, the EU does not want to expand new drilling in the region. European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said the EU's view "on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground."
Greenland submarine cable route project bypasses US
Regarding economic interests in the Arctic, the bloc may take further steps to bypass the US. The strategy calls for "resilient submarine cable connectivity linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions towards Canada and Japan."
The EU also outlined new plans regarding the residents of the Arctic region. The bloc wants to strengthen dialogue with Indigenous people along with expanding Erasmus+ opportunities for Arctic youth.

articles.title: Lower capital requirements are no shortcut to European competitiveness - CEPR
articles.summary: Lower capital requirements are no shortcut to European competitiveness  CEPR
articles.full_text:
Europe faces substantial investment needs in defence, energy, and innovation. Geopolitical tensions have made these needs more urgent, particularly in defence and energy security (Vissers et al. 2025). Given Europe’s heavy reliance on bank financing, banks are expected to play a key role. The European Commission's report on the competitiveness of Europe’s banking sector highlights regulatory complexity, market fragmentation, and uneven implementation of international standards. This has revived a contentious question: are prudential rules holding European banks back? The debate has gained urgency as the US has renewed efforts to roll back parts of its post-crisis regulatory framework under the second Trump administration (European Commission 2026).
The European Banking Federation argues that EU-specific additions to international standards, supervisory add-ons, and national buffers unnecessarily constrain banks’ lending capacity, and calls for supervisory add-ons and national buffers to be reduced (European Banking Federation 2026). Industry analysis has also argued that regulatory requirements contribute to European banks’ historically lower profitability relative to their US peers (Oliver Wyman 2023, European Banking Federation 2026). Assessing that case requires separating three questions. Are capital requirements generally higher for European banks than for US banks? Do they explain European banks’ historically lower profitability? And would lowering them generate more lending, especially for Europe’s investment priorities? The answers differ in detail, but they do not add up to a case for an across-the-board reduction.
Are European capital requirements higher than US requirements?
Headline capital ratios cannot answer this question. European and US banks calculate risk-weighted assets differently and face different stress tests, leverage constraints, and supervisory requirements. US banks generally face higher risk weights, so the same loan portfolio results in more risk-weighted assets. A lower required capital ratio in the US can therefore still require as much or more capital against that portfolio than a higher European ratio. 
Recent comparisons that take these differences into account do not find that European capital requirements are generally higher. A counterfactual application of current US rules to EU banks finds that the largest EU banks would face stricter requirements under US rules whereas mid-sized ones would face lighter ones. Whether US or EU requirements are more demanding depends on bank size and the interaction of risk weights, add-ons, and leverage constraints (Bank of England 2025, Baudino et al. 2026, Dzezulskis et al. 2026). Current US proposals would narrow rather than overturn this picture: requirements for the largest US banks would fall, but are not expected to fall below those of comparable EU banks (Bank of England 2026, Theurer 2026).
Do capital requirements explain lower European bank profitability?
The profitability claim starts from the way banks are funded. Equity investors generally demand a higher return than depositors and senior creditors, because they bear greater downside risk. More equity can therefore appear to raise funding costs. More equity also lowers leverage and, for a given amount of net income, mechanically lowers measured return on equity because that income is spread over a larger equity base. This helps explain why retur-on-equity figures feature prominently in calls for lower requirements. However, this is not the whole story. Reducing leverage also makes equity less risky, as gains and losses on the bank’s assets translate into smaller fluctuations in returns to shareholders. This lower risk, in turn, reduces the return investors require on equity. In addition, it increases a bank’s capacity to absorb large losses in times of crisis, thereby reducing risks for bondholders and debt funding costs.
More important for the current debate, however, is whether capital requirements explain the gap in return on equity between European and US banks. European banks had substantially lower return on equity than US banks after the Global Crisis. Yet the gap largely disappeared as European interest margins recovered, even though capital requirements were not eased (Figure 1). In 2025, banks in both regions recorded returns on equity of about 10–12% on average (Hoendervangers et al. 2026). This development is a result of different underlying business models: large US banks earn more from fees and trading in deeper capital markets, while large euro area banks depend more on interest income and were therefore more exposed to very low and negative rates (Di Vito et al. 2023). Bank-level evidence finds no indication that lower capital requirements make banks more efficient at generating profits. If anything, higher actual capital ratios tend to be associated with greater efficiency for less well-capitalised banks (Behn and Reghezza 2025). Capital rules affect funding choices and measured returns, but they do not appear to be the main reason European banks historically lagged their US peers.
Figure 1 The US–EU bank return-on-equity gap largely closed as ECB rates rose
    
  
      
  
Source: Hoendervangers et al. (2026).
Would lower capital requirements translate into more lending?
The idea that lower capital requirements automatically free up money for new lending rests on a mistaken image of bank capital. Capital is not cash that banks must set aside; it is a source of funding: the equity-financed part of a bank's balance sheet. A bank can fund the same loans with more equity and less debt. Lowering its capital requirement therefore does not directly release money for new loans.
Lower capital requirements can support lending only when requirements genuinely bind and banks cannot or do not want to raise equity or retain earnings. Whether these conditions hold in practice is therefore crucial. Studies generally find that higher capital requirements have only a modest effect on lending over the longer term (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision 2022). The effect tends to be larger when banks have little spare capital or during periods of financial stress. Looking at the recent post-pandemic increases in capital buffers, Behn et al. (2024) find no statistically significant change in corporate lending by the average euro area bank. Banks with less headroom experienced slower loan growth, but firms partly replaced the affected credit with loans from elsewhere. That the effect is concentrated among banks with little headroom is unsurprising: capital requirements are meant to ensure that additional risk-taking is backed by sufficient capacity to absorb losses. In this case, the effect on particular bank–borrower relationships did not translate into a material reduction in aggregate corporate lending.
Broadly binding capital constraints, however, do not describe Europe's banking sector today. Banks are profitable, hold capital above regulatory minima, and made record payouts to shareholders in 2025 (European Banking Authority 2026, Vissers et al. 2026). Any additional headroom created by lower requirements could support more lending, but it could also enable further payouts or investment in other assets. More headroom does not itself create viable loans: firms must want to borrow, and banks must expect returns that justify the credit risks.
Finally, reducing bank capital can impose broader social costs and also affect lending in periods of market stress. Better-capitalised banks are less likely to fail and draw on public funds, and are better able to continue lending after losses (Soederhuizen et al. 2021, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision 2022). The idea behind releasable buffers is precisely to allow banks to absorb losses in a downturn without cutting credit (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision 2022, Miettinen and Nier 2025).
Would lower capital requirements help finance the EU’s investment priorities?
Even if capital requirements were binding and lowering them increased lending, the additional credit would not necessarily finance the investments at the centre of the EU agenda. Banks are well suited to provide loans backed by collateral and predictable cash flows. Some defence, energy, and infrastructure projects meet those conditions. Early-stage technologies and innovative firms often do not: they have uncertain returns, few tangible assets, and a greater need for investors who share the firms’ risk (Brouwer et al. 2026). Lower capital requirements would not turn these projects into suitable bank debt. Deeper equity markets, well-designed securitisation, and targeted risk-sharing are needed for these investments instead (Vissers et al. 2025).
Simpler rules, not a lower common denominator
Across-the-board capital relief is poorly matched to Europe's competitiveness problems. European requirements are not uniformly higher than US requirements, and capital rules do not mainly explain the past gap in return on equity. Lower capital requirements are also unlikely to unlock additional lending, especially the risk-bearing finance needed for innovative and strategic projects.
There is nevertheless substantial scope for reform. Simplifying the interaction between different capital requirements could make buffers easier to use in periods of stress, while more consistent implementation and streamlined reporting would lower the cost of operating across borders (European Commission 2026, European Central Bank 2026, Miettinen and Nier 2025). Reform also needs to go beyond prudential rules: completing the Banking Union would help banks achieve cross-border scale, while the Savings and Investments Union could expand risk-bearing finance for projects that do not fit bank balance sheets. The relevant distinction is between simplifying the framework and weakening it. The Eurosystem has argued that unnecessary complexity can be reduced while preserving the banking system's overa

articles.title: Beyond the riots: Europe's migration and social cohesion challenge - Counterview
articles.summary: Beyond the riots: Europe's migration and social cohesion challenge  Counterview
articles.full_text:
Europe’s experience since 2015 offers a useful case study in the difficult trade-offs between humanitarian obligations, border governance and social cohesion. Germany’s decision under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel to admit large numbers of asylum seekers was presented as a humanitarian response. Some critics warned at the time that the scale and speed of arrivals could strain housing, schools, welfare systems and public confidence. Several years later, the debate is more nuanced than either the open-borders or restrictionist camps suggest.
Germany and other Western European countries have advanced economies and strong institutions. Many new arrivals, however, came with limited formal education, weak language skills and qualifications that were not easily recognised in Europe. This is common among displaced populations and does not by itself indicate unwillingness to integrate. Integration outcomes depend heavily on language training, affordable housing, labour-market access, recognition of qualifications and early asylum processing. Where these supports have been underfunded or slow, integration has lagged. Outcomes vary widely by country, origin, age and time since arrival.
Within the Schengen area, movement across borders means that arrivals in one country can affect others. This has made asylum a European-wide governance challenge rather than a purely national one. The EU’s response has been uneven, and responsibility-sharing remains contested. Many migrants and refugees have integrated into labour markets and communities; others remain in precarious conditions. Generalisations about entire groups are not supported by the evidence.
Demographic change is real but driven by multiple factors: ageing populations, low fertility, intra-EU mobility and migration. Migration can help offset labour shortages, but it can also create short-term pressures where arrival is rapid and integration capacity is limited. The policy question is not whether migration should occur, but how to manage it in a way that is orderly, lawful and publicly legitimate.
Recent protests and unrest in France, Belgium, Italy and the UK have complex and multi-causal origins, including labour-market conditions, policing, housing and social exclusion. Immigration is part of the public debate, but it is not accurate to attribute such incidents solely to refugee arrivals. Similarly, the UK’s external processing arrangement with Rwanda has been legally contested and operationally limited; it illustrates the difficulty of “externalising” asylum obligations rather than a simple policy failure.
European governments now face a difficult political balance: maintaining humanitarian and legal commitments while restoring public confidence in border control and integration. This requires better asylum processing, fair responsibility-sharing, adequate funding for integration, and honest public communication about costs and benefits. It also requires avoiding language that stigmatises migrants or treats cultural diversity as inherently threatening.
The debate should not be framed as a choice between open borders and exclusion. A credible policy can be both humane and orderly. Europe’s challenge is to design a migration and asylum system that upholds legal obligations, supports integration and retains public trust. That is a difficult but necessary task, and it is not served by exaggeration in either direction.
---
*Trustee, Nandini Voice For The Deprived, Chennai

articles.title: Europe's Power Demand Returns to Growth - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: Europe's Power Demand Returns to Growth  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.full_text:
Despite weakening industrial activity and high energy costs, European electricity demand is bucking years of flailing power consumption.
Rising electrification rates and the data center boom are the key drivers of this new trend in Europe's power demand, which is set to gather momentum in the coming years amid the EU's energy transition and the global AI boom.
Europe's electricity demand growth is nowhere near the pace seen in the United States and China in recent years, but it's a marked shift nevertheless, after years of declining or stagnant power consumption.
The Age of Electricity, as the International Energy Agency (IEA) put it in its 2026 Electricity report, is gathering pace even in Europe. The renewed growth in power demand is changing long-term assumptions and forecasts about power markets, and posing new challenges for policymakers and grid operators.
Return to Growth
Electricity demand in the European Union inched up by 0.5% in 2025, below the 2024 increase of 1.9%, according to data by clean energy think tank Ember.
Then, over the past year, top European economies, including Germany, Italy, and Spain, saw power demand growth in most months, according to data by BloombergNEF. Portugal and the Nordic countries are also seeing steep growth in electricity consumption this year, with all figures adjusted for weather impacts, per BNEF's analysis. Related: Copper Needs $332 Billion in New Mines to Avoid Deficit, BloombergNEF Says
The weather impacts, especially the several extreme heat waves in Europe this past summer, are prompting a growing number of households to consider air conditioning. Last year, 23% of European households had AC at home, according to data by the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Electrification for heating is also gathering momentum now amid soaring natural gas prices in the wake of the war in Iran.
Not to mention record electric vehicle (EV) sales amid record-high fuel prices and a record number of newly available affordable models.
In a landmark achievement, battery electric vehicles (BEVs) outsold gasoline-fueled cars for the first time over a full quarter in the second quarter of 2026, Transport & Environment, a European advocacy group for clean transport and energy, said in a report earlier this month.
Home-charged electric cars cost 50% less to run than gasoline and diesel cars as of the middle of September 2026, according to Transport & Environment's analysis.
Official automotive figures also confirmed the findings-the fuel crisis is shifting buyer preferences to EVs.
BEV sales in Europe, including the UK, Switzerland, and Norway, surged by 52.2% in August from a year earlier as record-high gasoline and diesel prices prompted drivers to flock to battery and hybrid vehicles, according to data by the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association, ACEA.
The growth in Europe's power demand is not a short-term trend, analysts say. It's the beginning of a shift toward rising demand - even at lower rates than in the U.S. - due to the electrification drive and the data center boom.
"A growing share of energy use is through electricity, and even if energy demand goes down, electricity demand is going up," Per Lekander, CEO of London-based hedge fund Clean Energy Transition, told Bloomberg.
"It's unstoppable and it's going to go on for decades."
Europe's data center capacity is also growing and the UK and Germany are set to remain the largest markets through 2035, with 7.7 gigawatts (GW) and 5.1 GW, respectively, BNEF said in an outlook on Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA) last month.
Spain and Finland will jump up the rankings as currently early-stage projects start to come online toward the end of the decade, while ongoing constraints in Ireland and the Netherlands will see them both drop out of the top five largest markets, according to BNEF.
In total, the power capacity of European data centers is expected to double to top 30 GW by 2032, and further grow to 39 GW by 2035, BNEF reckons.
Grid Constraints
As power demand grows, the electricity supply is increasingly leaning into renewable energy as Europe and the UK stick with emission-reduction goals to become carbon-neutral by 2050. In the EU, solar power generation overtook coal generation in 2024. Last year, wind and solar combined exceeded fossil fuels in power generation for the first time, after drawing level in 2024, according to Ember's data.
This rise of renewable energy is placing a strain on Europe's grids, which need a lot of investment to be able to incorporate soaring solar and wind output. That's a pressing problem for the EU and the UK, with trillions of dollars needed to make the grids of the past suitable for future power generation and demand.
At the end of last year, the European Commission unveiled the European Grids Package to fast-track grid upgrades and renewable project permits, and boost cross-border cooperation.
The European Commission has estimated that $2.25 trillion (2 trillion euros) to $2.6 trillion (2.3 trillion euros) is required to meet grid needs until 2050, a review of the EU's electricity grids by the European Court of Auditors showed last year.
By the end of the decade, the EU would need $656 billion (584 billion euros) in investments as 40% of its distribution grids are over 40 years old, and cross-border transmission capacity is set to double by 2030, the Commission says.
By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

articles.title: EU Tightens 'European-Made' Rules in IAA, Threatening South Korea - 조선일보
articles.summary: EU Tightens 'European-Made' Rules in IAA, Threatening South Korea  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Germany and France, Europe’s two leading automotive powers, are pushing to tighten the criteria for recognizing “European-made” products in the European Union’s proposed Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), a form of trade barrier, deepening concerns in the global automotive industry. While the move targets Chinese eco-friendly vehicles, South Korea—a country with a free trade agreement (FTA) with the EU—could also face unintended repercussions if the regulations become overly stringent.
The IAA includes non-tariff barriers aimed at expanding EU production of eco-friendly vehicles and secondary batteries. For eco-friendly vehicles, the draft law stipulates preferential treatment, such as subsidies, if the final assembly occurs in an EU member state and at least 70% of components (excluding batteries) are sourced from Europe.
According to industry sources on October 20, Germany and France agreed on October 16 to narrow the scope of “European-made” components to the EU’s 27 member states and select European countries like the UK. The March draft of the IAA had initially proposed extending European status to parts produced in FTA partner countries, including South Korea. However, recent factors such as France’s fiscal challenges and Volkswagen’s historic restructuring have reportedly influenced the two nations to advocate for stricter origin criteria.
Hyundai Motor and Kia sold approximately 200,000 electric vehicles in Europe from January to September this year, with 37% produced locally, including in Turkey. However, Turkey is not an EU member state, raising concerns that its components might not qualify as “European-made” under the final IAA. Additionally, Hyundai and Kia’s factories in EU member states like the Czech Republic and Slovakia rely heavily on Korean-sourced parts, meaning they may need to increase local procurement to meet the 70% threshold. This could necessitate costly expansions of European component facilities and negatively impact South Korean auto parts exporters.
In response, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources launched a public-private task force on October 15 to address the IAA. It has also urged the EU to treat South Korea, as an FTA partner, equally with EU member states. The ministry argues that South Korean companies have significantly contributed to the EU’s economy and supply chains through investments in local production facilities, making discriminatory treatment unjustified.

articles.title: Chinese imports force Germany to change strategy ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - Business - Fakti.bg
articles.summary: Chinese imports force Germany to change strategy ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - Business  Fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
Germany is facing a major change in its economic relations with China. While for decades German companies profited from exporting cars, machinery and industrial equipment to the Chinese market, today increasing imports from China and increasing competition are questioning the advantages of this model. This is shown by data and analyses published by Deutsche Welle.
In the first five months of 2026, German exports to China fell by 14.5% year-on-year to 29.6 billion euros. Over the same period, imports from China grew by 6.2% to 72.4 billion euros. Thus, Germany's trade deficit with the Asian country reached 42.8 billion euros compared to 33.5 billion euros a year earlier.
Two of the traditionally strong German industries - automotive and mechanical engineering - were most seriously affected. Exports of cars and automotive parts to China decreased by 26.1%, and those of machinery - by 17.5% during the period under review. Already in 2025, the value of German automotive exports to the Chinese market fell by 33% to 13.6 billion euros.
The reasons lie both in the weakened domestic demand in China and in the growing competitiveness of local manufacturers. Chinese companies are now offering their own technology solutions in sectors where German industry has long held leading positions.
At the same time, the German economy remains heavily dependent on Chinese supplies. In the first five months of 2026, approximately 81.8% of notebook computers, 66.3% of smartphones and 64.1% of lithium-ion batteries imported into Germany were of Chinese origin, measured by value. For photovoltaic cells, the share reaches 86.1%.
The change in trade relations is intensifying the debate about the need for a new German strategy towards Beijing. The main challenge for Berlin is to maintain access for German companies to the Chinese market while simultaneously reducing dependence on strategic supplies and protecting the competitiveness of its own industry.
At the European level, concerns about the trade imbalance are also growing. In 2025, the European Union imported 559.4 billion euros worth of Chinese goods, while its exports to China amounted to 199.6 billion euros. This means a deficit of almost 360 billion euros.
The European Commission sees Chinese competition as a serious challenge for industry, especially in electric vehicles, batteries and renewable energy technologies. China, for its part, disputes accusations of unfair competition and insists on maintaining open trade relations.
For Germany, the situation is particularly complicated, as China remains an important trading partner and production base for German companies. Therefore, the change in strategy does not necessarily mean limiting economic ties, but seeking a new balance between trade benefits, industrial competitiveness and security of supply.

articles.title: Britain is not at war with Russia, says minister - UK Defence Journal
articles.summary: Britain is not at war with Russia, says minister  UK Defence Journal
articles.full_text:
Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe and is constantly probing and testing Britain, but the two countries are not at war and Britain does not seek confrontation, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Richard Holden, the Conservative member for Basildon and Billericay, asked whether the description of Russia’s actions as being short of war by officials in the department reflected a political or a military analysis.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. Russia is constantly probing and testing us, including through military posturing.
“We are not at war with Russia, nor do we seek confrontation but with an increase in threats the UK will increase its warfighting readiness and meet its NATO commitments. The government is also acting against threats on our own shores.
“Russia should be in no doubt that we are ready to defend every inch of NATO territory and will not be deterred in our unwavering support for Ukraine.”
Officials have been more forthcoming about Russian activity in other published material. The government’s Arctic Policy Framework, published last week, named the threat to critical national infrastructure from Russia’s Main Directorate for Deep-Sea Research, said Britain has exposed its operations and demonstrated a capability to respond, and described the shadow fleet as a systemic risk. The Lunna House Agreement with Norway commits the two navies to protecting undersea cables and pipelines in the North Atlantic.

articles.title: ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers | Datacentres - UK - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers | Datacentres - UK  The GuardianGoogle Cloud says services are recovering after outage hit banks, businesses, and courts  BBCRevolut hit by major outage  The TelegraphGoogle Cloud's London zones takes a nap, multiple services disrupted  The RegisterGoogle cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
It happened again. A power outage hit a datacentre in London, and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app.
The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients.
The outages – which have affected, according to the website Downdetector, Royal Mail, Revolut, HSBC and Lloyds bank, among others, are so far not of the scale of a similar cascade this time last year, when Amazon Web Services went down for nearly half a day.
That outage hit a far bigger node – Amazon’s us-east-1 – in a concentrated region of Virginia, which hosts the greatest density of datacentres on Earth. It saw cascading effects worldwide: taking out the Roblox game and Signal messaging app and causing smart mattresses worldwide to suddenly heat overnight and toast their occupants.
It lasted about 15 hours.
Today’s problems appeared to peak at about 9am, and by mid-afternoon were somewhat resolved, according to reports submitted to Downdetector. Because Google Cloud stores data and runs operations for a number of businesses, there were widespread knock-on effects – mostly confined to UK businesses.
Revolut confirmed “a service disruption affecting multiple services”, but added that “all our customers’ money and data are safe”. Lloyd’s said its app was working, but “we understand some [people] are having issues with certain online services this morning”.
HM Courts and Tribunal Service, which handles remote video hearings in courts across England and Wales, said it was “aware of an issue affecting Cloud Video Platform,” and was “working with our technology partners to restore service”.
Like the far bigger outage last year, it’s a reminder of the physical infrastructure – often creaking and provisional – that underpins most of the virtual world.
Michał “rysiek” Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said the outages were a reminder of the increasing concentration of the internet and vital services on the infrastructure of a few key companies – the “hyperscalers”.
“Hyperscalers have become too big to not fail. But worse, they’ve become so deeply ingrained into the very fabric of our digital lives that switching away from them seems unimaginable.”
The Guardian has reported that British police keep vital data on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, despite being apparently aware that this exposes sensitive information to US government insiders, hostile foreign actors and outages like today’s. Up to 60% of the UK government’s infrastructure is hosted on cloud services – mostly Amazon, Microsoft and Google.
“I am sure Google’s engineers are doing everything they can to mitigate them, but it is unreasonable to have a handful of gigantic companies whose outages time and again cause public institutions or large swaths of the digital economy to stop working en masse,” said Woźniak.
Last year’s AWS outage was later revealed to have been caused not by a power outage, but by a bug in automation software. A separate outage was caused by an AI tool that Amazon had adopted after laying off tens of thousands of staff last autumn.
Woźniak pointed at an announcement this year from Google indicating that it was also embracing AI, with 75% of all new code “now AI-generated and approved by engineers”.
“One can only wonder how that affects the reliability and quality of Google’s services. Multiple large outages at another hyperscaler, AWS, a year ago have been linked to internal AI tooling.”
A Google spokesperson said: “We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event. Services have been restored. We will update our public status dashboard with an analysis of the incident.”

articles.title: After the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le Pen | Paul Taylor - The Guardian
articles.summary: After the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le Pen | Paul Taylor  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
There is only one clear winner so far from France’s chaos: Marine Le Pen. The violence and rioting that engulfed towns and cities across the country over the weekend, six months before a pivotal presidential election, is a godsend for the hard-right, Eurosceptical, anti-immigration candidate. As buildings burned, shops were looted and police attacked, the rioting largely drowned out peaceful mass protests over the dilapidated state of schools , fuel prices and the cost of living.
Across France and the rest of Europe, people are in shock at scenes of arson and pillage in city centres, the wrecking of symbols of the republic such as the 19th-century town hall in peaceful provincial Limoges and the bust of Marianne in Marseille’s city hall, and the looting of more than 2,000 shops.
Though France has a long revolutionary tradition, this was not the work of egalitarian insurgents or working-class warriors, but nihilist, anarchist “black bloc” gangs, with opportunist looters and rioters along for the ride.
Emmanuel Macron is a lame-duck president who has no practical answers to a crisis that is ruining his legacy. Macron expressed his “anger and shame” at the violence and the damage to France’s global image in a Sunday-night broadcast to the nation, but he is so widely loathed, including by many who voted for him in two presidential elections, that his pleas for order and dialogue were largely ignored.
Le Pen, in contrast, issued a solemn video message, looking presidential as she sat at a desk with the national tricolor (but no EU flag) and bookshelves as her backdrop. Millions of suffering French people were angry about “anarchic immigration” and the cost of living without smashing or burning anything, she said. They would have an opportunity in six months’ time to vote for a different path of “restored authority and security”.
Macron’s minority government is trapped in a vicious circle. France’s debt and deficit squeeze leaves him no spare cash left to buy off protesters. A decade of his centre-right presidency has failed to reform a bloated public sector or improve public services. The country has a youth crisis, characterised by anxiety over an economically uncertain future and amplified by social media, as well as a geopolitical crisis with Russia’s war on Ukraine spreading into a covert war against Europe.
Foreign critics of progressive European social policies are fanning the flames with incendiary commentaries. Donald Trump gloated on social media that “France is burning!”. Blaming the situation on immigration, he urged the French to “close your borders and take control before it is too late”. Vladimir Putin’s close aide Kirill Dmitriev described events in France as “the suicidal fall of Europe” and also ascribed it in part to chaotic migration.
The convergence of crises leaves little room for manoeuvre for a French government struggling to push even a mildly cost-cutting budget through a hung parliament. For now, it is trying to extinguish the violence with selective curfews. One presidential hopeful, Dominique de Villepin, who was a Gaullist prime minister 20 years ago, has even compared the situation to the eve of the fall of the ancien regime in 1788, a year before the outbreak of the Revolution, when France was stricken by drought, failed harvests and empty state coffers.
That may be a far-fetched parallel. But the sense of a fraying state, a discredited political class and an ossified bureaucracy unable to staunch a slow-motion financial crisis that might suddenly accelerate makes the stakes in next year’s presidential race ever-higher.
Until last weekend’s explosion, the school and student protests, unrest over the cost of living and outrage at instances of police brutality against young demonstrators all seemed to be lifting the campaign of radical-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who in some opinion polls had overtaken the centrist Edouard Philippe for second place. However, Mélenchon’s apparent refusal to clearly condemn the looting or attacks on the police, and his belittling of the violence as “disorder that is part of the events in the life of a society”, may cost him support among more moderate leftwing voters who have boosted Socialist candidate Raphaël Glucksmann in the latest opinion surveys.
Investors are taking fright at the violence and political instability, selling French stocks and bonds. A deepening market run on France could yet change the dynamics of the presidential campaign, rallying a frightened middle-class behind a seasoned centrist candidate seen as a safe pair of hands in a crisis.
A month after the May 1968 student-worker uprising that rocked Charles de Gaulle’s staid regime, voters scared by the spectre of civil unrest delivered a landslide victory to his party, which promised to restore order and authority. A year later, De Gaulle was disavowed in a referendum on regional devolution and resigned.
Historical comparisons are risky. Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy. Economics is Le Pen’s weak spot.
So far, neither Philippe nor other centrist and centre-right rivals have set the campaign alight. But six months is a long time in French politics.
- Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

articles.title: Driving law changes to ban common practice impacting thousands of cars across the UK - GB News
articles.summary: Driving law changes to ban common practice impacting thousands of cars across the UK  GB NewsSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Labour has announced sweeping new rules to crack down on the scourge of second-hand car dealers taking advantage of motorists.
The Government will crack down on vehicle dealers winding back odometers to hide a vehicle's true mileage.
The process is often referred to as "clocking" and will now result in dealers facing "tougher action" for misleading motorists.
Selling a clocked car is already illegal, but the Government will go one step further and will add winding an odometer to the list of banned practices.
It said that this would make it easier for enforcers to crack down on unscrupulous sellers, protect buyers and support honest businesses.
Data from carVertical suggests that 2.7 per cent of checked UK cars had signs of clocked mileage between September 2024 and August 2025.
The average odometer rollback on affected UK cars was roughly 35,000 miles, making the UK one of Europe's hotspots for clocking.
Research found that electric cars were now the most clocked fuel type in Britain at three per cent, compared to diesel (2.8 per cent), petrol (2.5 per cent), and hybrids (two per cent).
The Government said it was banning the practice of car clocking as part of the Prime Minister's "series of everyday fixes".
It comes alongside similar measures to stop unfair airline charges, tackle subscription traps and rip-off school uniform costs.
Minister for Consumer Action, Kate Dearden, said: "Nobody works hard for their money just to be deceived by a dodgy trader, and this is exactly the kind of everyday rip-off this government is going after.
"By making it easier to take action against car clocking, we are protecting consumers' hard-earned money and supporting businesses that play by the rules."
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
Car clocking will now be added to the banned practices list (Schedule 20) under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024.
It will be placed alongside claiming to be a signatory to a code of conduct when the trader is not, falsely stating that a product will only be available for a limited time to elicit an immediate decision, and establishing, operating or promoting a pyramid promotional scheme.
The Government states that the clocking change will apply to businesses selling cars to consumers.
Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at The AA, said: "Buying a car is a major purchase, so making it easier to crack down on those trying to deceive consumers is welcome."
Alongside the new rules regarding car clocking, the Government confirmed that it would be introducing new parking rules to protect motorists from "rip-off" operators.
Through the new Private Parking Code of Practice, drivers will be given five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends.
Operators risk being blocked from accessing the DVLA's vehicle records if they fail to adhere to the rules, which would make it much harder for them to issue fines.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes, while going after the deliberate scams that rip drivers off."

articles.title: Advantech and DEKRA target industrial cybersecurity gaps as EU Cyber Resilience Act implementation advances - Industrial Cyber
articles.summary: Advantech and DEKRA target industrial cybersecurity gaps as EU Cyber Resilience Act implementation advances  Industrial Cyber
articles.full_text:
As the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) enters its implementation phase, cybersecurity compliance is becoming an increasingly important requirement for industrial equipment and Edge AI products entering global markets. Advantech announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with DEKRA. By combining the expertise in industrial computing, cybersecurity testing, and global certification, the partnership aims to help end customers and system integrators address cybersecurity requirements from the product design stage, accelerate compliance with EU CRA requirements and international standards such as IEC 62443, reduce compliance risks, and shorten time to market.
Miller Chang, President of Advantech’s Embedded Sector, said at the MOU signing ceremony: “As Edge AI continues to advance rapidly, compliance is evolving from a certification procedure before product launch into a critical consideration that customers need to address from the early stages of product design. By combining Advantech’s expertise in industrial computing and Edge AI with DEKRA’s global certification expertise, we aim to enable customers to identify regulatory requirements earlier, reduce compliance risks, and shorten time to market, enabling trusted Edge AI innovations to reach global markets more efficiently.”
Stan Zurkiewicz, CEO of DEKRA, said: “Digital trust is essential for industrial innovation to succeed in global markets. As AI and connected technologies become integral to manufacturing, energy and transportation, companies need verifiable evidence of safety and cybersecurity to build confidence in new technologies. Our collaboration with Advantech combines its industry experience with DEKRA’s third-party independent testing and certification expertise. DEKRA’s role is to provide independent assurance, helping companies navigate evolving international requirements and build trust in new technologies.”
Advantech and DEKRA are bringing testing and compliance expertise into the early stages of product development, helping customers identify regulatory and technical requirements across different markets from the design stage, plan certification pathways in advance, and identify and address potential cybersecurity gaps throughout development. The collaboration covers technical and feasibility assessments, documentation review, certification preparation, vulnerability management, and secure development support. This approach helps customers reduce the time and costs associated with late-stage design changes while establishing a comprehensive compliance process from product concept and design development to testing, certification, and market deployment.
As an initial outcome of the collaboration, Advantech’s AFE-E630 industrial edge system has passed an independent assessment by DEKRA and received an Attestation of Conformity (AoC). Designed for commercial and industrial energy storage management applications, the AFE-E630 security functions meet IEC 62443-4-2 SL2 requirements within the assessed scope. This provides a verified basis for product cybersecurity in these applications and a reference for customers’ subsequent product integration and system-level compliance assessments.
Beyond established industrial applications, Advantech and DEKRA plan to extend the collaboration to emerging technology areas, including AI-enabled industrial systems, semiconductor manufacturing, robotics, drones, other mission-critical unmanned systems, as well as energy site equipment and transportation management, to accelerate global market access.
As Edge AI becomes increasingly integrated with physical devices, product safety, functional safety, and cybersecurity requirements are becoming increasingly interconnected. Advantech and DEKRA will combine Advantech’s edge computing platforms and industry application knowledge with DEKRA’s expertise in cybersecurity, testing, and functional safety to enhance the safety and trustworthiness of next-generation intelligent devices.
As cybersecurity regulations continue to evolve across global markets, Advantech and DEKRA will continue to combine their respective expertise to help customers address compliance requirements across different markets more efficiently, reduce risks associated with global deployment, and accelerate time to market, further supporting the expansion of Edge AI and intelligent industrial applications into global markets.

“The EU has the world’s largest network of free trade agreements. We invest years in getting these deals right, ensuring they are balanced, ambitious and offer benefits for both us and our partners,” Commission trade spokesperson Olof Gill told POLITICO. “Once negotiations are done, they are done.”
Gill was asked whether Brussels would return to the table if the deal could not get the backing it needs in the Australian Senate. He said the Commission aims to propose the agreement for signature and conclusion in early 2027.

articles.title: Germany’s Rearmament: From Fiscal Power to Strategic Capacity - https://debuglies.com
articles.summary: Germany’s Rearmament: From Fiscal Power to Strategic Capacity  https://debuglies.com
articles.full_text:
Scope: Germany’s defence expansion and its industrial, economic and European consequences, assessed against the official record available on 20 October 2026, with an outlook to 2031.
Executive Summary / BLUF
Germany has created the financing conditions for a substantial military expansion; its strategic and economic returns depend on procurement execution, industrial capacity and technological diffusion.
The 2027 proposal combines €109.7 billion in the defence ministry’s regular budget with €29.9 billion from the Bundeswehr special fund, compared with €108.2 billion combined in 2026. These are budget allocations and proposals, not measures of delivered readiness. Deutscher Bundestag
The constitutional exemption removes qualifying security expenditure above a defined threshold from the domestic borrowing calculation; European fiscal constraints remain a separate consideration. Einzelnorm
Industrial expansion is visible, but corporate revenue and order books cannot establish military availability or economy-wide productivity gains.
The principal policy requirement is to connect sustained demand with competitive procurement, production investment, deployable capability and European interoperability.
The decisive uncertainty is whether Germany can achieve that conversion before rising operating and financing costs narrow its room for adjustment.
Germany Can Borrow for Rearmament. It Still Has to Deliver It.
Germany’s rearmament will strengthen European security only if procurement buys complete military capabilities rather than a growing inventory of obligations. The federal draft budget for 2027 provides the immediate test: Berlin is expanding defence commitments while manufacturers finance production, infrastructure authorities prepare facilities and the armed forces absorb new equipment. These processes run on different clocks, but the bill ultimately reaches the same taxpayer. The Bundeswehr’s special fund approaches its endpoint, European fiscal flexibility has conditions, and industrial expansion creates operating costs that survive the acquisition cycle. Germany’s decisive choice is therefore how to allocate its enlarged financial capacity: towards contracts that demonstrate expenditure, or towards deployable formations whose personnel, software, maintenance and supply arrangements are available together.
The budget measures effort; the financing plan reveals exposure
The federal draft provides €139.6 billion for defence in 2027, comprising €109.7 billion in the regular budget and €29.9 billion from the Bundeswehr special fund, against €108.2 billion in 2026. The increase establishes purchasing capacity. It does not establish how much additional military capability will enter service, because acquisition expenditure, industrial production and operational acceptance occur at different times.
The Finanzplan des Bundes 2026 bis 2030 exposes a second distinction. Gross federal borrowing is planned at €487.9 billion in 2027 and €760.8 billion in 2030, but refinancing accounts for €361.6 billion and €583.8 billion respectively. These are not annual deficits. They show why financing conditions reach the budget through both new borrowing and the rollover of existing obligations. Defence commitments become harder to sustain if the government preserves acquisition contracts by squeezing the support expenditure that makes their deliveries useful.
Corporate accounts reveal the same timing problem inside industry. In the first half of 2026, Rheinmetall reported operating free cash flow of minus €1.616 billion, HENSOLDT adjusted free cash flow of minus €136 million and Leonardo free operating cash flow of minus €249 million. Their definitions and business perimeters differ, so the figures cannot be aggregated. They nevertheless demonstrate that production expansion can consume cash even when demand is strong.
BAE Systems reported a different outcome: group-defined free cash flow of £1.791 billion in the first half of 2026, supported by material customer advances. That contrast identifies a procurement mechanism rather than a ranking of companies. Payment schedules influence who can finance inventories, equipment and subcontractors before final acceptance. An order book supplies commercial visibility; cash supplies the means to execute it.
A stronger prime contractor does not finance every supplier
The procurement question raised by HENSOLDT’s first-half 2026 results is whether government advances reach the production constraint. The company attributed improved cash flow partly to advance payments while noting the concentration of deliveries and acceptances later in the year. Earlier payment can accelerate output, but only if it supports the materials, specialist labour and equipment required along the supply chain.
Germany’s Bundeswehrbeschaffungsbeschleunigungsgesetz permits advance payments under specified conditions, including the prospect of accelerating industrial capacity expansion. The instrument should therefore be judged by additional productive capacity and accepted deliveries. Government takes exposure before receiving the capability; its protection depends on verified milestones, oversight of subcontractor payments and enforceable arrangements for publicly financed tooling and unfinished work.
The Bundesrechnungshof’s May 2025 audit of additive manufacturing illustrates what happens when expenditure and usable capacity become detached. It recorded the purchase of 33 printers for €3.4 million while the central database contained design information for only ten spare parts in July 2024. The finding is historical, not an October 2026 inventory. Its relevance lies in the mechanism: machinery without the necessary information and manufacturing rights cannot reliably perform the task used to justify its purchase.
The same acceptance discipline should govern the Bundeswehr’s wider expansion. A delivered platform requires trained personnel, functioning communications, repair arrangements and suitable facilities. If procurement, infrastructure and service commands each report success against separate targets, the government can meet its expenditure plans while leaving the operational package incomplete.
Faster permission does not mean earlier production
The Council’s final approval of the defence simplification package on 9 October 2026 removes part of the administrative obstacle to expansion. The adopted permitting text provides an ordinary decision period of 42 working days, with exceptional extensions bringing the total to no more than 102 working days. But the principal clock starts after notification that an application is complete.
That qualification determines what the reform can accomplish. Under the permitting regulation, relevant assessments prepared by the applicant belong in the completeness process; construction, utility connections, installation and production qualification remain distinct delivery stages. A manufacturer can obtain a faster administrative decision and still miss the date on which qualified output was expected. Measuring permits alone would reward the reform’s intermediate result while overlooking its industrial purpose.
The European Commission’s selection of 46 additional strategic raw-material projects on 9 October 2026 presents a similar distinction. The projects include extraction, processing, recycling and integrated operations. Their designation advances the supply policy, but it does not establish that qualified material is available to defence manufacturers. A diversified mine supply remains vulnerable if the material depends on the same processing facility or cannot yet meet a downstream customer’s specification.
AGILE, adopted by the Council on 12 October 2026, should be evaluated further along the same chain. The €115 million programme aims to help smaller companies move from prototypes towards operational capability, with a first call expected at the beginning of 2027. Its institutional value will depend on whether testing leads to acceptance and funded procurement. Faster grants cannot resolve a missing military customer or an absent purchasing route.
Fiscal flexibility can encourage the wrong contracts
Germany’s European fiscal settlement allows qualifying military-equipment deliveries after 2028 to benefit from flexibility when the equipment was contracted before the end of 2028, within the applicable cap. The provision accommodates long production cycles. It also creates an incentive to sign before the window closes, even where requirements, delivery schedules or support costs remain insufficiently settled.
The Bundeswehrbeschaffungsbeschleunigungsgesetz adds another timing distinction by permitting procurement procedures to begin, under specified conditions, before financing is secured. Starting earlier can remove delay from the process. It cannot turn a prospective purchase into an affordable commitment. Parliamentary oversight must preserve the difference between a procedure opened, a contract funded and a capability supported throughout its operating life.
Rheinmetall’s August 2026 results supply a reminder that an expanding defence market does not validate every programme. The company attributed an approximately €300 million reduction in its current-year sales outlook to the F126 cancellation decision. That figure is a reported revenue effect, not a measure of total public losses or replacement costs. It demonstrates why termination and restructuring remain necessary instruments during rearmament.
The F126 case also defines the proper comparison. Government needs the remaining cost of completion, the credibility of technical recovery, available replacements and the consequences for suppliers and operational bridging. Preserving past expenditure is not itself a reason to incur further expenditure. Equally, cancellation does not produce a capability: the replacement route must be executable.
Europe needs common operating rules before common declarations
The NATO Hague

articles.title: Prices of bread, milk and meat to rise on back of heatwaves and war, ECB warns - Irish Independent
articles.summary: Prices of bread, milk and meat to rise on back of heatwaves and war, ECB warns  Irish Independent
articles.full_text:
The cost of bread, pasta, dairy and meat is set to climb over the next year as extreme weather and high energy prices bite, the European Central Bank (ECB) says.
In a blog post on Tuesday, ECB economists said some forecasts see food inflation rising to almost 4pc by next autumn as the effects of war and drought filter through.
Annual food inflation in the eurozone picked up to 1.3pc in September and 0.8pc in Ireland, the first rise since the start of the Iran war.
Food inflation is set to keep climbing throughout the next year, the ECB said, and is not likely to ease until at least next autumn.
While food prices have been rising all year, the rate of inflation had been slowing thanks to good 2025 harvests and low prices for staples like coffee, tea, cocoa and sugar.
For instance, In Ireland, the average price of butter, cheddar cheese, full-fat milk and brown bread had fallen in the year to September, according to the Central Statistics Office.
But droughts caused by a series of heatwaves this summer and the ongoing US war in Iran, which has throttled oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, are set to feed through to people’s shopping baskets this winter and beyond, the ECB said.
The price shock will be far less severe than it was after the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the ECB said. But food prices in the 21-member eurozone are already 30pc higher than they were at the end of 2021.
“It is too early to assume that food inflation has lost its bite,” the ECB said on Tuesday. “With pipeline pressures building and the summer’s weather yet to feed through, food prices look set to pick up again.”
Overall eurozone inflation was 3.8pc in September, the same rate as in Ireland, due mainly to surging energy prices.
Food prices tend to rise more slowly than overall prices.
But energy costs are now trickling down through higher fertiliser, animal feed, packaging and transport costs, the ECB says, as well as the rising cost of heating greenhouses.
That is most likely to affect wheat, maize and barley, putting pressure on prices of bread, pasta and other baked goods.
High grain prices mean it is costlier to feed animals, which will impact dairy and meat prices.
Fresh vegetables, potatoes and other greenhouse-grown products are also set to become more expensive due to higher heating costs.
“Higher energy costs and weather-related pressures are working their way through to the food chain, with the factors that previously kept food inflation low fading away,” the ECB said.

articles.title: Europe’s €800bn defence borrowing hides a reality of every country buying on its own - EUobserver
articles.summary: Europe’s €800bn defence borrowing hides a reality of every country buying on its own  EUobserver
articles.full_text:
Europe is supposed to be financing its defence together. It barely is.
Of the €800bn announced under ReArm Europe in March 2025, €650bn is not common money. It is an estimate of the extra room governments get under the national escape clause to spend up to 1.5 percent of GDP more on defence for four years.
Each country still pays for that spending itself.
The room is also temporary: EU Commission simulations suggest that maintaining higher defence spending after 2028 could require additional annual fiscal adjustment of 0.25 to 0.4 percentage points of GDP from 2029.
The other €150bn is SAFE, and it is loans, not grants.
The EU borrows and lends the money on, and each country repays its share. Grants are small: €1.5bn from the European Defence Industry Programme for 2025-2027, plus the European Defence Fund for joint research.
Not every country has used these tools, as Table 1 shows. The Netherlands and Sweden have used neither. Like Germany, which has taken only the clause, they can borrow at least as cheaply as the EU, so SAFE gets them nothing.
France has taken SAFE but not the clause, to protect the credibility of its budget plans.
Table 1. Who uses SAFE and the national escape clause
Source: Council of the EU, European Commission. Data as of 17 October 2026. * Hungary: allocated €16.2bn, now requesting €5.4bn; still pending. ** Italy: the Commission backed its request on 8 October 2026; the Council has yet to decide.
Where SAFE does matter is on the eastern flank. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia can borrow the equivalent of five to eight percent of their GDP, and Poland almost five percent.
Graph 1. SAFE loans as a share of GDP, by country (%)
Source: Council of the EU, European Commission, Eurostat. SAFE loans only, as a share of 2025 GDP. Amounts approved by the Council, except Italy and Hungary (* revised requests of €8bn and €5.4bn, September 2026). Data as of 17 October 2026.
That leaves private money.
The European Investment Bank and the European Investment Fund are trying to bring in private investors, partly by removing the reputational stigma of financing defence.
But defence is almost a monopsony: the state is nearly the only buyer. Without a clear flow of public orders, private investment will be hard to come by.
So Europe barely borrows together. And it buys alone.
