articles.title: Why Macron is visiting the UAE amid protests in France - Operativ Məlumat Mərkəzi
articles.summary: Why Macron is visiting the UAE amid protests in France  Operativ Məlumat Mərkəzi
articles.full_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron held talks with United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi on Monday, October 19. The meeting covered energy supplies, investment and other issues, as rising fuel prices and violent protests over the cost of living increase pressure on the French government. AnewZ reports that Macron’s Gulf tour began in Kuwait and will continue in Bahrain and Qatar.
According to the Abu Dhabi Media Office, the talks covered maritime security, global energy supplies, investment and artificial intelligence.
Macron’s visit began after violent unrest in France over the weekend. More than 2,500 people were arrested after protests over the cost of living escalated into clashes, looting and property damage, Le Monde reported.
Alongside restoring public order, Macron faces another urgent task: securing energy supplies as the war between the United States and Iran disrupts traffic along one of the world’s most important oil shipping routes.
Energy prices and household finances in France
Official figures from France’s National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE) show that petroleum product prices in mainland France rose 36.8% in September from a year earlier.
Overall energy prices climbed 21.4% year on year, while consumer prices excluding energy rose by just 1.6%. The figures show that energy costs are increasing faster than prices in other parts of the economy.
According to INSEE, annual inflation in France rose to 3.1% in September, from 0.9% in February.
The change in petroleum product prices has been particularly pronounced: after falling 2% year on year in February, prices rose 18.9% in March and 36.8% in September.
Eurostat figures show that in 2025, 28.8% of France’s population lived in households unable to cover an unexpected expense without borrowing money or receiving financial assistance. Meanwhile, 41.1% of respondents said they faced at least some difficulty making ends meet.
Although these figures predate the latest unrest, they highlight the financial pressure on households facing rising energy costs.
Energy agenda on Macron’s Gulf tour
According to the French Presidential Administration, one of the aims of the visit is to secure agreements for additional oil and diesel supplies. Macron left for Kuwait just hours after addressing the nation following the weekend’s violence.
He acknowledged failures in maintaining security and condemned the destruction. However, he said the Gulf tour was necessary to protect France’s energy supplies.
Executives from French energy companies TotalEnergies and Engie are also taking part in the visit, underscoring its commercial significance.
France is seeking additional supplies and alternative shipping routes. Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz are increasing uncertainty in global energy markets. Even if Macron secures new agreements, however, prices for French consumers are not expected to fall immediately. Fuel prices will depend on the volumes secured, delivery terms and the overall state of international energy markets.
The Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, is one of the world’s most strategically important sea routes and a key passage for exports of Gulf oil and gas.
The US-Iran war, which began in February, has severely disrupted vessel traffic through the strait. Attacks on energy facilities and ships elsewhere in the region have also heightened concerns about supplies.
France and the United Kingdom have proposed an international maritime mission to help reopen the strait, including by clearing mines, after Washington and Tehran reach a political agreement. No such agreement has been reached so far.
Macron’s talks with Gulf leaders therefore have two main aims: securing energy shipments and finding alternative ways to transport supplies while existing routes are disrupted. These efforts form part of a broader international push to stabilise energy markets.
G7 countries agreed in early October on a plan to release up to 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves to ease supply pressures, Le Monde reported. A joint release from reserves is separate from the supply agreements Macron is seeking on his Gulf tour.
UAE and France expand trade and technology cooperation
At Monday’s meeting, Macron and Sheikh Mohamed discussed expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy, advanced technologies and artificial intelligence.
According to the Abu Dhabi Media Office, the leaders also reviewed regional developments and efforts to limit their impact on maritime security and global energy supplies. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening coordination on regional security and stability.
The talks took place amid rapidly expanding economic ties between France and the UAE. Trade in goods between the two countries reached 10.8 billion euros in 2025, according to figures from the French Treasury, up from 8.5 billion euros in 2024 and 7.4 billion euros in 2023. Trade therefore increased by about 27% in one year and 46% over two years.
The UAE was France’s largest export market in the Gulf region in 2025, according to the French Treasury. However, the agency noted that the UAE has historically accounted for a limited share of France’s direct energy imports.
For that reason, Macron’s visit is not limited to buying oil from the Emirates. Its aims also include strengthening regional energy security, investment and infrastructure links, as well as deepening cooperation with companies active in global energy markets.
New energy and artificial intelligence agreements signed
The commercial agenda of the diplomatic visit expanded on Tuesday, October 20, when Macron and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan attended the UAE-France Business Dialogue at Qasr Al Watan.
According to the Abu Dhabi Media Office, French and Emirati companies signed contracts and memorandums of understanding in energy, artificial intelligence and advanced technology.
In the energy sector, ADNOC Gas and Schneider Electric signed a memorandum of understanding to explore new technologies and operational improvements. ADNOC Refining and Technip Energies signed two agreements, including one on a project to increase refining capacity and another related to sustainable aviation fuel.
In the technology sector, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, G42 and Analog each signed a separate memorandum of understanding with AMI Labs. The discussions also covered France’s Campus AI initiative, involving investment partners from the UAE and other countries.
The agreements show that Macron’s Gulf tour covers long-term industrial and technological cooperation in addition to urgent energy needs.
Can the visit ease pressure in France?
Macron’s Gulf tour comes at a politically sensitive time: France is facing some of its most serious civil unrest in recent years, while the next presidential election is due in 2027.
Securing additional energy supplies and alternative shipping routes remains a near-term priority. But the outcome will depend largely on factors beyond Paris’s control, particularly the US-Iran conflict and restrictions on vessel traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
New energy and technology agreements have already been reached during the visit, strengthening France’s economic partnerships with Gulf countries. For French households struggling with higher fuel prices, the key question is whether Macron can turn diplomatic agreements into more reliable energy supplies and, ultimately, lower prices.

articles.title: EU enlargement could strengthen economic ties between Moldova and Romania - logos-pres.md
articles.summary: EU enlargement could strengthen economic ties between Moldova and Romania  logos-pres.md
articles.full_text:
This is evidenced by an analysis published on 13 October 2026 by the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS). The document identifies opportunities for Moldova linked to closer ties with Romania and participation in European supply chains.
However, the study notes that capitalising on these opportunities requires reforms, infrastructure and investment, which must be initiated before EU accession.
Moldova’s potential
The authors see Moldova’s potential in the development of the production of electronic components, wiring harnesses and automotive parts, as well as in strengthening the agri-food sector and business services. These activities could benefit from bringing production closer to European markets, a process known as ‘near-sourcing’.
Moldova already has a Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Agreement with the EU, but administrative barriers, regulatory differences and logistical costs are holding back investment. The EU accession process could reduce these obstacles by introducing more predictable rules on competition, public procurement, customs clearance and investment protection.
For Romanian companies, links with Moldovan manufacturers and cross-border projects could open up opportunities in the areas of supply, transport and services. Rail, road, energy and digital connections are vital for the movement of goods and for reducing costs.
The European Commission has already mentioned support through the ‘Connecting Europe’ facility to improve transport links between Moldova and Romania. This is an example of pre-accession cooperation, which in itself does not determine the scale of future economic benefits.
CEPS warns that attracting manufacturing solely on the basis of low costs may trap candidate countries in low-value-added activities. The development of local suppliers, staff training and technology transfer are essential for boosting productivity. Labour mobility has mixed consequences. EU firms may be able to recruit specialists, whilst Moldova risks losing skilled personnel.
The authors recommend the circulation of skills, including the return of specialists, investment by the diaspora and the transfer of knowledge, accompanied by economic opportunities in the country of origin.
Every country has its own path to the European Union
The experience of previous enlargements serves as a guide, but does not guarantee the same results. IMF research shows that in 2019, per capita income in countries that were EU members before 2004 was approximately 10 per cent higher than it would have been in a scenario without enlargement that year. This percentage reflects the aggregate level estimated 15 years on, rather than the annual growth rate or the increase for each country.
Romania joined the EU in 2007, and this figure does not represent an estimate of its benefits from future enlargement. The studies compiled by CEPS cover different time periods and make different assumptions, and do not contain individual forecasts for Romania or Moldova.
Existing financial support should be considered separately from these scenarios. The Reform and Growth Fund for Moldova covers the period 2025–2027 and amounts to approximately €1.9 billion. According to the Council of the EU, it comprises up to €385 million in grants and €1.5 billion in concessional loans on favourable terms and at favourable interest rates. Disbursements are conditional upon the implementation of reforms under a programme agreed with the EU, and the amount does not represent funds that have already been spent in the economy.
On 5 October 2026, the European Commission announced an additional payment to Moldova of €157 million following a positive assessment of the implementation of 18 reforms. These reforms relate, amongst other things, to private sector development, economic governance, the labour market, energy and good governance. The payment is part of an already established mechanism, distinct from the CEPS recommendations on accelerated economic integration.
The analysis is signed by Tinatina Akhvlediani, Pierre-Alexandre Ballan and Andrea Renda, and forms part of the ‘Enlargement without Illusions’ project, supported by the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Enlargement and the Situation in Eastern Europe. The views expressed by the authors are their own and do not represent the official position of the EU.
However, the experts’ views are of undoubted interest to Moldova as a candidate country. They recommend accelerating investment in infrastructure, industry and skills prior to EU accession, with phased access to the single market linked to verifiable reforms.
For businesses and employees, the benefits will depend on the investments made, labour productivity and the local economy’s ability to sustain value-added activities.

articles.title: HIPTHER launches dedicated AI and cybersecurity summit in Prague - European Gaming
articles.summary: HIPTHER launches dedicated AI and cybersecurity summit in Prague  European Gaming
articles.full_text:
The new standalone day extends HIPTHER’s Prague event to three days and introduces a €40,000 startup competition.
With high-risk obligations under the EU AI Act due to apply from December 2027, AI governance and security are moving up the agenda for companies in regulated industries, including iGaming. HIPTHER announced on 20 October 2026 that it will launch the HIPTHER AI Summit 2027 in Prague on 25 March 2027, adding a third day to its Prague programme and hosting its first startup competition.
A third day added to HIPTHER’s Prague programme
HIPTHER has run its Prague summit annually since 2017, broadening the programme from iGaming to include fintech, AI, compliance, and cybersecurity.
The new summit takes place at OREA Hotel Andels Praha immediately after the HIPTHER Prague Summit on 23–24 March 2027. Where previous editions included AI within a wider multi-track agenda, the new day focuses entirely on artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. For operators and suppliers attending both, the format adds a dedicated programme on AI governance, fraud detection, and security.
The one-day event will run across two conference stages and a separate HIPTHER Academy room.
- The main stage will host keynotes, panels, and technical sessions on generative AI, large language models, AI agents, enterprise adoption, threat intelligence, fraud detection, Zero Trust architecture, and EU AI Act governance.
- The second stage will host the HIPTHER AI & Cybersecurity Startup Challenge, while the Academy room will run four practitioner-led courses, with separate enrolment and limited places.
€40,000 startup competition: Structure and timeline
The Startup Challenge is the first competition of its kind in HIPTHER’s event history. Applications open on 16 November 2026 and close on 31 January 2027. A jury will select a Top 20 longlist in February 2027, followed by online semi-finals in March. Eight finalists will pitch on stage in Prague on 25 March 2027, and the winner will receive a €40,000 investment.
The competition is open to early-stage AI and cybersecurity companies from Europe and beyond. HIPTHER says the full investment structure, eligibility criteria, evaluation framework, and rules will be published when applications open.
Programme scope and regulatory context
The summit’s focus on AI governance coincides with a shift in the EU AI Act timeline. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, which entered into force on 27 July 2026, moved obligations for stand-alone high-risk AI systems under Annex III from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 — less than nine months after the Prague summit. Transparency obligations under Article 50 have applied since 2 August 2026.
Zoltan Tündik, co-founder and head of business at HIPTHER, said:
‘The conversation around artificial intelligence has evolved rapidly from theoretical potential to real-world deployment, governance, and security.’
Tündik added that the summit was built to connect builders, security experts, and innovators directly with investors and industry leaders.
About HIPTHER
HIPTHER is a media and events organisation incorporated in Estonia, operating across iGaming, fintech, AI, blockchain, cybersecurity, and compliance. It runs boutique conferences across Europe, including the HIPTHER Prague Summit, HIPTHER Warsaw Summit, and the HIPTHER Baltics series, with an event portfolio spanning CEE, the Baltics, D-A-CH, and beyond.

articles.title: Ukraine Introduces Nine New Asbestos Safety Standards for Reconstruction - Oj - Odessa Journal
articles.summary: Ukraine Introduces Nine New Asbestos Safety Standards for Reconstruction - Oj  Odessa Journal
articles.full_text:
Ukraine's Ministry of Economy and Environment, together with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Ukraine and with the support of the Government of Japan, has presented nine new national standards for detecting asbestos and monitoring its presence.
The new standards establish procedures for collecting samples, testing construction materials and demolition debris for asbestos, and measuring the concentration of asbestos fibres in the air. Their implementation brings Ukraine closer to European requirements, particularly Directive 2009/148/EC on the protection of workers from risks related to asbestos exposure at work.
According to UNDP, as of September 2025, approximately 17.2 million tonnes of demolition debris had been generated by damage to and destruction of residential buildings in areas under Ukrainian government control. Some of this waste may contain asbestos.
The standards will help identify asbestos in a timely manner, safely separate contaminated materials and determine which materials can be recycled and reused.
To support the practical implementation of the standards, a handbook titled Asbestos: Monitoring Content in Accordance with European and International Standards has been prepared.
More than 300 specialists from government authorities, environmental monitoring bodies, occupational health and safety organisations, local communities, research institutions and the private sector have already received training based on the handbook.
This initiative forms part of broader cooperation between the Ministry and UNDP, including work related to Chapter 27, "Environment and Climate Change", of Ukraine's EU accession negotiations.
"The introduction of international standards, the provision of modern equipment to laboratories and the training of specialists are of direct practical importance for protecting human health and the environment. At the same time, our task is not only to identify and safely remove hazardous materials, but also to make maximum use of the resource potential of demolition waste. Combining proper laboratory monitoring, modern methodologies and practical recycling mechanisms will reduce the burden on the environment and waste disposal sites, enable more efficient use of resources and integrate circular economy principles into Ukraine's reconstruction process," said Olena Kramarenko, Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment of Ukraine.
The standards and handbook were developed by the NGO Living Planet and the Institute for Environmental Recovery and Development of Ukraine, which has served as the secretariat of Technical Committee for Standardisation TC 82, "Environmental Protection", since 2026.
With financial support from the Government of Japan, UNDP is helping Ukraine develop a safe demolition waste management system by improving national standards, strengthening laboratory infrastructure and training specialists. One of the outcomes of this cooperation has been the opening of Ukraine's first national asbestos detection laboratory, equipped with transmission electron microscopy technology.

articles.title: Germany to make funding available for industrial decarbonisation and carbon capture - oEnergetice.cz
articles.summary: Germany to make funding available for industrial decarbonisation and carbon capture  oEnergetice.cz
articles.full_text:
Germany is launching a new funding round to help industrial companies develop technologies that reduce greenhouse gas emissions and support the transition to climate neutrality. The programme will fund research and innovative solutions in these areas.
The Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) announced the latest call on its website under the Federal Funding Programme for Industry and Climate Protection (BIK). Companies can submit project proposals by 6 December 2026. The proposed funding is subject to the availability of budgetary resources.
Eligible activities include industrial research, experimental development and feasibility studies focused on specific greenhouse gas emissions reduction projects. Companies can apply for support to develop new or significantly improved products, test innovative production processes, manufacture prototypes and carry out pilot projects. Projects involving the exploration, development and monitoring of CO₂ storage sites may also be eligible under the new programme.
The programme covers two main areas: industrial decarbonisation and carbon management. The first focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions from industrial processes, while the second supports technologies for capturing and using carbon dioxide or storing it underground.
These opportunities are particularly relevant to sectors where process emissions are difficult to eliminate through electrification or energy efficiency alone. According to the BMWE, the programme has already supported projects across a wide range of sectors, including cement and construction materials, chemicals, steelmaking, glassmaking, paper and pulp, waste processing, food production and mechanical engineering.
The portfolio also includes the direct capture of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and technologies that incorporate captured CO₂ into products.
In the previous funding selection round in 2025, 38 industrial projects were selected to receive approximately 476 million euros in public funding, including contributions from regional governments. The ministry expects these projects to attract approximately 1.05 billion euros in private investment.
Supported initiatives include waste recycling, carbon capture, waste heat utilisation, low-carbon concrete and technologies designed to generate negative emissions. The new funding round comes as German industry faces the challenge of reducing emissions while maintaining its international competitiveness.

articles.summary: Ukrainian Drone Strike Sparks Fire at Oil Transit Hub in Tambov Region  The Moscow TimesOil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg  BBCSt Petersburg endures biggest Ukrainian drone attack  Financial TimesUkraine launches over 1,000 drones at Russia, setting oil facilities ablaze  Al JazeeraFirst War Death Reported in Putin's Hometown After Kyiv's Record Drone Assault  Kyiv Post
articles.full_text:
A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at an oil pipeline hub in central Russia’s Tambov region, authorities said early Tuesday.
Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov confirmed that a blaze had broken out at “one of the enterprises in the Michurinsky district” without identifying the facility. He said no one was hurt in the attack.
The district is home to the state pipeline operator Transneft’s Nikolskoye linear production and dispatch station, a key transit node along the Druzhba oil pipeline, which supplies countries in Eastern and Central Europe.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of the fire to identify the targeted facility in the Tambov region as the Nikolskoye station.
Nikolskoye receives, stores and transports crude oil and refined products, including diesel, gasoline, jet fuel and fuel oil. Its pumping capacity is estimated at 300,000 metric tons per day.
The attack comes after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an agreement with the Kremlin to increase Russian diesel exports to global markets in order to offset energy prices driven by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, three people were killed after a Russian drone struck near a highway that connects Kyiv to the Black Sea port of Odesa in the south, according to the prosecutor’s office.
More than 32,700 families in the Odesa region were left without electricity after an overnight Russian attack on three facilities of Ukraine’s largest private energy company DTEK.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it struck four commercial cargo vessels, one of them bound for Odesa, alongside logistics hubs in the Volyn and Khmelnytskyi regions.
Reuters contributed reporting.

articles.summary: At least five killed and thousands evacuated as Storm Adam batters eastern Spain  EuronewsDrivers rescued from rising floodwaters in Costa Blanca motorway tunnel after deadly Storm Adam dumps 70mm of rain in less than an hour  Olive Press News SpainResidents winched from rooftops as torrential rain hits eastern Spain  ReutersTwo killed and thousands evacuated after Storm Adam batters Spanish coast with heavy rain  The IndependentFour dead as torrential rai...
articles.full_text:
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will visit Valencia on Tuesday to see the impact of the storm.
The DANA weather system Storm Adam began to ease on Tuesday after leaving at least five people dead and causing severe flooding in eastern Spain. In the Valencia region, the Civil Guard evacuated more than 2,100 people and rescued almost 500 since the start of the storm, according to the latest update released by the force.
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will visit Valencia on Tuesday to see the impact of the storm. The visit is scheduled for around 12:30, after which the premier is expected to speak to the media.
The Valencian town of Oliva is among the worst affected, with rainfall of 600 litres per square metre in 24 hours. Around 600 people received assistance at the municipal centre and 400 spent the night there from Monday into Tuesday.
Emergency operations have deployed more than 1,300 Civil Guard officers, with helicopters, boats and specialised units for water and mountain rescues.
Although the rain has lost intensity in the Valencia region and stay-at-home orders have been lifted, the State Meteorological Agency (Aemet) is keeping warnings in place in nine provinces on Tuesday, with particular attention to the rainfall forecast in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands.
Historic rainfall of more than 700 litres per square metre
Aemet has described the rainfall as exceptional in the Valencian counties of La Safor and Marina Alta, where some of the largest rain accumulations in recent decades have been recorded.
In L'Atzúvia in Alicante province, 713 litres per square metre fell during the episode, while Pego registered 632 litres in 36 hours, 430 of them in just six hours.
The intensity of the rain caused the rivers Girona and Vernisa and the Beniopa ravine to overflow, as well as flooding in numerous municipalities.
According to RTVE, the episode ranks among the most intense ever recorded in Spain, behind the historic rainfall in Oliva in 1987, when 817 litres per square metre fell in 24 hours, and the rains from the 2024 DANA, with 772 litres in Turís.
In Oliva, the streets were left completely under water and many residents had to take refuge on the upper floors of their homes or climb onto rooftops as they waited for rescue teams to arrive.
The severe flooding forced the Generalitat Valenciana to temporarily lock down 145 municipalities in Valencia and Alicante on Monday. Authorities urged people to avoid travelling and seek shelter on upper floors because of the risk of further surges. The restrictions were gradually lifted in the afternoon.
The storm also caused road closures, transport disruption and the suspension of classes for more than 100,000 pupils.
Balearic Islands and Catalonia also suffered
The storm has also hit the Balearic Islands, particularly Ibiza and Formentera, where the rain has caused torrents to burst their banks, flooding and numerous road closures.
In Ibiza, more than 130 incidents have been recorded, including fallen trees and problems accessing the airport, where standing water forced some operations to be suspended.
In Formentera, up to 203 litres per square metre were recorded in 24 hours. The UME has also been deployed on the islands to help with emergency work and remove the accumulated water. The Balearic government suspended classes in Mallorca, Ibiza and Formentera on Monday, a precautionary measure affecting around 160,000 students.
In Catalonia, the heaviest rain shifted towards the provinces of Barcelona, Girona and Tarragona on Monday afternoon, after Aemet issued warnings for heavy and persistent rainfall.
Mobile phone alerts, key to the response to the storm
The Generalitat Valenciana has used the ES-Alert system to send warnings directly to the mobile phones of citizens in areas threatened by the rain.
The first messages were sent over the weekend, before the storm reached maximum intensity, and were repeated on Monday as the flood risk increased.
The alerts urged people to avoid travelling, stay away from rivers and ravines and seek shelter on higher ground or on the upper floors of buildings.
The rollout of these warnings marks a difference from the handling of the October 2024 DANA, when delays in emergency communications were the subject of fierce criticism.

articles.title: FPT, France’s Quandela sign MoU to advance quantum technology cooperation - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: FPT, France’s Quandela sign MoU to advance quantum technology cooperation  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| Delegates at the signing ceremony on October 19 evening in Hà Nội. — Photo quandela.com | 
HÀ NỘI — Vietnamese technology group FPT and French quantum computing company Quandela have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to cooperate in quantum technology research, computing access and workforce development, marking a step forward in scientific and technological cooperation between the two countries.
The agreement was signed on October 19 at the French Embassy in Việt Nam as part of efforts to translate the strategic cooperation commitments between Việt Nam and France into concrete initiatives in advanced science and technology.
Éléonore Caroit, France's minister delegate for Francophonie, International Partnerships and French Nationals Abroad, welcomed the first French business delegation specialising in quantum technology to visit Việt Nam.
The event was organised by Business France, the French national agency responsible for internationalising the French economy, supporting French companies' exports and attracting foreign investment to France. It also provided an opportunity to connect businesses and partners from the two countries.
Caroit said the agreement between FPT and Quandela was a concrete step in implementing high-level commitments reaffirmed by Party General Secretary and State President Tô Lâm and French President Emmanuel Macron during their recent high-level meeting in Paris.
She said the MoU opened up opportunities for broader cooperation in applied research, access to quantum computing resources and, in particular, the training of highly skilled personnel, reflecting the spirit of the comprehensive strategic partnership between France and Việt Nam.
Nguyễn Xuân Phong, FPT's chief technology officer and chief AI transformation officer, said the two countries shared scientific potential and strong ambitions for development.
Combining Quandela's expertise in photonic quantum computing with FPT's engineering capabilities and global research network would help advance research, workforce training and the development of practical applications, he said.
Phong described the agreement as more than a partnership between two companies, saying it also served as a bridge connecting science with industry and ideas with the shared future of the two countries.
Marine Xech-Gaspa, Quandela's director of Institutional Affairs and Public Policy, said the cooperation was significant because it represented the first concrete realisation of the ambitions shared by the two countries in this field.
She expressed hope that the initial step would pave the way for specific joint projects in research, access to cloud-based quantum computing and the development of applications for industry and cybersecurity.
Under the MoU, Quandela will provide FPT with access to its cloud-based quantum computing platform to support testing and development activities in Vietnam.
The two companies also agreed to coordinate applied research in quantum computing, quantum communications, information security and quantum algorithms, as well as explore potential industrial use cases.
The cooperation framework is non-commercial and will run for two years. It is intended to lay the groundwork for training activities, knowledge transfer, expert exchanges and collaboration with universities and research institutes.
The agreement brings together Quandela's quantum computing capabilities and FPT's technical expertise and research network, with cooperation expected to focus on research, access to computing resources and the development of applications. — BIZHUB/VNS

articles.title: Spain versus Morocco: this is how the military forces of both countries stand in 2026 - Euronews
articles.summary: Spain versus Morocco: this is how the military forces of both countries stand in 2026  Euronews
articles.full_text:
Spain spends three times more on defence than Morocco and leads in air and naval power, but Rabat has more troops and rockets. US-backed rearmament boosts its strength and narrows the gap.
The Royal Moroccan Air Force's first F-16 Block 72 carried out its maiden flight on 6 October in Greenville, South Carolina, Lockheed Martin has announced. It is now progressing through pre-delivery testing after some delays in the programme. It is the most eye-catching piece of a rearmament drive that is being closely watched in Spain.
But, with the numbers in front of us, how much military weight does Morocco actually have today compared with Spain? Spain is still far ahead in terms of budget and easily dominates at sea. Rabat, by contrast, has more soldiers and rocket artillery, a capability the Spanish Army has lacked for the past 15 years.
Defence spending: more than six to one
The clearest gap is in spending. According to the latest report by Sipri (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute), Spain allocated around 34.287 billion euros to Defence in 2025, 50% more than the previous year, pushing its military burden up to 2.1% of GDP. Morocco came to 5.645 billion euros, up from 4.920 billion in 2024. That increase keeps it as Africa's second-biggest military spender, behind Algeria, which spent 22.660 billion.
Behind that lies the size of each economy. Morocco closed 2025 with a GDP of 138.668 billion euros, according to the World Bank, while the Spanish economy was around 1.69 trillion euros. Twelve times larger.
Does Morocco really spend 10% of its GDP on Defence?
It is one of the figures most often circulated, but it does not fit with Sipri's time series. The institute itself puts Morocco's 2025 military spending at 3.54% of GDP. The 10% looks much more like another indicator: Defence's share of public expenditure, which Sipri calculates at 10.28% for 2025.
Something similar happens with the budget figures. Morocco's 2026 finance law authorised future spending commitments for the National Defence Administration of 157.170 billion dirhams, around 14.7 billion euros, a multi-year line that is often presented as if it were spending in a single year. What will actually be disbursed in 2026 in payment appropriations comes to 55.300 billion dirhams (5.157 billion euros).
Spain, meanwhile, hit 2% of GDP in 2025 and aims to consolidate that in 2026, although it remains the only ally to have refused to sign up to the 5% target for 2035.
Manpower: more troops south of the Strait
Here the balance tips the other way. Several sources converge on Morocco having between 195,000 and 200,000 active-duty personnel and some 150,000 reservists. In addition, unlike Spain, Morocco maintains compulsory military service, reintroduced in 2019. In troop numbers, Morocco's military strength comfortably exceeds Spain's.
This is where the oft-quoted 400,000 figure, which has gone viral in various media, should be treated with caution. The number comes from Global Firepower's profile updated on 21 January 2026, which also credits the African country with some 250,000 reservists, and, as of publication, no other independent record backs it up.
The Spanish Armed Forces have a staffing problem. On 1 January 2025 there were 116,739 military personnel in active service, below the legal minimum of 130,000 set by the Military Career Act, and the year ended with 832 fewer troops. The reserve is even weaker: at the start of 2024 there were 3,091 voluntary reservists.
Aviation: Eurofighter versus F-16 Viper
Spain flies more aircraft, but faces a longer-term question mark. FlightGlobal's World Air Forces 2026 directory credits it with 81 EF-18 Hornets and 67 Eurofighters, with another 45 on order. The first Halcón, a twin-seater, rolled out of the Getafe plant on 1 June, and the second batch will start to be delivered in 2030.
The problem is what comes next. Spain shelved the F-35 in August 2025 in order to buy European, and in June 2026 the FCAS, the fighter it was banking on, fell apart between France and Germany. Paris will now develop its own aircraft on its own.
Morocco is taking a different path. Washington approved in 2019 the sale of 25 F-16 Block 72s for some 3.380 billion euros, plus 23 kits to upgrade the F-16s it already operates.
And the F-35? There are signs of advanced talks, but the deal remains in the realm of the possible and would still need final approval from the US administration and Congress. Specialist media have spoken of 32 aircraft costing around 13.5 billion euros spread over 45 years, including maintenance, but there has been no official confirmation.
In helicopters, Rabat already has 12 of the 24 AH-64E Apaches it ordered and is expecting the rest in phases between 2026 and 2027. Spain will upgrade its 18 Tigers to the MKIII standard. Morocco has also completed delivery of the Israeli Barak MX system, with three batteries and 225 interceptor missiles with a range of up to 70 kilometres, according to Sipri's database.
Ground forces: where Rabat presses hardest
It is on land that Morocco's military strength comes closest to Spain's. Rabat operates the US M1A2 Abrams and, although opacity makes an exact count impossible, some 200 units are estimated to be in service and another 150 on order. Spain fields 220 Leopard 2E tanks and around 50 2A4s, and plans to upgrade them to the 2A8 standard.
The most striking asymmetry is in multiple rocket launchers. Global Firepower credits Morocco with 185 systems and Spain with none; the Army lost that capability when the Teruel system was withdrawn in 2011. Morocco, by contrast, combines Chinese systems with Israel's PULS, already in service, and is awaiting the US HIMARS, of which Washington has approved the sale of 18 launchers.
There is a paradox here. Spain's Silam programme was to be based precisely on PULS, but the contract was cancelled because of the embargo on Israeli military technology imposed by the government; on 30 December 2025 Escribano and Rheinmetall Expal presented the Defence Ministry with a national alternative. In the meantime, the Moroccan Army is already receiving 8x8 WhAP armoured vehicles assembled in the country.
At sea, the gap is vast
The Navy is Spain's big safety cushion. Its backbone consists of five Álvaro de Bazán-class F-100 frigates, whereas Rabat's flagship is a single FREMM frigate. On top of that Spain has the LHD Juan Carlos I, which serves as an aircraft carrier, and two Galicia-class amphibious assault ships.
Under water there is simply no comparison, as submarine capability is one of Morocco's historic shortfalls. The S-81 Isaac Peral has been in service since November 2023, and the S-82 Narciso Monturiol has been undergoing port and sea trials since the summer, with delivery scheduled for the last quarter of the year; it will be the first to be fitted from the outset with air-independent propulsion. On the surface, the F-111 Bonifaz frigate, first in the new series, will join the fleet in 2028.
The Washington factor in Morocco's military strength
What has changed in 2026 is the political backing behind the purchases. Morocco and the United States signed at the Pentagon a military cooperation roadmap for 2026-2036, and by February the Royal Armed Forces had already tested the Link-16 tactical communications system, until now reserved for NATO members.
The US Senate has gone a step further: a clause in its defence bill instructs the Pentagon to deliver within 180 days a ten-year plan to turn Morocco into its most capable military partner in Africa. The United States already accounts for around 60% of Morocco's arms imports.
Rabat also wants to manufacture at home. The government has authorised ten defence industrial projects worth around 231 million euros in investment, and a letter of intent envisages producing in the country a long-range autonomous strike system, the Irifi, with a declared range of around 2,000 kilometres.
Spain has other cards to play. Its defence industry places it among the few countries capable of designing and building its own conventional attack submarines, and it belongs to NATO, although the geographical scope set out in Article 6 of the Washington Treaty does not explicitly include Ceuta and Melilla.
What the rankings don't measure
In the 2026 Global Firepower index, Spain ranks 18th out of 145 and Morocco's military strength appears in 56th place. It is the most frequently cited ranking, but it does not publish an auditable methodology and acknowledges that it relies on the CIA World Factbook and unidentified sources.
The trend, in any case, is upward. Morocco's military strength was ranked 59th in the 2025 edition and 61st in 2024. Nor does the index keep pace with deliveries: it gives Spain zero tanker aircraft, even though the Air Force is taking delivery of its third A330 MRTT this year.
The real friction between the two countries has not, moreover, involved fighters or armoured vehicles. At the end of July, the arrival of migrants in Ceuta led to a mass crossing by sea and over the breakwater at the border, the most serious crisis between the two countries since 2021.
The next figure to be scrutinised in Madrid will arrive soon. Mohammed VI on Saturday chaired in Rabat the Council of Ministers that approved the general guidelines of the 2027 budget, and the Defence allocation will be known once the draft reaches Parliament.

articles.title: Europe’s Defence Spending Surge: Billions More, but Procurement Remains National - Pagenews.gr
articles.summary: Europe’s Defence Spending Surge: Billions More, but Procurement Remains National  Pagenews.gr
articles.full_text:
English Edition
Europe’s Defence Spending Surge: Billions More, but Procurement Remains National
Πηγή Φωτογραφίας: AP Photo//EU defence expenditure is projected to reach €454 billion in 2026, yet only 24% of equipment procurement in 2025 was collaborative — The challenge for SAFE and the competition over industry, contracts and national control.
Europe is rapidly increasing its defence budgets. The harder question remains: can governments translate higher spending into joint procurement and military capabilities that work effectively together?
Russia’s war against Ukraine and uncertainty over Washington’s future stance have accelerated European decisions. Governments are seeking to address shortages in ammunition, air defence, drones and infrastructure.
Financing, however, is only part of the equation. Different military requirements, procurement schedules and national industrial interests continue to shape purchasing decisions.
€418 Billion in 2025 — €454 Billion Projected for 2026
According to the European Defence Agency, spending by the EU’s 27 member states reached €418 billion in 2025, a 20% increase compared with 2024.
For 2026, expenditure is projected at €454 billion, equivalent to 2.4% of EU GDP.
Defence equipment procurement totalled €115 billion in 2025, with 24% involving collaborative purchases.
EDA Chief Executive André Denk stressed:
“EU Member States are making unprecedented investments in defence.”
The figures demonstrate both the scale of the increase and the scope for greater cooperation. Most equipment purchases are still organised outside collaborative arrangements.
Compatibility Starts Before the Order Is Placed
An armed force can acquire modern equipment and still struggle to support it during joint operations.
Differences in spare parts, maintenance, training and communications increase complexity. Cooperation therefore needs to begin when requirements are defined and continue throughout the equipment’s service life.
Joint procurement can support standardisation and economies of scale. It nevertheless requires agreement on what to buy, when it should arrive and how it will be maintained.
These decisions shape military capabilities for decades, helping explain why governments remain protective of national control.
The €800 Billion Headline Is Not a Single European Fund
The ReArm Europe / Readiness 2030 plan is associated with the potential mobilisation of approximately €800 billion.
That figure brings together different mechanisms. A large share reflects additional fiscal space that national governments can use for defence expenditure. Another component is SAFE, which provides up to €150 billion in loans.
The distinction matters politically. The European initiative facilitates financing and creates incentives for cooperation, while governments retain the central decisions over their budgets and purchases.
The Commission also seeks to strengthen production, innovation and military mobility so that additional resources address specific readiness gaps.
SAFE: Loans Designed to Encourage Joint Orders
Security Action for Europe provides up to €150 billion in long-term loans to member states.
The EU raises money on capital markets and lends it to participating countries, which remain responsible for repayment.
In principle, a joint procurement must involve at least two participating countries, although temporary exceptions allow national purchases.
Eligible areas include ammunition, missiles, air defence systems, drones, cyber capabilities, maritime capabilities and military mobility.
Rules on component origin and technological control also aim to strengthen Europe’s industrial base and security of supply.
The financial incentive brings partners to the negotiating table. Reaching a shared contract still requires political and operational agreement.
Fiscal Flexibility Leaves Costs With National Governments
The national escape clause permits temporary deviations from certain fiscal requirements to accommodate increased defence expenditure.
This flexibility is subject to conditions and limits, with debt sustainability remaining a central consideration.
For governments, it facilitates the planning of additional spending. Financing and servicing the resulting obligations nevertheless continue to affect national accounts.
Countries facing different borrowing costs and budget pressures consequently have unequal room to participate. Aligning the availability of funding is another challenge for joint orders.
The Industrial Politics Behind Defence Contracts
Every major defence purchase involves jobs, expertise, production facilities and export opportunities.
A joint European procurement can generate collective benefits, while the distribution of industrial work prompts negotiations among participants.
Governments must explain why they have chosen a particular supplier and how much economic value will return to their own country.
This competition can slow decisions. Addressing it requires early agreement on requirements, production and support so that negotiations produce workable contracts.
Manufacturers Need Predictable Orders
Expanding production capacity requires investment in facilities, equipment, workers and suppliers.
For businesses, political announcements signal intent. Binding orders and credible delivery schedules enable more concrete investment planning.
Combining demand from several countries can support larger production runs. It also requires stability in specifications and quantities so that manufacturers can respond.
Lessons From Ammunition Procurement
The European Defence Agency’s joint ammunition procurement initiative, launched in 2023, demonstrated how pressure from a shared need can accelerate cooperation.
It established a framework through which countries could coordinate purchases while retaining decisions over their requirements and commitments.
The broader challenge is extending that approach to programmes with longer timelines and greater technological complexity. In those cases, differences in planning and industrial interests carry greater weight.
What the Debate Means for Greece
For Greece, European cooperation raises questions about operational capability, financing and industrial participation.
Assessing a joint programme requires examination of lifetime costs, timely delivery, spare-parts availability and reliable support.
The potential involvement of Greek companies in production, maintenance, software and technical services is equally important.
These criteria can guide the assessment of cooperation proposals alongside the specific requirements of the Greek Armed Forces.
European Readiness Will Be Tested in Contracts
Higher expenditure creates opportunities. Its operational value depends on equipment choices, cooperation and industry’s ability to deliver.
Europe now has more financing tools. The next test is whether governments will align their requirements sufficiently to sign joint orders and secure dependable support.
That will determine how much of the new procurement surge translates into effective European defence readiness.
Source: pagenews.gr

articles.title: France Protests: Why Is France Perpetually Rioting? - Foreign Policy
articles.summary: France Protests: Why Is France Perpetually Rioting?  Foreign Policy
articles.full_text:
Protest and radicalization are the answer to an authoritarian, centralized state.
When I first started studying contemporary France as a graduate student in 2006, the country was still reeling from a convulsion of urban violence triggered by the deaths of two teenagers in an electrical substation as they were hiding from police. For several weeks in late 2005, the country had gone up in flames as angry young people protested against police violence, racism, social inequality, and the broken promises of France’s social contract.
Fast forward 20 years, and the images of France being broadcast to the world are the same. What began as a protest by high school students has escalated into a nationwide cry of exasperation, punctuated by looting, the ritual burning of public buildings, and a cascade of violence meted out by riot police armed with smoke grenades and tear gas.
When I first started studying contemporary France as a graduate student in 2006, the country was still reeling from a convulsion of urban violence triggered by the deaths of two teenagers in an electrical substation as they were hiding from police. For several weeks in late 2005, the country had gone up in flames as angry young people protested against police violence, racism, social inequality, and the broken promises of France’s social contract.
Fast forward 20 years, and the images of France being broadcast to the world are the same. What began as a protest by high school students has escalated into a nationwide cry of exasperation, punctuated by looting, the ritual burning of public buildings, and a cascade of violence meted out by riot police armed with smoke grenades and tear gas.
No less predictable has been the cascade of hot takes by commentators, politicians, shock jocks, and activists, all looking to capitalize on the spectacle of French people taking to the streets. For the most part, this has involved endless platitudes about the French—who are said to be especially revolutionary or pathological, depending on your view—or outright untruths about a supposed invasion of migrants destroying French and Western civilization.
For those of us who have worked on contemporary France for much of our careers, the rush to commentary is exhausting. But it does at least highlight one of the signature questions of our field: Why is it that modern France seems to be a land of protest? And no less importantly, why does anyone still care about what happens in a medium-sized European country that has long ceased to be a global power?
The answer to the first question—about the omnipresence of protest—does not have an easy answer, but the facts are beyond doubt. According to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, which monitors political violence and protests worldwide, there have been about 20 protests a day in France in recent years. These are often small and localized, but sometimes they are nationwide, with hundreds of thousands of people taking part.
Crucially, protesting is an activity for everyone in France. The idea that only young left-wing activists march in the streets is wildly inaccurate: Some of the biggest protest movements of the last 50 years have been led by the right, most famously the huge demonstrations against reforms to private schooling in 1984 and same-sex marriage in 2013.
For such a culture of protest to develop across the political spectrum, two basic elements are needed: the politicization of the fight against injustice and a belief in the power of the street. Both of these have been present in France for a long time.
The idea that opposition to any perceived injustice must be politicized—and that any such politicization can take the form of insurrectionary violence—has a long and distinguished pedigree in France. It was the French, after all, who first showed the world what ideology-driven revolutionary insurrection looked like. France also bequeathed to the world the perennial distinction between “right” and “left,” a divide that became the basic coordinates of parliamentary and extra-parliamentary politics worldwide. Time and again, from 1789 onward, the French have made protest more than the sum of its parts.
This politicization of discontent has not translated into stable institutions. France has had multiple republics and dictatorships since the French Revolution; compared with other Western countries, it has had relatively weak intermediary bodies. It is not a land of strong political parties or powerful trade unions. In fact, rates of union membership in France have long been much lower than elsewhere in Europe. Contrary to widely held perceptions of the French as perpetually “on strike,” the speed with which popular protest develops is an indication of the weakness of institutions that might channel discontent.
The presence of a strongly authoritarian, centralized state has not helped. For at least a century, if not more, the French state has been top-heavy and technocratic. Its grand plans for reconstruction after World War II, for instance, were elaborated by the central government with no real popular consultation, and the foundation of today’s constitutional settlement—the Fifth Republic—was explicitly anti-democratic in its elevation of presidential authority and the subservient role given to the French Parliament when it was devised in 1958.
All of which means that protest is one of the few ways in which French people can make themselves heard beyond the ballot box. Memories of earlier struggles are passed down through the generations as older activists tell their youthful comrades stories of their first protest, parents come out in support of their children, and teachers stand in solidarity with their students. As any good French protester knows, the symbols, language, and power of protest resonate across decades and even centuries.
And it sometimes works: Protesters do get their way, and reforms do get reversed. Every French government knows—and fears—the judgment of the street, which can be harsh and uncompromising.
This is one of the reasons that French governments frequently take preemptive action in the form of violent, sometimes murderous, repression. From the crushing of the Paris Commune in 1871 to today’s police violence, the French authorities often shoot first and ask questions later. Remarkably resistant to 21st-century de-escalation strategies, they still operate according to 19th-century ideas about the irrational mob, and they see everyone from schoolchildren to football fans as a potential threat.
Yet this only hardens the resolve of protesters. Some take to outright violence, joining petty criminals in the destruction of private and public property, while others record TikTok videos in front of riot police, lampooning a state that sees its citizens as a perpetual nuisance.
Of course, many contemporary protest movements go through a similar cycle. At the same time as the protests in France were taking place, hundreds of thousands of young Indians were launching their own movement to protest against another authoritarian state—and they met with an equally robust response.
So why do protests in France continue to capture the public imagination?
Some of this no doubt has to do with a tendency, especially in the Anglosphere, to imagine France as a volatile dystopia. Much of 19th-century British politics was built around a myth of stability that was positively contrasted with France’s revolutionary upheavals, and this characterization of France is still very much alive. More recently, the great conservative intellectual Roger Scruton attributed more or less his entire political outlook to his experiences in Paris during May 1968.
But there is something deeper than simply prejudice and national stereotypes. Despite its much-reduced global status, France has managed to maintain its status as the vanguard of European radical politics on both sides of the political spectrum. Protesters in Paris—like the teenager Elwan, whose eloquent paean to left-wing politics quickly went viral—appear to be more articulate than their peers elsewhere, and the intensity of their revolutionary symbolism gives them global appeal.
It is surely no coincidence that much of the protest imagery of the contemporary far left is French in origin. So is one of the biggest slogans of the global far right—the “Great Replacement” theory, which posits that a cabal of liberal elites seeks to replace the native population with migrants.
Although the French do not have a monopoly on protest—far from it—they have spent more time than anyone else packaging it for public consumption, and their ideas continue to shape political movements around the world. This alone makes it worth examining closely what happens on the streets of Paris, Lyon, and Marseille.
Emile Chabal is a professor of contemporary history at the University of Edinburgh and the author, most recently, of The Age of Hobsbawm: The Life of a Revolutionary Historian.

articles.full_text:
On Oct. 12, NATO's top military commander told the Warsaw Security Forum that the alliance does not seek war but is " ready to fight tonight" if attacked. U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich laid out what he called NATO's theory of victory: block an initial attack, blunt it if it persists and, if required, break the enemy's forces along with everything that sustains them. He added that conflict is neither imminent nor inevitable and that the surest way to keep the peace is to prepare for war while keeping lines open with Moscow. The setting mattered as much as the message. Western officials have blamed Russia for at least 211 sabotage and covert incidents since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, from an arson attack on an Estonian defense company to a failed drone plot against a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig airport. Danish military intelligence sees a low but growing risk of a limited Russian attack on a NATO state bordering Russia, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that Moscow may disguise strikes as accidents to sap the allies' will to respond.
A day later, at the same forum, Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski made Warsaw's request explicit: a permanent American base on Polish soil. He urged President Karol Nawrocki to use his rapport with Donald Trump to secure that presence and to make it clear in Washington that Russia is the aggressor and Ukraine cannot be pushed into surrender. In late September, at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York, Sikorski said the two governments were discussing a facility for up to 10,000 troops, a presence that would reassure Poland but not threaten Russia. The timing is striking. Washington has announced a drawdown of roughly 5,000 troops from Germany, drained Europe's stock of air defense interceptors for its war with Iran, and struck a diesel deal with Moscow ahead of the midterms. Poland is asking for more Americans, not fewer. The reason lies in its history.
For Poles, Russia is not an abstraction in a strategy paper. In September 1939, Britain and France declared war on Germany to honor their guarantee to Poland, then offered almost no practical help. Sixteen days after the Wehrmacht crossed from the north, south, and west, the Red Army invaded from the east under the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. In the spring of 1940, the NKVD shot roughly 22,000 Polish officers, policemen, and intellectuals at Katyn and other sites. After the war came a satellite regime, a secret police, and four decades without freedom. Poles drew two lessons from that history, and both still shape their strategy: Moscow fills every vacuum it finds, and a guarantee is worth exactly as much as the soldiers standing behind it.
When resistance finally broke through, it came from the shipyards. In August 1980, some 17,000 workers occupied the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk after the firing of crane operator Anna Walentynowicz. Their leader, Lech Wałęsa, was an electrician who had been sacked for union activism and who climbed the shipyard wall to join the strike. On Aug. 31, the regime signed the Gdańsk Agreement, and Solidarność became the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc. Within about a year, it counted close to ten million members, roughly a quarter of the country.
Moscow's answer was force. On Dec. 13, 1981, under Soviet pressure, Gen. Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law, outlawed the union and jailed its leaders, Wałęsa among them, for nearly a year. In 1984, the secret police murdered Solidarity's chaplain, Father Jerzy Popiełuszko. None of it worked. The Round Table talks of 1989 produced semi-free elections that Solidarity swept; Tadeusz Mazowiecki became the first non-communist prime minister in the Soviet bloc, and in December 1990 Wałęsa was elected president. It can be argued that the end of the Cold War started in Poland.
Memory explains why Poland wants American soldiers. Money explains why it can ask for them. When Poland joined the EU in 2004, its GDP per capita adjusted for purchasing power stood at 49 percent of the bloc's average. In 2025, Eurostat put it at 81 percent, the highest on record, level with Portugal and well ahead of Greece. The economy grew 3.6 percent last year. According to Poland's foreign ministry, cumulative growth between 2003 and 2025 reached almost 130 percent, against 34.5 percent for the EU as a whole, while unemployment fell from 19 percent to 3 percent. Poland is now the world's 20th-largest economy, with more than $1 trillion in annual output.
That wealth has turned into hard power faster than anywhere else in the alliance. Defense spending has risen from 2.2 percent of GDP in 2022 to 4.8 percent in the 2026 budget, about 200 billion zloty, and is one of the highest shares in NATO. According to NATO's own estimates, the United States spends about 3.2 percent and France about 2 percent. The bill is real. In September, Moody's downgraded Poland's credit rating and said it expects the deficit to stay near 7 percent of GDP through 2027, with public debt rising from 59.7 percent to 68.9 percent. Warsaw is betting that being unprepared would cost more.
This is the paradox of the transatlantic relationship in 2026. The broader American posture in Europe is contracting, and even the general who promised to fight tonight conceded that troop deployments are ultimately a political decision. In Poland, the line points the other way. Roughly 10,000 U.S. service members are already in the country, most of them on rotation, alongside the forward headquarters of the Army's V Corps in Poznań. Earlier this year, the Pentagon reversed a decision to cancel a 4,000-troop deployment. A permanent base, which Nawrocki has already baptized "Fort Trump," is now under negotiation.
Poland earned that exception by speaking this administration's language. It outspends every ally relative to the size of its economy, buys American hardware from Patriot batteries to Abrams tanks, and frames the U.S. presence as a good deal rather than a favor. Washington has called it a model ally and on burden sharing, the label is hard to dispute. Yet reading this as Poland choosing America over Europe would be a mistake. According to the foreign ministry, about 85 percent of foreign investment in Poland comes from other EU states, and Brussels has allowed Warsaw and fourteen other capitals to keep defense spending outside the bloc's fiscal rules. Poland is Atlanticist because it is European and European because it is Atlanticist. It wants an American tripwire and a European rearmament at once.
That combination makes Poland the EU's most credible safeguard, on three counts. The first is ideological. The European project rests on the promise that the continent will never again be carved up by empires, and Poland is the member state that knows from living memory what the absence of that promise looks like. Solidarity was the moment the Iron Curtain began to crack, and that memory gives Warsaw a clarity on Russia that Paris, Rome, and Berlin have often lacked. The second is economic: a country that has more than doubled its output in two decades and spends close to 5 percent of GDP on defense is no longer the junior partner of the 2004 enlargement but one of the Union's engines. The third concerns the future. With nearly 38 million people and one of the largest land armies on the continent under construction, Poland is the natural anchor for the frontline states that see Russia as it does: the Baltic republics, Romania and the other Bucharest Nine members, along with Finland.
That role has a precedent. In 1569, the Union of Lublin merged Poland and Lithuania into a Commonwealth. For two centuries it ranked among the largest states in Europe, and it held together because its members pooled what neither could defend alone. Today's frontline states face the same choice. Poland, the Baltic republics and their Nordic and Romanian partners share a reading of the Russian threat and defense budgets well above the European average. Coordinating procurement, air defense and the Suwałki Gap, the narrow strip between Belarus and Kaliningrad that forms the only land link between Poland and the Baltics, would turn them into a coherent eastern bloc inside the EU and NATO rather than a row of exposed borders. The Lublin Triangle, which Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine launched in 2020 and named for the 1569 union, shows Warsaw already thinks in these terms.
The Commonwealth also shows how such a bloc dies. It fell not for lack of soldiers but because the liberum veto let a single deputy paralyze every decision, giving Russia, Prussia and Austria the opening to partition it by 1795. An EU in which one government can stall sanctions or aid by veto should recognize the pattern. So should Poland, where the standoff between Tusk's government and Nawrocki's presidency over the Constitutional Tribunal is exactly the kind of fracture Moscow knows how to exploit. Warsaw must also lead as a first among equals, not an heir to the empire. Lithuanians remember the Commonwealth too, and not all of those memories are warm.
Grynkewich's message was that NATO will not be caught by surprise. Poland's is that it refuses to be caught alone again. The open question is not whether Poland is ready. It has spent, built, and lobbied as if its existence depended on it, because twice in the last century it did. The question is whether the rest of Europe treats the security of its eastern frontier as its own or as a problem to subcontract to Washington. In 1980, a shipyard electrician climbed a wall and helped bring down an empire. Whether Europe defends the country where that happened will show what European integration is worth. That is why Poland is Europe's stress test.

articles.title: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest - The Guardian
articles.summary: Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
As Republicans confront mounting political headwinds ahead of November’s midterm elections, Donald Trump is attempting to turn unrest in France into a cautionary tale for American voters, recasting the demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living as evidence of the dangers of immigration and the erosion of western civilization.
At a rally in Kansas on Monday evening, Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said.
Nationwide protests in France on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they erupted into looting and clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris.
“This is what’s happening to France – they want to happen to our country. It’s never happening here,” Trump declared, drawing loud cheers from the thousands-strong crowd in ruby-red Kansas where the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Earlier in the day, Trump repeated his baseless claim that migrants had “taken over” France, writing on Truth Social that the country’s leaders must “CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”
The rhetoric echoes France’s far-right National Rally, whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.
As Trump set off for the Kansas rally on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.
“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
The demonstrations in France began weeks ago, when high school students began marching against teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes in effect shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.
As the midterms loom, the unrest in France offers Trump a familiar political opportunity: the chance to transform a crisis on the other side of the Atlantic into an argument in favor of the hardline immigration policies that helped propel Trump’s return to the White House.
“If you import the third world, you become the third world,” the official White House X account posted earlier in the day.
JD Vance and array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument.
Sharing a video that showed the historic city hall in Limoges alight, Vice-President JD Vance argued that the rioting was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” he wrote on X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.
Mike Johnson, the House speaker, posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS – just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets across Europe, in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.
Neither has the president commented on protests in Albania, where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
But Republicans are eager to keep the attention on France, as they warn of threats to the national identity and seek to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.
The vice-president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.
“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” Vance concluded.

articles.title: European coil and green steel round-up: EU coil largely stable on slow apparent demand - EUROMETAL
articles.summary: European coil and green steel round-up: EU coil largely stable on slow apparent demand  EUROMETAL
articles.full_text:
Domestic steel coil prices in Europe remained largely unchanged in the week to 16 October, while distributors were focused on reducing inventory volumes and restocking was limited.
Bullish sentiment, however, prevails in the market, as buyers will have to rely more on domestic producers when they replenish their stocks due to the effects of regulations restricting access to imports – tariff-rate quotas (TRQs), which have been in place in the EU since July this year.
Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) duties have also made prices of imported coil comparable to those from European mills, and some buyers have switched to less risky local suppliers.
“The additional costs related to CBAM and potential tariffs if the quota is exceeded will be triple-digit, and I am not sure that the supply chain could digest such an additional burden from imports,” a German service center said.
Transactions for domestic hot-rolled coil (HRC) in Northwest Europe have been settled at EUR740-760/t ex-works. In Italy, the material has been available at EUR750/t delivered.
Some Northwest European steelmakers have been more active in the Italian and Spanish markets, taking market share previously occupied by overseas suppliers.
Domestic prices are expected to start rising after distributors’ stocks decrease. The severe competition among distributors as they focus on destocking by the year-end and generate cash flow prevents a price recovery at both mill level and further down the supply chain.
“The current situation in distribution is tough – there is a battle for volumes and severe competition to reduce stocks by the year-end. But there is an understanding that the next round of restocking will be done at higher prices,” an Italian distributor said.
European steelmakers have started negotiating long-term contracts with end consumers, notably the automotive industry. The mills seek an increase of EUR100/t for contracts covering the first half of 2027 compared with those for the second half of 2026. Market sources believe that the long-term agreements will be settled with an increase, but it is unlikely to reach the target of EUR100/t.
Some market participants also reported increases in extras for coil grades and sizes of around EUR50/t, particularly for downstream products, pushing for further increases in effective prices.
Imports have been limited, and prices offered on a DDP basis were largely uncompetitive. In addition, some origins, such as Turkey, are expected to exhaust their quota for the first quarter of next year.
HRC offers from Japan and South Korea have been heard at EUR640-650/t CIF Italy, while offers from Asian suppliers have been reported at EUR740-760/t DDP South European ports.
Green steel market
Demand for green steel coil in the spot market remains subdued, with deals mainly limited to small trial batches. Automotive and construction companies remain the main sources of demand for low-emissions steel.
Premiums for trial volumes have averaged around EUR150/t, while spot premiums for green hot-rolled coil (HRC) produced via the electric-arc furnace (EAF) route have been reported at around EUR100/t.
Most buyers remain focused on adjusting to new trade restrictions and securing sufficient supplies of conventional steel. Distributors continue to show limited appetite for low-CO2 material, typically purchasing it on a back-to-back basis against confirmed orders from end users.
