articles.title: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers - Tech Times
articles.summary: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry formally approved a revised production plan for TSMC's second fabrication plant in Kumamoto Prefecture on October 16, 2026, certifying what will become Japan's first facility capable of manufacturing 3-nanometer logic semiconductors. The approval is a genuine milestone — but the story behind the numbers is more technically revealing than the headline suggests. The original plan called for 48,000 wafers per month at 6nm and 12nm. The approved plan calls for 6,000 wafers per month at 3nm. That 87.5% capacity reduction is not a setback. It is a direct consequence of what 3nm manufacturing actually requires — and of who makes the equipment that enables it.
Japan's Node Upgrade — and the Volume Reckoning It Reveals
When TSMC first laid out plans for the Kumamoto second fab in February 2024, the blueprint called for producing 6nm and 12nm chips at a monthly capacity of 48,000 wafers, according to the JASM second fab announced in 2024 — a volume-first approach geared largely toward Japan's automotive and industrial sectors. Under the now-approved plan, the facility will produce 3nm chips at an initial monthly target of just 6,000 wafers, an 87.5% reduction in output volume compared to the prior design. METI approved the plan change on October 16.
The reduction is not a sign of diminished ambition. It reflects what happens when a facility moves from mature-node mass production into frontier-node manufacturing. At 3nm, a chip requires extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography — a technology that prints circuits with light at a wavelength of just 13.5 nanometers (0.000000053 inches), roughly one-fifteenth of a wavelength of visible light. EUV lithography is used on more than 20 critical layers at the 3nm node, compared to approximately 14 layers at 5nm. And only one company in the world is the sole manufacturer of EUV systems at commercial scale: ASML, the Dutch equipment maker.
TSMC and METI framed the revised plan explicitly around the requirements of 3nm manufacturing, which demands EUV equipment and carries a significantly heavier investment burden per wafer than the more mature nodes it replaces. METI's Director of the Information Industry Division, Tomonari Nanbu told reporters that "given the progress of AI transformation, 3nm cutting-edge logic semiconductors that power AI are indispensable," signaling that the ministry views the node upgrade as a strategic necessity.
TSMC has indicated that the 6,000-wafer figure represents only the first phase, and that production capacity will expand depending on the level of additional government support it receives.
Why EUV Scarcity — Not Strategy — Governs the Capacity Figure
Understanding why the Kumamoto II fab will start at 6,000 wafers per month instead of 48,000 requires understanding EUV tool availability.
ASML's EUV systems — the NXE series, which uses an optical system with a numerical aperture of 0.33 — are the workhorses of every advanced-node fab in the world. Each machine uses EUV plasma generation technology in which a pulsed laser fires at liquid tin droplets more than 50,000 times per second, producing photons at the 13.5nm wavelength that then pass through a reflective optical system to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers.
ASML produces roughly 50 to 60 EUV systems per year globally. Every major foundry — TSMC in Taiwan and Arizona, Samsung in South Korea, Intel in the United States, and now Rapidus in Hokkaido — competes for allocation from that limited production line. Each EUV tool costs in excess of $150 million; installing and qualifying a single tool at a new fab takes months. A 3nm production line requires multiple such tools running in concert.
The 6,000-wafer-per-month figure represents what EUV tool allocation and yield ramp-up can realistically support at a new Japanese site in the 2026–2028 installation window, given that TSMC is simultaneously prioritizing equipment for its Fab 21 Phase 2 in Arizona (targeting 3nm production in the second half of 2027) and its continued 3nm and 2nm expansion in Taiwan. There was earlier reporting of a 15,000-wafer monthly figure when Taiwan approved the 3nm investment in March 2026; the official METI-certified plan lists 6,000 wafers per month. METI's official documents do not explain the difference, but the discrepancy is consistent with a first-phase ceiling set by tool availability rather than demand.
METI is explicitly considering increasing its support, and METI included the subsidy request in its fiscal year 2027 preliminary budget — a process that will determine whether TSMC can raise the 6,000-wafer ceiling before mass production begins in December 2028.
Subsidy Structure and Investment Scale
METI designated the Kumamoto II plant as a subsidy recipient under Japan's semiconductor reindustrialization program. The government originally planned to provide ¥732 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in subsidies tied to the prior 6nm/12nm plan. With the revised blueprint now approved, that figure has been adjusted to ¥645.15 billion (approximately $4.1 billion), reflecting the reduced initial production volume, as documented in the METI official revised plan document.
The first Kumamoto fab's subsidy was also revised downward — from ¥476 billion to ¥409.5 billion (approximately $2.6 billion). Between the two plants, total committed public support fell from ¥1.208 trillion to ¥1.055 trillion (approximately $6.7 billion). However, METI is considering increasing the second fab's support as the full scale of the 3nm investment becomes clearer. TSMC's own statement confirmed total Kumamoto capital spending exceeds $23 billion (approximately ¥3.63 trillion) across both facilities.
Timeline: December 2028
Commercial production at the second Kumamoto fab is targeted for December 2028. Under METI's certification conditions, JASM commits to ten-year operation and to increasing production in the event of a domestic shortage — conditions attached to all Japanese government semiconductor subsidies.
The 2028 production date means Kumamoto's 3nm node will come online approximately one year after TSMC's 3nm capacity at its second Arizona fab, where Arizona 3nm production targets 2027 in the second half. That sequence reflects TSMC's global capital allocation priorities — Taiwan first, then Arizona under US CHIPS Act pressure, then Japan — rather than any deficiency in the Japanese site itself.
Kumamoto I Also Revised
METI's October 16 approval package extended to the existing Kumamoto I plant as well. Originally planned to run both 12–16nm and 22–28nm processes at a combined 55,000 wafers per month, the first fab plan revised to 22-28nm phases out all 12–16nm production, concentrating the facility on 22–28nm nodes (plus 40nm processes reserved for Japanese domestic customers) at 45,000 wafers per month across the subsidized facility footprint, and 50,000 wafers per month across the full plant.
JASM attributes this revision to how automotive and industrial customer demand has evolved — an implicit acknowledgment that sluggish electric vehicle adoption has moderated demand for the advanced-mature nodes originally planned for Kumamoto I. The move effectively repositions Kumamoto I as a stable-node workhorse for Sony image sensors, automotive chips, and industrial electronics, freeing the second facility to serve as the campus's leading-edge AI-oriented anchor.
The first fab has been operating since late 2024, when volume production began at 12–28nm. Its resilience was tested on July 28, 2026, when a magnitude 7.1 earthquake halted JASM Fab 1 operations for equipment inspections. The facility recorded a maximum seismic intensity of 5 at the fab site; analysts estimated a one-week shutdown could represent approximately $14 million in potential lost revenue, according to the TSMC Kumamoto earthquake impact estimate. The fab subsequently returned to normal operations.
What 3nm Means: Density, Power, and Why Artificial Intelligence Drives It
A 3nm chip is not merely a faster version of a 6nm chip. The performance gap is structural. TSMC's N3 process delivers 70% logic density over 5nm, plus a 15% performance improvement at the same transistor count, and a 30% reduction in power consumption compared to its 5nm node — the previous generation widely used in high-performance AI chips.
For AI workloads — the inference and training pipelines that power large language models, image generators, and autonomous systems — transistor density and power efficiency are the primary engineering constraints. More transistors per square millimeter means more compute per die; lower power per transistor means larger dies can be built without exceeding thermal limits. The combination makes 3nm the node at which AI accelerators cross from constrained to capable at the scale AI infrastructure requires.
TSMC CEO C.C. Wei met Prime Minister Takaichi in Tokyo in February 2026 to signal the shift in direction, citing "strong demand driven by AI" as the driving rationale for moving the second Kumamoto fab from 6nm to 3nm. Japan's PM Office stated that "there is a huge significance to have the world's most advanced semiconductor factory in Japan from the perspective of economic security."
By installing 3nm capacity in Japan, TSMC can serve GPU and AI accelerator customers who require geographically diversified supply chains, while also positioning the facility to capture Japanese hyperscaler and defense-adjacent demand. JASM's ownership structure — TSMC holds 86.5% of JASM with Sony Semiconductor Solutions at 6%, Denso at 5.5%, and Toyota at approximately 2% — ensures that Japan's largest technology, automotive, and electronics companies have direct investment stakes in the outcome.
Japan's Two-Track Advanced Semiconductor Strategy

articles.title: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried. - Latin Times
articles.summary: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried.  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Vietnam did not wait for Latin America to catch up.
While South American and Mexican exporters were still absorbing the ripple effects of their own hard-won market openings, Hanoi moved — completing a sweeping trade pact with Europe's second commercial bloc one day after the rest of the world's attention was focused elsewhere. The consequences for Latin American manufacturers are not theoretical; they are structural, and they are already in motion.
A 14-Year Deal With Immediate Market Consequences
Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association formally concluded a comprehensive free trade agreement on October 18, 2026, in Hanoi, after fourteen years and 21 rounds of negotiations that began in 2012 and were interrupted for years before resuming in 2025. The ceremony brought together Lê Mạnh Hùng, Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade, who signed the document on Hanoi's behalf, alongside the heads of government of Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, and Liechtenstein.
President and General Secretary Tô Lâm — Vietnam's top leader, holding the country's two most powerful positions simultaneously — attended the Hanoi ceremony in person, a signal that this was not a routine trade formality but a presidential-level strategic commitment.
The scope of the agreement is broad: it addresses trade in goods and services, rules of origin, intellectual property rights, government procurement, investment, sanitary measures, and sustainable development. But it is the tariff architecture that carries the most immediate competitive weight.
Under the deal, EFTA members immediately liberalize more than 90% of tariff lines, representing 99.5% of Vietnam's current exports to the bloc. Covered products include textiles and garments, footwear, seafood, computers and electronic components, and machinery and equipment. Vietnamese agricultural goods — including rice, honey, and fruit — also receive tariff reductions. Selected European products such as cheese and chocolate will gain duty-free access to the Vietnamese market, but only after a transition period of up to 16 years.
The EFTA Prize: A $630 Billion Market With Room to Grow
The commercial opportunity at stake is considerable. EFTA's annual import turnover runs to roughly $630 billion, and Vietnamese goods currently account for just 0.65% of that figure. Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam totaled €4.8 billion in 2025, with Vietnam running a €2.5 billion surplus — a gap that has widened sharply compared with a decade earlier.
For Colombian garment producers, Brazilian footwear exporters, and Mexican electronics assemblers competing for shelf space in Zurich or Oslo, the arithmetic is straightforward: their Vietnamese rivals now pay zero import duties, while Latin American goods still face standard EFTA tariff rates. The competitive floor has shifted, and there is no reversal mechanism built into the agreement.
The Mercosur Flank: Vietnam Takes the Competition South
The EFTA pact drew the headlines, but a simultaneous diplomatic push may ultimately prove more consequential for the region. Vietnam is negotiating directly with South America's largest economic bloc — not just for market access in Europe, but for preferential access to Mercosur's domestic markets themselves.
The first round of negotiations for the Vietnam–Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement concluded on August 28, 2026, after five days of technical sessions in Buenos Aires, with Argentina coordinating the bloc's side. The framing on both ends was optimistic: Argentine officials highlighted that bilateral trade had doubled over the past decade, growing from approximately $6.6 billion in 2015 to more than $12 billion in 2025, without any preferential framework in place.
If a preferential deal is reached, the implications for Brazilian and Argentine manufacturers extend beyond export competition in third markets. Vietnamese electronics — which generated nearly $165 billion in export revenue in 2025 — would gain improved access to the Brazilian and Argentine consumer market, the very domestic revenue base that regional producers depend on when global export conditions tighten.
Latin American Textiles and Electronics Face a Structural Squeeze
For the textile sector on both continents, the combined effect of Vietnam's European trade moves represents a pincer movement.
Brazil's textile and apparel industry counts 25,700 businesses employing approximately 1.3 million workers and generating $40.9 billion in annual revenue. The sector had cautiously welcomed the EU–Mercosur agreement — signed in Asunción on January 17, 2026 — as a pathway to expanded European market access. Industry associations representing Brazilian manufacturers (ABIT), their Argentine counterparts (FITA), and Europe's own textile lobby (EURATEX) issued a joint statement in February calling the deal "essential" for competitiveness on both sides of the Atlantic.
Vietnam's EFTA deal partially neutralizes that advantage. European buyers who might have shifted sourcing toward Mercosur suppliers under the new EU framework now have an equally competitive Vietnamese alternative — one that operates under zero tariffs across both EU and EFTA channels simultaneously.
The overlap in export categories is not coincidental. Vietnam's textile and garment industry posted $46 billion in exports in 2025 and has set a $50 billion target for 2026, driven by the same European and American buyers that Latin American producers compete for. Vietnam is already the world's second-largest garment exporter. The EFTA deal adds one more preferential lane to a network that already covers most of its major trading partners.
Hanoi's Export Pivot and the U.S. Tariff Pressure
The aggressive pace of trade diversification is not a coincidence of timing. Vietnam has been under sustained pressure to reduce its dependence on the U.S. market, which absorbs roughly 30% of Vietnam's total exports. That reliance became a structural liability after Washington imposed reciprocal tariffs that left Vietnamese textile and garment exports facing a 12.5% U.S. import duty — 2.5 percentage points above the 10% rate applied to some regional competitors — according to the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association.
Vietnam's response has been systematic: conclude the EFTA deal, push for EU-market access under the existing EU–Vietnam FTA (in force since 2020), and now open negotiations with Mercosur. Taken together, the strategy is to spread export volume across so many preferential lanes that no single market disruption — however large — can destabilize the country's export-driven growth model.
What Latin American Trade Ministries Must Reckon With Now
The Vietnam–Mercosur PTA remains at an early stage, and the EFTA deal must pass parliamentary ratification in each member country before entering full force. But direction matters as much as timeline in trade policy, and the direction here is unambiguous.
Vietnam is no longer simply an Asian competitor in Asian-facing supply chains. It is now an active rival in European markets — and a prospective entrant to South American domestic ones. For trade ministries from Bogotá to São Paulo, the question is no longer whether to respond; it is how fast a coordinated response can be assembled, and whether the advantages secured under the EU–Mercosur agreement will be enough to offset what Hanoi has just put in place.

articles.summary: France Vows Business Aid After Riots Damage 3,000 Shops  logos-pres.md
articles.full_text:
He noted that the final assessment of the damage has not yet been completed and announced support measures following a meeting of the inter-ministerial crisis unit. According to the Prime Minister, many business owners need urgent financial assistance: some of them have already purchased goods for the Christmas season. According to Boursorama, the government intends to prevent further job losses and provide businesses with the resources they need to recover.
The authorities have also instructed prefects to impose partial curfew restrictions in certain areas on the evening of 19 October to prevent further riots. These are local measures, but the government has not ruled out declaring a state of emergency if the situation so requires, reports Reuters.
In Paris, Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire described the damage to shops as unprecedented in scale. He said that further incidents of looting at retail outlets continued on Sunday and into the night. The city authorities intend to help business owners document the damage and claim insurance payouts.
Widespread unrest (clashes, arson and the looting of retail outlets) has swept through Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities across the country. According to the French authorities, around 2,400 people were arrested over the weekend. Meanwhile, President Emmanuel Macron refused to accept the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and instructed him to ensure a transparent investigation into errors in the planning of police operations and the gathering of intelligence.
Although the full extent of the damage to businesses has not yet been calculated, traders estimate the losses to be in the hundreds of millions of euros.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy formed a delegation to participate in negotiations with the European Investment Bank (EIB) regarding the conclusion of the Financial Agreement "Infrastructure of Ukraine’s Western Border".
According to order No. 121/2026-rp, the delegation is headed by the First Deputy Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine Serhiy Derkach.
The delegation also includes representatives from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Economy and Environment, Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport, as well as the State Agency for Restoration and Development of Infrastructure of Ukraine.
Specifically, the negotiation participants include Deputy Minister of Finance Olha Zykova, Deputy Head of the State Agency for Restoration and Development of Infrastructure Ivan Lukerya, Director of the European Union Department of the MFA Olha Bohonska, and other officials from relevant agencies.
The head of the delegation is authorized, with the consent of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to make changes to its composition.
Additionally, the President approved directives for the Ukrainian delegation regarding the conduct of negotiations. The document with the directives is marked "For official use only."
Separately, the order authorizes the Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine Mykola Kalashnyk to sign the Financial Agreement "Infrastructure of Ukraine’s Western Border" between Ukraine and the European Investment Bank.
At the same time, the order does not specify the amount of funding, specific infrastructure projects, or timelines for the implementation of the future agreement. The document provides for the formation of the delegation, approval of negotiation directives, and granting authority to sign the agreement, but does not confirm the fact of its conclusion.

articles.title: ECB rate decision Oct 29: what it means for crypto - CryptoTicker
articles.summary: ECB rate decision Oct 29: what it means for crypto  CryptoTicker
articles.full_text:
Which topics should we dive deeper into?
Select what genuinely interests you. Your picks feed directly into our editorial planning.
On Thursday, October 29, 2026, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank decides on euro area interest rates. The decision falls on the second day of the meeting, after which ECB President Christine Lagarde steps in front of the press. For your crypto portfolio this ECB rate decision matters for a reason that has little to do with the price on the day: the risk-free rate in euros now sits above the yield Ethereum staking delivers. Hold crypto and from this autumn you are no longer comparing against zero but against 2.5 percent.
This piece sets the date in context: where the rates stand today, why the central bank raised them at all, what a further step would mean for the price, for staking yields and for leveraged positions, and which points can be settled calmly in the ten days before the meeting. You will not find price forecasts for October 29 here. Anyone telling you how Bitcoin reacts to a decision nobody yet knows is guessing.
The Governing Council of the European Central Bank meets on October 28 and 29
The meeting calendar of the European Central Bank lists October 28 as day one of the monetary policy meeting in Frankfurt and October 29 as day two, followed by the press conference. That is the usual sequence: deliberation starts on Wednesday, the decisions and their reasoning come on Thursday. The decision is published in the early afternoon Central European Time, with the press conference following a good half hour later.
What matters for planning is the date after it. The next monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council is not in the calendar until December 16 and 17, 2026. Whatever is decided on October 29 therefore holds for around seven weeks. There is normally no interim decision; the central bank departs from that only in severe market disruption.
Deposit rate 2.5 percent: where the policy rates have stood since September 16
The ECB steers the money market through three rates. The most important is the deposit facility rate, the rate banks receive for overnight deposits with the Eurosystem. Since the decision of September 10, 2026, effective from September 16, the central bank's official rate table carries these values:
- Deposit facility: 2.50 percent. The rate that overnight money and short-term euro deposits take their bearings from.
- Main refinancing operations: 2.65 percent. The rate at which banks borrow weekly against collateral.
- Marginal lending facility: 2.90 percent. The overnight credit rate, the ceiling of the corridor.
The path to those levels explains why the subject counts right now. In June 2025 the deposit rate stood at 2.00 percent, the trough of the easing cycle. On June 17, 2026 the ECB lifted it to 2.25 percent, and on September 16 to 2.50 percent. Two increases in one year, after years of falling rates: since the summer of 2026 the euro area has been in a tightening cycle again, not in a phase of cuts.
Inflation at 3.8 percent: the reason for September's rate step
Price developments supply the reasoning. On October 16 Eurostat confirmed the annual euro area inflation rate for September 2026 at 3.8 percent, after 3.2 percent in August. That is the highest reading since September 2023 and sits well above the two percent target the central bank has set itself.
The rise comes almost entirely from one direction. Energy grew 18.9 percent more expensive within a year and so accounted for the bulk of the jump; without that rise in energy prices the rate would sit close to target. Core inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, by contrast, edged up only slightly to 2.5 percent. For Germany, Eurostat reports 3.3 percent.
That breakdown is decisive for assessing the date. A central bank can treat inflation driven mostly by energy prices differently from inflation that has settled into wages and services. Energy prices act with a lag and can fall back just as quickly. Whether the Governing Council adds another step on October 29 or waits hangs on precisely that question.
Fed on the 28th, ECB on October 29: two rate decisions in 24 hours
The week carries a peculiarity that often gets lost in European calendars. The US Federal Reserve meets on October 27 and 28 according to its own meeting calendar, the ECB on October 28 and 29. About a day lies between the two decisions.
For the crypto market the order carries weight. The Fed decides first, and the crypto market trades in US dollars: Bitcoin dominance stood at 60.2 percent on October 19, with total market capitalisation at around $2.77 trillion. If a marked move runs through the market on the evening of October 28, it very probably originates in Washington rather than Frankfurt. The ECB decision lands the following day on a market that has already priced the Fed in.
In practice that means anyone planning an order or a savings plan execution around those days should reckon with two jolts rather than one. And anyone seeing a large move on Thursday should check first whether it has anything to do with the ECB at all.
ECB rate decision and crypto: the three channels the policy rate works through
The link between monetary policy and cryptocurrencies runs through three channels, and none of them is magic.
The price of money
A higher policy rate makes credit more expensive. Companies and households have less free money, and some of it would otherwise have flowed into risky assets. Crypto sits well down that order of preference, behind equities and bonds. It shows up in inflows from companies and funds, not in a single day's price.
The alternative without price risk
As long as overnight money paid nothing, holding Bitcoin cost no forgone interest. At a deposit rate of 2.50 percent that changes. Any asset delivering no running income now competes with a rate you receive without price risk. The same applies to Bitcoin and to gold. Specialists call it opportunity cost.
The euro-dollar exchange rate
If euro area rates rise faster than US rates, the euro tends to firm against the dollar. Bitcoin is quoted in US dollars. A firmer euro lowers the euro price of a coin even when the dollar quote does not move. On October 19 Bitcoin stood at around $82,700 and around €73,700; Ethereum at about $2,428 and €2,164. Count in euros, then, and you never see exactly the same move as an observer watching the dollar quote.
Staking yield against the risk-free rate: 2.20 against 2.50 percent
This is where the rate decision gets concrete for crypto investors. The yield from Ethereum staking currently sits below the ECB deposit rate. DefiLlama data show an annual yield of around 2.20 percent for Lido, the largest liquid staking provider, on roughly $23.4 billion of deposited capital, and around 1.98 percent for Rocket Pool. Our own measurement of October 18 came to 2.21 percent and set it against the ECB rate of 2.50 percent; the assessment is in our analysis of the staking yield below the ECB rate.
The comparison limps in one place by design, and that belongs in the picture. A staking yield accrues in ether and carries the cryptocurrency's full price risk, plus smart contract risk and, at some providers, a withdrawal period. The central bank's deposit rate, by contrast, is interest on euro balances. Two yields in two different currencies with two different risks cannot be set cleanly against each other.
Something shifts nonetheless. Hold ether solely for the staking yield and above a certain rate level the argument weakens. If the ECB raises again on October 29, that gap widens. Which platform pays out how much and which lock-up periods apply is shown in our comparison of staking platforms; a look at the actual net yield after fees pays off before any renewal.
Bitcoin on rate days: leverage and liquidation in a thin order book
Dates with a fixed time create a pattern of their own. Ahead of publication many traders pull their orders out of the book, because nobody wants to stand on the wrong side of a surprise. The order book thins out, and in a thin book the same order size moves the price further than usual.
For leveraged positions that is the dangerous part. A liquidation is the forced closing of a position when the margin no longer suffices. It is triggered by the brief spike in between, not by the closing price. Trade with leverage and you check the distance between the current price and your own liquidation price before days like these, then decide deliberately whether that buffer is enough for a rate decision.
Without leverage the subject is calmer. A spot holding survives a swing of a few percent without consequence, as long as you do not have to sell.
Euro balances, stablecoins and overnight deposits between the dates
A rising deposit rate also affects the money sitting on an exchange between two purchases. Three routes are open, and they differ in one point that is easily overlooked.
A euro balance in a German overnight deposit account earns interest, and the level follows the central bank's deposit rate at some remove. A euro balance on a crypto exchange as a rule earns nothing; it sits there ready as a means of payment. Euro stablecoins, in turn, are tokenised euro claims; the interest income from the backing reserves accrues to the issuer, not to the holder.
At a deposit rate near zero that difference was immaterial. At 2.50 percent, a larger balance sitting unremunerated on a trading platform for months costs noticeable money. Leave longer gaps between purchases and you move the part you do not need back to the bank account. Which venues offer a euro deposit without the detour through a stablecoin is set out in our crypto exchange comparison.

articles.title: More than half of UK first-time buyers paying more for mortgage than they did for rent - The Guardian
articles.summary: More than half of UK first-time buyers paying more for mortgage than they did for rent  The GuardianHow much more expensive is it to buy a home than five years ago?  This is MoneyFirst-time buyers paying more on mortgage than they did on rent  The TimesMajority of former renters now pay more on mortgage than rent  LandlordZONEIt is now impossible to buy a home  The Independent
articles.full_text:
A majority of first-time UK buyers now pay more towards their monthly mortgage bills than they used to pay in rent, the estate agent Hamptons has found.
Last month 56% of first-time buyers said their monthly mortgage bills exceeded their previous rent, the highest proportion in at least a decade, according to Hamptons. They paid £39 more on average.
Mortgage rates have been climbing in the UK since the outbreak of war in the Middle East, as volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate deals.
Earlier this month the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years. On Monday morning the average rate stood at 5.99%, while the average rate for a two-year fixed mortgage was 5.96%, according to the financial analyst Moneyfacts.
Aneisha Beveridge, the head of research at Hamptons, said when interest rates were low “the financial case for tenants to buy as soon as they could was fairly straightforward”.
She added: “Higher mortgage rates have turned that equation on its head. The long-term benefits of home ownership – building equity, greater security and eventually owning a home outright – remain, but the immediate monthly saving that once rewarded tenants for making the leap has largely disappeared.”
First-time buyers in their 40s faced the biggest jump in their housing costs, with 67% taking on a mortgage that was more expensive than their rent, Hamptons found. On average, their monthly mortgage costs were 18% higher than their rent.
Meanwhile, the price of renting continues to climb. Newly agreed rents across Great Britain rose at by 2.7% on an annual basis in September, the fastest pace in almost two years.
The average rent now stands at £1,433 a month nationally, up from £1,396 in September last year.
In Greater London the average monthly rent on new lets stood at £2,357, up 1.5% compared with last year. It increased the most in the south of England, where the average rose by 3.7% to £1,419, Hamptons found.
Beveridge said: “So far this year, higher rents have mainly been felt by tenants moving home. But if growth continues to pick up, it is likely to feed through to more existing tenants in the coming months as the gap between new and existing rents widens.”
